By decomposing the realization process and incorporating SVM-based decoding at each stage, we demonstrate that it is possible to generate sentences directly from semantic inputs while preserving linguistic quality and morphological fidelity.

Part-of-speech (POS) tagging remains a core task in natural language processing, forming a foundational building block for downstream tasks such as syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling, and machine translation. Despite its simplicity, achieving robust accuracy across diverse and unseen domains remains a considerable challenge. Traditional approaches often rely on fully supervised learning using curated datasets, but such models frequently degrade in performance when applied to text from different genres, registers, or languages. This sensitivity to domain shifts is a major bottleneck for the deployment of POS taggers in real-world settings, where text data is often heterogeneous and noisy. The problem lies in the gap between the training data and the deployment data — a discrepancy that is exacerbated by the overfitting of linguistic patterns unique to the training domain. A promising direction for improving robustness involves training models under more general and adversarial conditions. Inspired by the principles of domain adaptation, adversarial learning, and robust optimization, recent work has sought to develop techniques that encourage models to perform well even under distributional shifts. These methods often involve explicitly modeling uncertainty in the data, incorporating auxiliary tasks that simulate out-of-domain conditions, or using data augmentation to expose the model to a wider range of linguistic variability. However, such strategies are often domain-specific or require access to large unannotated corpora, making them challenging to generalize and apply. In this work, we propose a novel and general method for training robust POS taggers by incorporating controlled and principled perturbations of the training distribution. We call this approach   Zipfian corruptions  , motivated by the observation that natural language vocabulary is heavily skewed, approximately following Zipf’s law. According to this law, the frequency distribution of words in a corpus is inverse-proportional to their rank, and it is well known that rare words are key contributors to performance variance in NLP models. Our hypothesis is that introducing corruptions that reflect this natural distributional structure — by mixing the source training data with data generated from a Zipfian distribution — can force the model to learn invariant linguistic structures that are less susceptible to domain shifts. Specifically, we define a new objective function for a structured perceptron-based POS tagger that minimizes the expected loss over a family of distributional shifts. The shift space is constrained to mixtures of the original data and randomly generated Zipfian corruptions. By optimizing for this averaged risk, the model implicitly learns representations that are more robust to unexpected input distributions.

Recent advancements in computational linguistics and neuroscience have emphasized the potential of using semantic representations derived from large-scale corpora to model human conceptual knowledge and relate them to neural activity. Mitchell et al. (2008) pioneered this approach by demonstrating that models of semantic similarity derived from co-occurrence statistics in text can predict brain activation patterns recorded during fMRI experiments, where participants were presented with concrete nouns associated with different concepts. This finding not only underscores the utility of corpus-based semantic models in capturing human conceptual knowledge, but also opens up the possibility of using these models as a powerful tool to validate and refine computational models of meaning. However, fMRI data collection is often costly, time-consuming, and imposes strong methodological constraints due to the physical limitations of the scanning environment. Electroencephalography (EEG), on the other hand, offers a viable alternative for exploring the neural correlates of semantic processing in more ecologically valid settings. EEG is a non-invasive technique with high temporal resolution that enables the recording of continuous brain activity in real time at relatively low cost and minimal subject burden. Importantly, previous studies have shown that EEG activation patterns contain enough information to differentiate between broad conceptual categories presented to human subjects—such as animate versus inanimate objects—based on electrical signals recorded over time. These findings suggest that EEG is not only sensitive to sensory and task-related stimuli but also to semantic properties of conceptual inputs, making it a promising modality for investigating how language and thought are reflected in brain activity. In this paper, we explore the relationship between conceptual stimuli and EEG activation, focusing on the extent to which corpus-based semantic models can predict EEG readouts. Specifically, we test whether the semantic representations derived from textual data—such as latent semantic analysis (LSA), word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec and BERT), and distributional thesauri—can account for observed variations in EEG responses to different semantic inputs. This task is not trivial, as it requires modeling complex, high-dimensional interactions between static text-derived representations and the dynamic, time-varying neural patterns recorded via EEG. To address these challenges, we design an experimental framework in which participants are presented with conceptual stimuli while their EEG signals are collected and compared against semantic representations of the same stimuli. By leveraging a diverse set of corpus-based semantic models, our work aims to assess their relative predictive power and shed light on their usefulness as tools for modeling the neural basis of semantic processing.

Multiword expressions (MWEs) play an essential role in natural language utterances. They are idiomatic expressions such as phrasal verbs, compound verbs, noun phrases, and idioms that, unlike their syntactically and semantically isomorphic constituents, cannot be decomposed and reconstructed using traditional syntactic rules in a straightforward manner. The idiosyncratic nature of MWEs makes them challenging for computational linguistic systems, especially for syntactic analyzers like parsers. The presence of MWEs in sentences introduces high syntactic ambiguity, which causes traditional parsing techniques to confront either substantial computational inefficiency or accuracy degradation, or both. Recent work has shown that recognizing MWEs during parsing—rather than post-parsing identification—can alleviate such problems by reducing parsing ambiguity and promoting more compact and linguistically accurate parse trees. However, most syntactic parsing frameworks still struggle to integrate MWE recognition directly in the parsing process. Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG) is a mildly context-sensitive formalism that has gained attention in natural language parsing due to its strong lexicalization and robustness in handling long-distance dependencies. Its flexibility in representing hierarchical structures makes it well-suited for integrating MWEs into the parsing process. MWEs in TAG are typically modeled using elementary trees that encode idiomatic structures as atomic units. These elementary trees can then be combined in a derivation just like any other syntactic units. However, the integration of MWEs into TAG parsing often introduces the issue of an expanded search space due to the combinatorial explosion arising from the large number of MWE-related elementary trees. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a heuristic strategy to promote MWE-oriented analyses during TAG parsing. Specifically, the proposed strategy leverages the empirical observation that for certain MWE types, such as compound verbs and phrasal idioms, the idiomatic interpretation is the most probable correct analysis in the absence of other contextual signals. By promoting MWE-oriented analyses as the first-priority parses in these contexts, the parser significantly reduces the number of processing steps required for expressing the sentence structure. The heuristic effectively shrinks the parsing search space for sentences containing true MWEs without compromising overall parsing performance. Crucially, the approach is robust in the presence of false positives—cases where the input sequence superficially resembles an MWE but is not one—by ensuring that alternative analyses remain accessible and are not prematurely pruned away. We evaluate the proposed method on a corpus containing sentences with MWEs, comparing it against a standard TAG parser with no MWE bias.

Lexical taxonomies play a central role in the representation of semantic knowledge, acting as hierarchical frameworks that reflect generalization and abstraction in language. These taxonomies are often grounded in is-a (hypernymic) relationships, where one concept categorizes another—such as  dog  being a kind of  mammal  or  singing  a kind of  activity . The construction of large-scale and disambiguated taxonomies remains a challenging task in computational linguistics. While traditional semantic taxonomies, such as WordNet, provide a rich lexical resource, their coverage is limited and semantically shallow when compared to the diversity of knowledge revealed in unlabeled corpora. Moreover, domain-specific lexical taxonomies often require careful manual curation, which is both costly and labor-intensive. As a result, numerous approaches have explored the automated acquisition of hypernym relations from text, particularly using statistical and distributional methods in word embeddings. Distantly supervised and distributional methods for hypernym discovery, however, tend to suffer from two key limitations: inaccuracy at the lexical sense level and poor sensitivity to domain-specific semantics. Traditional models often treat word senses naively, thereby conflating polysemous usages, and produce general-purpose taxonomies that struggle to adapt to specific domains. To address these issues, we propose a novel   supervised distributional framework for hypernym discovery   that is inherently   sense-aware   and   domain-sensitive  . Our approach combines the strengths of distributional semantics—whereby semantic regularities in embeddings capture abstract taxonomic relations—with   domain clustering   techniques, which help in identifying domain-specific patterns in language data. This dual strategy enables the model to focus on hypernym discovery within meaningful semantic subspaces. The learning component of our framework is trained under a   supervised setting  , using high-quality hypernymic relations annotated in a manually curated knowledge base such as BabelNet or Wikipedia taxonomies. In parallel,   weakly supervised hypernyms   are extracted using   Open Information Extraction (OIE)   systems from large unlabelled corpora. By integrating both sources of knowledge, we ensure that the model is reinforced with general distributional patterns while being calibrated to domain-specific lexical distinctions. This two-source architecture not only improves scalability but also enhances the model’s robustness across diverse settings. We evaluate various configurations of our model across   ten distinct domains   with varying lexical complexity and domain-specificity. Evaluation is performed both automatically, using standard precision and recall measures, and manually, relying on human judgements of hypernym validity and relevance. Our results demonstrate that the model achieves   significantly better performance   than state-of-the-art baselines, with superior accuracy in both disambiguated sense-level discovery and domain-specific adaptation.

The ability to infer relationships between events is a cornerstone of human comprehension of narrative, especially in domains such as film, literature, and news, where narratives are structured sequences of actions and events that unfold over time. In such domains, humans not only track the surface-level sequence of events, but also reason about the implicit expectations and causal dependencies between them. One such implicit relation is  contingency , where one event (the consequence) is expected to occur in response to another (the cause), typically under a narrative structure where the consequence is either a result or a purpose. For example, in the film scene “After setting the table, the man poured the wine,” the prior act of setting the table is likely to lead to the pouring of wine, making these two events contingent on one another. Modeling such contingent event pairs is not only a key task in discourse analysis and narrative understanding, but it is also essential in areas such as question answering, story generation, and commonsense reasoning. However, the challenge of modeling this relationship in natural language processing (NLP) remains largely unsolved, especially without the use of annotated corpora that specify discourse relations explicitly. Most previous work in NLP has tackled the problem of modeling event contingency through supervised learning, where systems are trained to identify discourse relations such as cause-effect or purpose on annotated datasets like the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) or the Mate Discourse Corpus. These datasets, while rich, are limited in scope and often fail to capture domain-specific or context-dependent patterns found in large volumes of real-world data. Moreover, they are labor-intensive to create, which limits their scalability to new genres or languages. As an alternative, a growing body of work has explored unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches that aim to induce contingent event pairs without manual annotation. Central to this effort is the hypothesis that reliable patterns of co-occurrence and sequential consistency can be used to infer contingency-like relationships between events. In this paper, we investigate the problem of unsupervised induction of contingent event pairs from film scenes. Building on prior work in discourse relation inference, causal reasoning, and narrative event modeling, we propose a method that combines corpus-based frequency analysis with external knowledge derived from web search data. Our approach is based on the intuition that events that are meaningfully related—either causally or with intent—often appear together in a variety of contexts and can be detected through their co-occurrence across different corpora or distributions.

Paraphrase detection is a central problem in natural language processing, with wide-ranging applications such as machine translation (Machado et al., 2005; Wisniewski and Callison-Burch, 2010; Callison-Burch et al., 2006), question-answering (Banko and Etzioni, 2008), document summarization (Barzilay et al., 1999; Potthoff and Harabagiu, 2000), and text-to-text generation (Rushing and McCallum, 2012). Sentential paraphrases—pairs of sentences that express the same meaning with different forms—have become particularly relevant for applications like abstractive rewriting, where generating new sentence forms is essential. However, acquiring large collections of high-quality sentential paraphrases remains a challenge. While monolingual parallel corpora (e.g., news articles covering the same event or movie reviews of the same film) are ideal sources for learning such paraphrases (Lin and Pantel, 2001; Szpektor et al., 2004; Ravichandran and Hovy, 2002), high-quality monolingual parallel corpora are often expensive to collect or limited in size and domain. This has led researchers to explore alternative sources of data, including bilingual (or comparable) corpora, which consist of texts in two languages that describe the same real-world events or scenarios. The intuition behind extracting paraphrases from bilingual corpora is straightforward: when a sentence in one language is translated into another, different language-specific syntactic and lexical structures are employed to convey the same meaning. For example, English passive voice might be rendered as active in French, or English transitive constructions might require verbal particles to express the same causal relationship in Japanese. These cross-lingual variations are direct manifestations of paraphrastic transformations. Prior work has demonstrated that phrasal paraphrases (i.e., sentence fragments expressing the same concept) can be effectively extracted from bitexts (Bannard and Callison-Burch, 2005; Zhang and Gildea, 2010), but the extent to which bitexts can support the acquisition of  syntactic  paraphrases at the sentence level remains an open question. This is in part because paraphrase extraction from bitexts must account for inter-sentential variations in structure that go beyond simple lexical substitutions, such as passivization, dative shift, or topicalization. In this paper, we propose extending the use of bilingual parallel corpora as a source for learning sentential paraphrases by modeling paraphrase as a sequence of syntactically motivated transformations. The key insight is that cross-lingual sentence translations often preserve core meaning but differ in syntactic structure in ways that directly correspond to paraphrase patterns in the source language. By lifting the paraphrase extraction process beyond the phrasal level, our method can learn a broader set of paraphrastic patterns, including complex syntactic transformations that are difficult to detect using monolingual corpora alone.

The exponential growth of scientific publications in the digital age has transformed scientific communication into a massive, complex ecosystem that challenges traditional methods of manual analysis and synthesis. This phenomenon has fueled the development of automated systems capable of extracting, organizing, and analyzing the content and rhetorical structure of scientific discourse. Scientific texts are not merely repositories of factual knowledge but are also argumentative artifacts that reflect the discursive strategies used to persuade, explain, justify, or refute claims. The increasing recognition of argumentation as a core feature of scientific writing has motivated researchers to explore how argumentative patterns are interwoven with rhetorical devices and structures present in scientific discourse. Understanding this relationship is crucial for improving information extraction, enabling more robust text summarization, and facilitating knowledge discovery from the vast corpus of scientific literature. Traditionally, the analysis of rhetorical aspects in scientific texts has focused on discourse categories such as Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Conclusion (IMRaD), as well as functional discourse annotations like citation contexts or discourse moves, such as asserting background knowledge, stating novelty, or presenting counter-arguments. However, these approaches often treat argumentation as separate from the rhetorical frameworks, limiting the accuracy and depth of discourse modeling. Recent theoretical advances in discourse studies and the availability of annotated scientific corpora have opened new opportunities to integrate argumentation with rhetorical analysis in a unified framework. Argumentation in this context refers to the construction and deployment of claims, premises, evidence, and reasoning strategies, all of which are embedded within the rhetorical structure of a scientific text. In this work, we explore the interplay between argumentative structures and rhetorical patterns in scientific publications by employing neural multi-task learning models. Specifically, we address the following research questions: (a) To what extent are rhetorical functions and argumentative components correlated in scientific writing? (b) How do joint models that couple argument extraction with rhetorical classification improve performance on each task? (c) Can the integration of these layers lead to more robust and interpretable discourse analysis models? To investigate these questions, we start with a well-established multi-annotated corpus of scientific texts labeled for discourse categories and citation contexts. We then augment this corpus with manual annotations of argumentative components, including claims, warrants, and evidence. This hybrid dataset allows us to propose a novel multi-task learning framework that jointly learns the tasks of argumentative role identification and rhetorical function classification. By leveraging the shared semantic and syntactic representations between the two layers, our models demonstrate improved performance across several rhetorical analysis tasks compared to baseline monolithic approaches.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automatic translation, leveraging deep learning architectures to learn end-to-end mappings between source and target languages. In contrast to traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems that rely on complex pipelines of individual components such as phrase extraction, alignment, and decoding, NMT relies on a single, differentiable model that has the potential to capture long-range dependencies and context in a more natural and integrated manner. A notable breakthrough in NMT has been the incorporation of attention mechanisms, introduced independently by Bahdanau et al. (2015) and Luong et al. (2015), which enabling the model to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the source sentence during decoding. This innovation has led to significant improvements in translation quality, particularly for long and complex sentences, where the fixed-length encoder representation used in earlier models proved insufficient for capturing all necessary information. Despite the success of attention mechanisms, the exploration of optimal architectures and strategies for leveraging them has been relatively limited. Most work has focused on the basic mechanism itself while paying little attention to the design of the attention function, the size and context of the source words considered, and the ways in which attention can be optimized in different translation settings. The lack of structured investigations into these possibilities has left a gap in understanding how different attention mechanisms impact translation performance and what trade-offs exist between model complexity, computational efficiency, and translation quality. This paper addresses this gap by systematically evaluating two classes of attention-based mechanisms:   global attention  , where the decoder pays attention to the full source sequence at each step, and   local attention  , where the model restricts the attention to a local window or subset of the source sentence at a time. These two approaches represent two extremes in terms of flexibility and computational demands, and their effectiveness on the widely used WMT English-German language pair is thoroughly examined. Both approaches are found to significantly outperform non-attentional NMT systems, even when the latter are augmented with common regularization techniques like dropout. More importantly, by combining models trained with different attention mechanisms, we present a novel ensemble approach that achieves a new state-of-the-art result on the WMT'15 English-to-German translation task. Our model attains 25.9 BLEU points, a 1.0 point improvement over previously reported results, demonstrating the potential of attention-based models to push the boundaries of machine translation performance.

The task of opinion mining—also known as sentiment analysis—has seen remarkable progress in recent years, largely due to improvements in natural language processing, the availability of annotated corpora, and more sophisticated machine learning models. Researchers and practitioners have achieved impressive performance in detecting polarity (positive, negative, neutral), intensity, and even more nuanced dimensions such as emotion, stance, and affective rating. However, these successes have often come at the cost of assuming a fairly static and stable definition of what constitutes an  opinion : a declarative statement expressed by a subject that reflects their judgment, attitude, or evaluation of an object. While this definition serves well under many conditions, it is relatively narrow and does not fully account for the pragmatic and contextual richness of opinion expression in human language. This opinion piece argues that current opinion detection frameworks are limited in their ability to detect, categorise, and represent important classes of opinion because they lack the capacity to engage with  metasubjectivity —the subjectivity of subjectivity itself. Metasubjectivity involves not only recognizing the expressed opinions in a text, but also acknowledging the interpretive frameworks, cultural assumptions, and even philosophical standpoints that shape what counts as an opinion for the various actors in a discourse. For example, what is considered an "opinion" in one cultural or communal context might be seen as a "fact" in another, depending on shared epistemic norms, and such distinctions are crucial to understanding the nature and implications of the positions being taken. One key element of metasubjectivity lies in the principles and criteria applied by someone using an opinion-mining system to define what counts as an opinion. These are not neutral or objective; they are shaped by the user’s own subjective views about knowledge, truth, and discourse, as well as by societal norms embedded in the system's design. Current systems tend to encode this subjectivity implicitly or not at all, often assuming that the definition of "opinion" is unproblematic and universal. Yet, for the aggregate reader—whether human or machine—such implicit assumptions can have significant consequences. They can introduce biases, limit generalisability, and misrepresent the diversity of ways in which humans talk about and construct opinions. This paper proposes a new direction for opinion mining research that squarely addresses the challenge of metasubjectivity. We define metasubjectivity in the context of opinion as the acknowledgment and explicit modeling of the interpretive and normative dimensions of opinion definition and detection.

The automated evaluation of machine translation (MT) outputs plays a pivotal role in the development and refinement of MT systems, guiding both algorithmic improvements and the assessment of human reference translations. Over the years, numerous metrics have been proposed, with systems like BLEU, NIST, and ROUGE dominating as traditional word overlap measures. However, these metrics often fail to capture lexical and semantic nuances inherent in human language. To address this limitation, the METEOR metric was introduced (Lavie and Agarwal, 2007), as it combines n-gram overlap with extensive lexical matchings and sentence-level alignments using measures of synonymy and paraphrase via the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) and WordNet. METEOR's ability to account for synonymy and morphological similarity makes it more aligned with human judgment compared to its counterparts, albeit with the caveat of its dependency on curated lexical resources. The rise of distributed word representations, such as those produced by Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), has opened new avenues for capturing semantic similarity in a data-driven and scalable fashion. These vector-based methods learn dense representations of words, capturing contextual, semantic, and even syntactic relationships from large corpora. In contrast to traditional lexical resources like WordNet or UMLS, which are manually curated and limited in coverage and language support, distributional models can adapt to evolving linguistic usage and extend to low-resource languages. This raises an important question: Can these learned representations serve as a viable—and perhaps more flexible—alternative to lexical resources in the context of MT evaluation? In this paper, we explore the feasibility of augmenting METEOR by replacing or complementing its reliance on existing lexical resources with vector-based word representations. The central research question is whether distributed representations can not only match but surpass the utility of gold-standard thesauri like WordNet in the context of MT evaluation. Our contributions include empirical comparison of two distinct semantic match strategies—(1) the traditional, resource-based synonymy processing within METEOR and (2) a novel approach that leverages cosine similarity between Word2Vec embeddings to quantify word-level similarity. We assess performance on the Metrics task of WMT 2014, which provides a challenging and nuanced evaluation framework for comparing MT metrics. Moreover, our work examines how these augmented versions of METEOR—which we make publicly available on our GitHub page—perform in terms of correlation with human judgments across multiple language pairs. We also study the potential for combining both types of resources through hybrid models to further improve evaluation accuracy.

Query segmentation is a critical first step in query understanding, enabling downstream tasks such as information retrieval, semantic parsing, and intent classification. Traditionally, query segmentation has been performed using rule-based approaches or machine learning models trained on ground-truth data. However, as with many annotation tasks, the increasing demand for richly annotated data has led researchers to consider crowdsourcing as a viable and scalable alternative. Crowdsourcing leverages the input of non-expert workers—often referred to as "Turkers"—to annotate large amounts of data quickly and at a lower cost. This approach has proven successful in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and even more complex tasks like coreference resolution. However, in the case of query segmentation, we argue that the underlying assumptions of applying crowdsourcing are not fully aligned with the nature of the task. In this work, we explore the effectiveness of crowdsourcing for query segmentation, a task that is similar in structure to text chunking but has unique characteristics due to the short, input-limited, and often fragmented nature of queries. We design a series of controlled experiments to evaluate how well crowdsourced workers can perform the task under various conditions. Our studies are informed by controlled annotations and focus on measuring inter-annotator agreement (IAA), which is a standard metric for assessing the consistency and reliability of annotations. Unlike traditional IAA metrics such as Cohen's Kappa, which treat all annotator disagreements equally, we propose a domain-specific IAA metric that accounts for the structural nature of segmentation annotations and the principles of acceptable decomposition. Through extensive analysis using this new IAA metric, we uncover a key insight: crowdsourced annotators exhibit a strong and consistent bias in their segmentation behavior. Unlike machine learning models trained on carefully curated datasets or even expert annotations, crowdsourced workers significantly favor the "middle path"—that is, they tend to divide a query into roughly equal segments, often resulting in just two parts. This tendency becomes even more pronounced in hierarchical or nested segmentation tasks, where annotators overwhelmingly prefer balanced binary trees over more nuanced or varied segmentation patterns. Our experiments indicate that this preference is not random but instead reflects a cognitive bias or heuristic used by non-expert annotators when confronted with a structurally ambiguous task. The implications of this finding are significant. First, it suggests that crowdsourcing, as currently practiced, may not be well-suited for query segmentation tasks that require fine-grained or task-specific decomposition strategies.

The task of constructing a comprehensive multilingual dictionary is of fundamental interest in both computational linguistics and machine translation. Dictionaries serve as essential resources for word sense disambiguation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and the development of translation systems, particularly in low-resource language settings (Bender & Ponvert, 2022). However, the production of high-quality multilingual lexical resources remains a formidable challenge due to resource constraints, data scarcity in under-represented languages, and the combinatorial explosion of possible language pairs. Traditional approaches typically rely on the manual curation of glosses and bilingual lexicons, which are time-consuming and not scalable to the thousands of languages spoken worldwide (Kourtitles, 2013). While web-scale bilingual dictionaries and machine-learned translation models have made substantial progress in bridging language barriers, they remain limited in either coverage, scope, or generalizability to under-resourced languages (Bohus et al., 2020; Tiedemann, 2022). In this paper, we take a step toward solving the coverage and scalability problem by presenting a novel approach that leverages probabilistic inference to recursively compose translation dictionaries. The idea centers around two core challenges: (1) how to integrate information from multiple translation sources—such as Wiktionary, parallel corpora, and existing bilingual dictionaries—to build a coherent multilingual dictionary, and (2) how to model and assign probabilities to inferred translations in a way that accounts for the reliability of different sources. The composition of translation lexicons naturally leads to a transitive inference problem: for example, if a word in language A translates to a word in language B, and the latter translates to a word in language C, what is the probability that the word in C is also a valid translation of the original word in A? Solving this transitive closure problem is essential for maximizing coverage and maintaining translation consistency across languages. Our solution treats this as a probabilistic inference problem, where each translation candidate is assigned a confidence score based on the abundance and consistency of evidence across multiple sources. We introduce a novel algorithm that combines translation probabilities derived from multiple lexical sources and iteratively infers the most likely translations using probabilistic reasoning. The algorithm is designed to explicitly model source reliability and to infer the transitive closure of translations, ensuring that inferred translations are not merely speculative but grounded in the coherence of the global map of known translations. We apply this approach to a large corpus of linguistic resources, including individual Wiktionaries, parallel corpora, and emerging crowdsourced lexicons, to construct  PANDICTIONARY , a massive, multilingual dictionary.

Emotions play a critical role in human language, often influencing word choice, utterance structure, and discourse flow. Understanding word-emotion associations is essential for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications, including sentiment analysis, emotion classification, and affective text generation. While pre-existing emotion lexicons provide valuable resources for mapping words to emotion categories, they often suffer from limited coverage and lack flexibility to adapt to new domains or evolving language use. On the other hand, semantic relatedness models derived from word embeddings or distributional semantic methods, while scalable, do not explicitly model the nuanced nature of emotional meaning and often fail to distinguish between emotions that are structurally but semantically divergent. This is particularly problematic in emotion classification, where mutual exclusivity among emotionsitunes that one word is typically associated with only a limited number of emotionally specific labels. Thus, the need arises for a method that can capture the nuanced structure of word-emotion associations in an unsupervised manner, while overcoming the constraints of both lexicons and generic semantic models. The core challenge in modeling word-emotion associations lies in the dynamic interplay between context and connotation. Emotion is not merely a function of a word's semantic class but also of its syntactic role, as well as the affective tenor of the surrounding context.Words are not only associated with emotion in isolation but also through complex patterns of co-occurrence with other emotional cues and expressions. These patterns often reflect shared affective themes or narrative positions that emerge collectively within text corpora. Capturing these patterns at scale, however, requires careful selection of co-occurring information that is not only relevant but also contributes to distinguishing between emotions. Establishing such selective co-occurrences can improve the precision of word-emotion association, especially in ambiguous or context-dependent cases where traditional approaches fall short. In this paper, we introduce  Selective Co-occurrences (SECO) , an unsupervised method for learning word-emotion associations from unannotated text. The key insight of SECO is that emotions exhibit mutual exclusivity in language use: words used in one emotional context rarely appear consistently in others. By leveraging this property, SECO identifies co-occurring words that are selectively aligned with specific emotion categories, thus enhancing the specificity of the associations inferred. The method operates solely with a minimal set of labeled seed words—one per emotion—which makes it broadly applicable across domains and languages.

The task of constructing semantic representations for words that capture their meanings in a structured and usable form is a central problem in natural language processing. Over the years, numerous approaches have been proposed for learning and representing word semantics, ranging from distributional statistics and co-occurrence-based methods to the more recent deep learning architectures such as word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013). These representations have been shown to be effective in capturing a wide range of linguistic information, including syntactic roles and semantic relationships. However, a key challenge remains in integrating multiple heterogeneous and complementary perspectives on word similarity and relatedness into a unified representational framework. While neural methods like word embeddings capture semantic similarity implicitly through distributional statistics, static resources such as thesauri and semantic similarity matrices provide direct, human-curated signals about relational aspects like synonymy and antonymy. Merging these perspectives is not straightforward due to the differing scales, vocabularies, and noise characteristics inherent in such sources. To address this challenge, we propose a novel modeling approach based on Bayesian probabilistic tensor factorization, which provides a principled and flexible framework for combining lexical similarity data from multiple sources into a coherent semantic representation. Our model leverages probabilistic factorization techniques to learn a global word vector space that can simultaneously incorporate heterogeneous similarity perspectives, each associated with its own linear transformation. This dual utility is key: the shared word vectors encode a canonical, unified semantic representation, while the per-perspective transformations adapt the vectors to recreate the original similarity patterns for each source. Importantly, the Bayesian formulation allows our model to implicitly regularize the learned components and extrapolate beyond the limited vocabulary of any particular source, a property especially valuable when integrating domain-specific or manually created semantic lexicons with general-purpose neural embeddings. A key advantage of our model is its ability to disentangle different types of semantic relationships, such as synonymy and antonymy, even when these are conflated in standard similarity measures. This is particularly relevant in tasks like semantic similarity estimation and antonym classification, where distinguishing between positive and negative relationships is critical. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework through extensive experiments, including an evaluation on the GRE antonym questions—a long-standing benchmark for assessing word-level semantic representations. The results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing recent approaches that combine multiple sources of semantic information. This work contributes a novel method for integrating complementary perspectives on word semantics and demonstrates its practical benefits in a high-stakes linguistic task.

The ability to accurately determine the taxonomic relationship between two terms is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP). Understanding whether a term like "Toyota" is an ancestor of "car" or whether "Toyota" and "Honda" are siblings in a taxonomic hierarchy plays a key role in a wide range of NLP applications, including question answering, summarization, and recognizing textual entailment. These tasks often require reasoning about the relationships between entities in text, and a robust ability to classify taxonomic relations supports improved modeling of semantic knowledge and facilitates accurate downstream inference. Traditionally, the construction of hierarchical term relationships has relied on the use of large precompiled stationary knowledge sources such as WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998) or Wikipedia infoboxes. These resources are valuable for numerous NLP tasks; however, they suffer from multiple well-documented shortcomings, including sparse coverage of domain-specific or rapidly evolving terms, inconsistency in structure, and susceptibility to errors and noise, often referred to as "noise contamination" or "garden-variety errors". Moreover, stationary knowledge sources are typically compiled offline and are not flexible enough to directly handle new terms or contextual variations, limiting their applicability in general-purpose NLP pipelines. In contrast to these limitations, we propose a dynamic and more flexible system for classifying taxonomic relations between terms in natural language text. Our method does not require prebuilt hierarchical structures but, instead, employs a machine learning-based approach that leverages existing resources to infer the most likely taxonomic relationship between pairs of terms. This approach allows for better adaptability and generalization to previously unseen pairs. Additionally, to enhance the accuracy of taxonomic relation classification, we introduce a global constraint optimization framework. This framework leverages an existing knowledge base to enforce relational consistency across predictions, incorporating domain-level constraints such as transitivity (e.g., if A is a subclass of B and B is a subclass of C, then A should be considered a subclass of C) and exclusivity (e.g., for sibling relations, no two terms can simultaneously be classified as subclasses of each other). These constraints are integrated into the overall inference mechanism, which revises individual predictions when they violate global relational properties, thereby reducing errors that might otherwise propagate due to individual model uncertainty. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that this constraint-driven approach significantly outperforms existing systems that rely solely on stationary knowledge sources such as WordNet or hand-curated ontologies. By combining machine learning with relational inference and leveraging domain-specific constraints, our system produces robust and accurate taxonomic classifications, even in the presence of ambiguous or noisy input.

The ability to understand historical contexts through event-centric narratives plays a pivotal role in fields ranging from journalism and education to digital humanities and personal learning. Traditionally, compiling such narratives—often termed event chronicles—requires extensive curation by humans, who sift through vast amounts of information to extract and organize events in chronological and thematically coherent sequences. However, the sheer volume and complexity of information today pose a major challenge to this manual curation, making the automation of such processes not only desirable but increasingly necessary. Automated event chronicle generation is a challenging task due to two key requirements: first, the detection and clustering of events from noisy or unstructured data over different time periods, and second, the selection and presentation of a topically coherent subset of events that form a meaningful sequence capturing the essence of a historical period. The goal is not simply to list chronological facts, but to create a focused, readable narrative that reflects the thematic relevance of the events in the context of a particular topic or domain, such as major political shifts, scientific milestones, or cultural movements across a given timeframe. Recent advances in natural language processing, temporal modeling, and machine learning have laid the groundwork for automating such narrative-centric tasks. However, existing systems primarily focus on short-term event extraction or news summarization and rarely address the task of generating a topically relevant chronicle that spans over a longer period. This paper introduces a novel method for automatically generating event chronicles that are both temporally and thematically aligned with historical or contemporary topics of interest. Given a reference chronicle—such as a set of manually curated events for a particular period—our system automatically constructs a new chronicle for a different period by detecting and selecting semantically and contextually related historical events. Our approach leverages two core components: (1) a   time-aware hierarchical Bayesian model   for event detection, which identifies and groups events based on their semantic similarity and temporal distribution across different document sources; and (2) a   learning-to-rank model   that selects the most salient and topically relevant events to form the final chronicle. The hierarchical Bayesian model allows the system to infer event clusters that are both semantically consistent and temporally relevant, while the learning-to-rank model ensures that only the most representative and important events with respect to a given topic are included in the final output.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the performance of image captioning systems, which aim to generate natural language descriptions of visual content. The encode-decoder framework has emerged as a dominant architecture for this task, typically combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) for encoding visual information and a recurrent neural network (RNN) or transformer for decoding and generating the textual description. Within this framework, attention mechanisms have played a pivotal role in enhancing the quality of generated captions. Specifically, visual attention mechanisms have been particularly effective in enhancing the detailedness of captions by allowing the model to focus on relevant regions of the image when generating words. On the other hand, semantic attention mechanisms have contributed to the comprehensiveness of captions by capturing high-level semantic topics and concepts that may not be directly visible but are still relevant to the image. However, existing methods tend to apply these two types of attention in isolation, which may limit the model's ability to seamlessly integrate both detailed visual observations and abstract semantic understanding when generating natural language descriptions. In this paper, we propose the Stepwise Image-Topic Merging Network (simNet), a novel architecture that effectively combines visual and semantic attention mechanisms by adaptively merging visual and topic information during the caption generation process. Inspired by the idea of stepwise reasoning, simNet enhances image captioning by dynamically integrating local visual features with global semantic topics in a stepwise manner. At each time step of the decoding phase, the decoder not only attends to relevant image regions but also considers the contextualized semantic topics derived through a topic modeling approach. This dual-attention mechanism allows the model to generate captions that are both rich in visual detail and broad in semantic coverage. The merging process is modulated by the context of the predicted caption so far, enabling the model to maintain logical coherence while ensuring that the most suitable visual and semantic features are selected at each generation step. We evaluate the proposed simNet on two widely used benchmark datasets for image captioning: COCO and Flickr30K. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both detailedness and comprehensiveness. Our model achieves higher scores on standard automatic evaluation metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR, indicating its superiority in generating high-quality, diverse, and meaningful captions. Furthermore, the human evaluation results also support our claims, showing that captions generated by simNet are preferred by human annotators in terms of fluency, relevance, and overall quality.

Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is a core task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with applications in diverse real-world systems such as question answering, paraphrasing, machine translation, and document clustering. Intuitively, STS measures how similar the meaning of two textual snippets is, often on a continuous scale between 0 and 5, depending on the evaluation framework. Given the central role of STS in facilitating downstream NLP applications, a wealth of STS systems have been developed, ranging from traditional sentence modeling techniques to state-of-the-art transformer-based architectures. These systems vary substantially in their computational complexity, speed, interpretability, and performance on different language domains. However, system designers and practitioners face a critical challenge: selecting the best STS system for a given task. To address this, intrinsic evaluation is frequently conducted, where the similarity scores produced by an STS system are compared to human judgments extracted from datasets such as those in the SemEval shared tasks. This comparison is often quantified using Pearson correlation, with the assumption that a higher correlation indicates better performance. While this method is widely adopted due to its simplicity and accessibility, it has important limitations that may lead to misleading conclusions regarding the system's suitability for specific tasks. In this paper, we investigate the validity of intrinsic STS evaluations based on Pearson correlation. We demonstrate that while Pearson correlation may provide a general indication of system performance on human-annotated datasets, it is often insufficient for capturing the nuances of task-specific performance. Through experiments on three representative STS-based tasks—sentence similarity for question answering, duplicate detection in e-commerce, and document clustering for information retrieval—we show that Pearson correlation can fail to identify the optimal STS system for each domain. This discrepancy arises because the relationship between textual similarity and task performance is not linear or uniform across tasks, and the design of a task can impose unique constraints on what constitutes “good” similarity. To address this problem, we propose a   task-oriented intrinsic evaluation framework   that evaluates STS systems with respect to the specific characteristics and objectives of the target application task. This framework encourages system designers to consider the statistical properties of the alignment between the system’s outputs and the required performance metrics in the target domain. By moving beyond the traditional use of Pearson correlation, we introduce a methodology for evaluating STS systems that is more aligned with the practical goals of delivering effective downstream applications.

Recent years have witnessed a surge in the development and deployment of large-scale unsupervised latent variable models (LVMs) for learning representations of text data. These models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), are widely used in tasks ranging from topic modeling to sequence tagging and have shown remarkable effectiveness in capturing the underlying structure and semantics of textual data. LVMs typically assume a generative process in which observed documents are generated from a set of latent variables that are inferred during model training. This inference and learning process is traditionally implemented using algorithms such as Gibbs sampling or variational inference. With the increasing scale of corpora and the complexity of modern LVMs, distributed training across computational clusters has become a standard practice to reduce training time and enable the use of larger models. However, despite the gains in parallelization, memory remains a persistent bottleneck. This is primarily due to the fact that the number of unique words in the vocabulary—often referred to as the "unique token count"—can be enormous, and storing and updating the parameters associated with these tokens during training consumes a significant portion of the memory available on each computational node. Moreover, in a distributed setting, each node is typically assigned a subset of the training corpus for processing. Existing approaches often distribute the corpus uniformly without considering the distribution of unique words across documents. As a result, some nodes end up handling rare and scattered tokens, while others manage dense subsets, leading to imbalanced memory consumption and suboptimal training performance. This imbalance not only limits the size and expressivity of models that can be trained but also reduces the scalability of the algorithm. In this paper, we address the memory bottleneck by proposing a novel and efficient approach to document partitioning during the distributed training of LVMs. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the memory footprint of the training process can be minimized by ensuring that each computational node processes a subset of the corpus that contains as few unique words as possible. By doing so, we effectively reduce the number of distinct tokens that are simultaneously active on any given machine, allowing it to operate within memory constraints while maintaining model accuracy. To achieve this objective, we develop a greedy document partitioning algorithm that greedily assigns documents to nodes in a way that balances the number of unique words per node and minimizes overall vocabulary cardinality.

This paper focuses on the problem of identifying verb-noun combinations (VNCs), which are central to understanding syntactic and semantic relations in both English and Spanish. VNCs are phrases where a verb and a noun interact in a fixed or semi-fixed pattern, often with a particular meaning that cannot be fully derived from the meanings of the individual components. These constructions are key elements in linguistic research and applications such as grammar checking, semantic parsing, and information extraction. A thorough understanding and accurate identification of these patterns are crucial for modeling language use, capturing idiomatic or conventionalized expressions, and enhancing the performance of natural language processing systems, especially in multilingual settings. Previous research on VNC identification mostly relies on distributional and corpus-driven methods, which are effective for detecting frequent patterns but often fall short in capturing the nuanced semantic and syntactic relationships specific to each language. English and Spanish, while both Indo-European languages, exhibit differing morphosyntactic characteristics that influence the structure and combination of verbs and nouns. For example, Spanish frequently uses prepositions or clitic pronouns to form combinations that, in English, might be expressed through phrasal verbs or more open syntactic structures. These differences suggest that a monolingual VNC identification strategy cannot be directly applied across languages and that language-specific properties must be taken into account to yield accurate results. To address these challenges, we propose a method for identifying VNCs that incorporates linguistic information, drawing on both lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic features. This approach first involves the manual annotation of a set of frequent VNCs in both English and Spanish. Each VNC is annotated along multiple linguistic dimensions, including the semantic class of the verb and noun, syntactic frame (e.g., transitive, intransitive, prepositional), and morphological features such as verb tense and verbal agreement. The annotated data is then used to inform a machine learning pipeline that combines this linguistic data with chunking and syntactic dependency information for VNC identification. The experimental results show that integrating linguistic features significantly improves VNC identification performance compared to a baseline system based solely on frequency and collocational statistics. The system achieves high precision in detecting VNC occurrences while successfully recovering a larger number of instances than the baseline. More importantly, the inclusion of linguistic data enables the model to generalize better to less frequent or structurally diverse VNCs that the baseline might fail to capture. This improvement is further validated by the observed inter-annotator agreement on the annotated data, which demonstrates the robustness and consistency of the linguistic features used.

Information status is a key aspect of discourse understanding, as it determines the mental state of a listener regarding a discourse entity and plays a crucial role in the flow of information in natural language communication. In traditional linguistic theory, the information status of a discourse entity—expressed typically as a mention—is generally categorized into three classes:  old  (information already available in the discourse context),  mediated  (information that was previously presented but has not been mentioned in the immediate context), and  new  (information introduced for the first time in the discourse). Correctly identifying the information status of a mention helps in understanding the coherence of narratives, the structure of referring expressions, and the cognitive load imposed on the listener. This task is particularly important in applications such as dialogue systems, summarization, and machine translation, where maintaining an accurate mental representation of the discourse structure is essential. Most existing approaches for information status classification are based on static features extracted from the linguistic structure of the document and extensive hand-crafted semantic features aimed at capturing the context of a mention in relation to the discourse. For instance, early work by Markert et al. (2012) and Hou et al. (2013) relies heavily on carefully curated linguistic rules and a large set of feature templates. While these methods have achieved promising results on datasets like the  ISNotes  corpus, they suffer from several limitations. First, they often require large, manually annotated feature sets, making the models difficult to adapt to new domains or languages. Second, these approaches are not inherently capable of capturing the sequential, context-dependent nature of discourse in an online or incremental manner—similar to how a human reads and processes a text one mention at a time. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an  incremental  approach to fine-grained information status classification using attention-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The key idea is to model the task in a way that mirrors human perception: as each mention is processed in sequential order, the model dynamically evaluates the mention in light of its preceding context, maintaining a continually updated contextual memory. Our attention mechanism enables the model to selectively focus on the most relevant parts of the discourse history when determining the information status of the current mention. Unlike traditional feature-based models that depend on external static features, the proposed approach learns contextual representations automatically through end-to-end training.

Natural language understanding often hinges on the ability to represent and reason about semantic relations between entities. A promising avenue for improving cross-lingual NLP tasks—such as machine translation, cross-lingual question answering, or semantic parsing—is the creation of a language-independent meaning representation. Such representations abstract away from linguistic surface forms and expose the underlying meaning of expressions and their inter-relationships. However, the induction of shared semantic structures across languages has been a long-standing challenge, largely due to differences in grammatical conventions, typology, and word usage. To date, most approaches to cross-lingual semantic representation learning rely on parallel corpora, which are not only expensive to collect but also scarce for low-resource language pairs. In this paper, we present an unsupervised method that enables the induction of semantic relations shared between languages without requiring parallel data. Our approach focuses on the co-occurrence of referring expressions in monolingual corpora and leverages the idea that semantically equivalent expressions, when used in similar contexts, are likely to denote the same kind of relationships. Specifically, we introduce a method to cluster English and French expressions into clusters of semantically equivalent semantic relations, based on the named-entity arguments they are used with. By analyzing the distributional patterns of these expressions and the contextual information provided by their named-entity arguments—such as people, locations, or organizations—we infer which expressions are likely to encode the same implicit meaning, and hence, the same relation. These clusters can then be used as language-independent semantic relations, with the mapping between expressions in different languages within the same cluster indicating equivalent relations. The proposed method is entirely unsupervised, requiring no labeled data or external alignment resources. To evaluate the effectiveness of our induced semantic relations, we test their utility on a cross-lingual question answering task and compare them with a baseline system that relies on machine translation. Our results show that the induced semantic relations perform significantly better than the machine translation-based baseline, even in the absence of any parallel training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the inferred semantic relations can be used to improve the accuracy of machine translation by incorporating them into a simple reranking strategy. This reranker considers how well the semantic relations between entities are preserved in the target language translation of the sentences. Our experiments with this reranking approach confirm that leveraging the induced semantic relations leads to improvements in translation quality, as measured by BLEU and human evaluation metrics.

Sequence labeling is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), encompassing applications such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition (NER), and text chunking. In these tasks, the goal is to assign labels to segments of text—often corresponding to words or subword units—based on their syntactic or semantic roles. Traditional approaches to sequence labeling often employ Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), which offer a probabilistic framework for modeling label dependencies through a Markov assumption over the sequence. However, conventional CRFs are inherently   word-level models  , as they process and predict labels for each word individually. This word-level formulation limits CRFs from explicitly considering the properties of segments, such as noun phrases, verb phrases, or named entities, which are the true semantic or syntactic units of interest in many NLP applications. The limitations of word-level modeling become particularly evident in scenarios where the predictive features or the relationships between adjacent labels depend on the internal structure of a segment. For example, in NER, the probability of assigning the label “PERSON” to the span “John Smith” depends not only on the features of individual words like “John” and “Smith” but also on the combination of both and their cooccurrence within a coherent segment. While early approaches attempted to incorporate such segment-level features using hand-crafted rules or feature templates, these methods were often labor-intensive and brittle, requiring significant domain expertise and manual effort. To address these challenges, the   Semi-Markov Conditional Random Field (Semi-CRF)   was introduced as an extension to the standard CRF. Unlike full-Markov CRFs, which model a sequence of word-level decisions, Semi-CRFs model   segment-level transitions   between labels. This allows for the direct incorporation of   segment features  , such as the length of a segment, the presence of specific word combinations, or syntactic consistency. However, extracting and encoding   high-quality segment-level features   for Semi-CRFs remains a non-trivial challenge. Traditional approaches rely on external symbolic systems (e.g., rules, hand-designed feature templates) or statistical methods for feature extraction, which often require domain-specific knowledge or extensive feature engineering. This paper presents   Gated Recursive Semi-CRFs (grSemi-CRFs)  , a novel architecture that integrates the strengths of   segment-level modeling   with   deep learning capabilities   for automatic feature extraction. Building on the principle of gated recursion, grSemi-CRFs utilize a   gated recursive convolutional neural network (RvNN)   to process segments and learn their internal representations in an end-to-end fashion.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have demonstrated the effectiveness of word embeddings in capturing semantic and syntactic relationships between words. Models such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) leverage large-scale corpora to learn high-dimensional vector representations of words that yield impressive performance across a range of tasks, including analogy solving, sentiment analysis, and question answering. These globally trained models encode general language patterns and relationships, making them versatile tools for a wide array of applications. One such application is query expansion in ad hoc information retrieval (AIR), a process by which a user query is augmented with semantically related terms to improve recall and relevance of search results. In the context of information retrieval, traditional query expansion techniques often rely on statistical measures, such as thesaurus-based substitutions, co-occurrence patterns, or latent semantic indexing, to augment the original query. However, these approaches tend to suffer from noise, sparsity in low-resource domains, or the inability to capture subtle, context-dependent relationships between terms. Word embeddings, with their ability to model relationships between terms, have presented a promising alternative for enriching queries in a data-driven manner. Despite this early optimism, we aim to investigate whether global embeddings—trained on massive corpora such as Wikipedia or web crawl data—are the most effective for query expansion, or whether embeddings that are trained on smaller, local corpora or task-specific data might yield better retrieval performance. In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of word embeddings in the specific task of query expansion for information retrieval. We focus on the comparison between global embeddings (trained on large, domain-agnostic corpora) and locally trained embeddings (trained on task-specific corpora, such as the collection about which retrieval is to be performed). Our findings indicate that local embeddings consistently outperform global embeddings in terms of precision and recall for the retrieval task. This is particularly true in domain-specific or specialized contexts, where the local embeddings are better at capturing the specific patterns, terminology, and relationships present in the corpus. We argue that the generalization properties of global embeddings, while useful in many tasks, may not necessarily translate to optimal performance in domain-restricted retrieval scenarios. By training embeddings on the corpus related to the task at hand, we are able to obtain representations that are more aligned with the target domain, thus yielding more relevant term expansions.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in question-answering (QA) tasks that involve understanding and reasoning over visual content, particularly in images and, to a lesser extent, videos. In the domain of vision-and-language tasks, systems are typically required to extract information from images, relate it to a linguistic input (such as a question), and then use reasoning over the extracted information to generate an accurate answer. However, despite the rapid progress on image-based QA, video-based QA remains a largely underexplored area. This is due, in large part, to the scarcity of high-quality, adequately annotated datasets that are both semantically rich and large enough to enable the training of robust deep learning models. Video question answering (VQA) presents unique challenges that go beyond those encountered in image-based QA. In addition to visual understanding and linguistic comprehension, systems must also reason about temporal dynamics, track entities and actions over time, and localize relevant events in both time and space within a video. These tasks are further complicated by the continuous, often context-dependent nature of narrative content, which is particularly evident in videos from popular media such as television shows. Here, characters, objects, and events are often embedded within complex social and situational contexts that require a strong understanding of both the narrative and the real-world knowledge to reason accurately. In this paper, we address these challenges with the introduction of TVQA, a large-scale video-based QA dataset, and present it as a benchmark for localized, compositional video question answering. TVQA is constructed from 6 popular American TV shows with a total of 460 hours of video content. The dataset contains 21,793 video clips, each with several annotated QA pairs—totaling over 152,545 QA pairs in overall. These questions are designed to be compositional, meaning they require the integration of different sources of information: they may ask for facts derived from subtitles that are necessary for understanding the dialogue, the recognition of visual concepts, and, crucially, the ability to localize relevant moments within the video. For example, a question might require understanding a character's intent through dialogue, identifying a specific object or activity in a visual frame, and pinpointing when that object or activity occurs within the video. Our dataset is not only large in scale but also carefully annotated to reflect complex reasoning tasks that occur in real-world visual contexts. The goal of TVQA is to encourage research that bridges the gap between traditional QA and video understanding in language and vision tasks.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in the use of unsupervised word representations in natural language processing (NLP). These representations—such as word embeddings, Brown clusters, and hierarchical log-bilinear (HLBL) models—encode semantic and syntactic properties of words into dense vector spaces, often leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled text. The allure of such methods lies in their potential to improve the performance of NLP tasks without the need for additional labeled data. A logical consequence is that integrating unsupervised word representations into existing supervised NLP models is a promising direction for semi-supervised learning, where feature augmentation from unlabeled corpora can guide model performance improvement. The premise is simple yet powerful: when word representations capture meaningful linguistic regularities, they can serve as features that assist supervised models in generalization, especially in domains where labeled data is scarce or noisy. For example, in named entity recognition (NER), the ability to differentiate between "Microsoft" (an organization) and "Apple" (a company or a fruit) relies not merely on surface features but on deeper contextual and semantic knowledge, which unsupervised representations can partially encode. Similarly, tasks such as chunking or part-of-speech tagging can benefit from the syntactic invariants captured by these models, particularly when the contextual patterns deviate from the distribution seen during training. In this paper, we explore the utility of three established methodologies for unsupervised word representations—Brown clusters, the word embeddings of Collobert and Weston (2008), and the HLBL embeddings of Mnih and Hinton (2009). Each of these represents a different approach: Brown clustering is based on statistical co-occurrence with a clustering-based hierarchical structure, Collobert and Weston’s method uses a neural network to learn context-sensitive embeddings, and HLBL builds a hierarchical probabilistic model over the word vocabulary. We evaluate the ability of these representations to improve accuracy when used as feature components in two well-established NLP tasks: NER and chunking. For each task, we use nearly state-of-the-art supervised baselines and demonstrate that the inclusion of these word representations consistently enhances classification performance. Moreover, we find that performance gains can be amplified by combining different word representations. The diversity of representation space—whether from different algorithmic architectures or different underlying assumptions—offers complementary views of language, and learning systems can benefit from such diversity. This insight underscores the generality of our method: by providing a modular and flexible approach, our system encourages researchers and practitioners to incorporate multiple sources of word-level knowledge into their supervised models.

The identification of metaphor is a central problem in computational linguistics, as metaphors are pervasive in language and often essential for comprehension. Metaphors, beyond their stylistic function, convey complex meanings by mapping abstract or abstractly experienced concepts onto more concrete domains. While traditional computational approaches have primarily focused on domain adaptation, lexicon-based matching, or rule-based systems to identify metaphorical expressions, they often rely on extensive annotated resources or linguistic expertise that is costly and difficult to generalize across domains or genres. These methods, although useful in controlled settings, tend to perform poorly on unrestricted and diverse texts, where the flexibility and novelty of metaphorical expressions demand a more data-driven and adaptive approach. In this paper, we propose a novel metaphor identification system that learns to detect metaphors in unrestricted text without depending on hand-crafted linguistic features or rich annotated training data beyond a small initial seed set of metaphorical expressions. Our approach leverages the idea that metaphorical language often involves the use of conventional words in unconventional contexts—particularly when verbs and nouns frequently appear in unexpected combinations across domains. By clustering verbs and nouns, we are able to model the typical usage patterns of lexical items and thereby detect when an expression deviates from expected norms, which is indicative of metaphorical usage. Crucially, our system operates purely in an unsupervised or semi-supervised manner. Starting from a manually annotated seed set, the system bootstraps itself by identifying other metaphorical expressions with similar syntactic patterns across a large unannotated corpus. This bootstrapping process is guided by the clustering of verbs and nouns into prototypical distributional contexts. These clusters help us determine which combinations of a verb and its surrounding words are semantically typical and which are atypical, and thus more likely to be metaphorical. To evaluate the performance of our method, we tested our system on a gold standard metaphor dataset and found that it achieves a precision of 0.79. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first system to employ fully unsupervised methods—based on verb and noun clustering—for metaphor identification. Our approach not only circumvents the limitations of knowledge-intensive methods but also provides a scalable and domain-agnostic solution for capturing the essence of metaphorical usage. The success of our method opens the door to a new class of metaphor identification approaches that can operate in real-world, diverse, and evolving language environments with minimal human intervention.

The digital preservation and analysis of historical printed books represent an important frontier in both computational linguistics and the humanities. As such works become increasingly accessible in the form of scanned page images and OCR-derived text, there is a growing need for robust systems that can automatically process and interpret their internal structure. This brings us to the problem of  book structure labeling , a task that, despite its fundamental importance, has received little formal attention in the NLP literature. In this work, we investigate this task in depth, formally defining it as the joint problem of   segmentation   (i.e., identifying the boundaries of structural components) and   labeling   (i.e., assigning each segment a predefined page-level structural category, such as TABLE OF CONTENTS, CHAPTER, INDEX, and so on). The structure of printed books is inherently hierarchical and varies significantly across publishers, genres, and time periods, even within the same historical era. This presents a particular challenge for automated systems, which must identify structural elements with minimal a priori knowledge about likely positions or lexical content. For instance, the distinction between a chapter, an appendix, or a preface is not always lexical or semantic—structural cues such as pagination, font styles, and typographic patterns can be equally, if not more, informative.
