To address these complexities, we recognize the need for a machine learning approach that can integrate a wide range of features, including lexical content, formatting heuristics, and positional context. To support this research, we present a comprehensive and carefully curated   page-level annotation dataset   composed of 1,055 printed books spanning approximately 250 years (1750–1922), selected to ensure a representative sample of historical publishing practices and linguistic and typographic diversity. The total dataset includes   294,816 pages  , each annotated with gold-standard structural labels. This resource is the first of its kind and is intended to serve as both a benchmark and a foundation for future work in book structure interpretation. We evaluate several contemporary machine learning models for this task, including classical sequence models and more recent deep learning approaches. Our best-performing system is a   bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)   model enriched with a broad array of hand-crafted features, achieving an overall   classification accuracy of 95.8%   and a   class-balanced macro F1-score of 71.4%  , even in the presence of challenging and ambiguous classes. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the feasibility of accurate, automated structural labeling of historical texts and highlight the importance of rich multimodal features in achieving this goal.

Parsing a sentence accurately is a foundational task in computational linguistics, with wide-ranging applications in machine translation, question answering, and semantic interpretation. Traditional parsing methodologies, including probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) and data-driven systems like dependency parsers, have made significant strides in achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, these approaches often face trade-offs between model complexity, the richness of syntactic representation, and the ability to generalize over unseen or structurally complex sentences. An alternative approach that has gained attention for its modeling flexibility and adaptability is Data-Oriented Parsing (DOP). DOP leverages syntactic fragments from a treebank to build a probabilistic grammar, enabling the parser to imitate linguistic patterns observed in real-world data rather than being bound by a rigid, hand-written grammar. Despite its generative power, conventional DOP models suffer from scalability and overfitting issues due to the exponential growth of syntactic fragments in the grammar. To address these limitations, we propose a refined variant of DOP, which we call   Double-DOP  . Our approach is built on the core idea of using a compact yet representative set of syntactic fragments derived from a treebank. Specifically, we consider only those tree fragments that occur at least twice in the training corpus. This constraint ensures that the grammar is composed of linguistically robust patterns, rather than rare or spurious syntactic units. By reducing the size of the grammar, our model gains improved efficiency without sacrificing coverage or parsing accuracy. What sets   Double-DOP   apart is its ability to seamlessly integrate principles from standard PCFG parsing within a data-driven framework. We introduce a   transform-backtransform   parsing strategy that allows the parser to operate using classical PCFG technology while leveraging the rich hierarchical structure of DOP fragments. This hybrid approach not only ensures parsing accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art models—according to standard Parseval metrics—but also maintains the interpretability and theoretical clarity of PCFGs. In addition, the transformation step allows the parser to handle larger syntactic structures explicitly, which can be particularly beneficial for languages with complex or recursive syntax. The core strength of   Double-DOP   lies in its balance between empirical richness and formal simplicity. By selecting and reusing representative fragments, our model captures the diversity of syntactic variation while retaining the psychological and computational plausibility of a symbolic grammar. Our best-performing model achieves parsing accuracy that rivals or exceeds many well-known parsers, while offering a more transparent and human-interpretable parsing process.

Text classification is a foundational task in natural language processing (NLP), with wide-ranging applications in areas such as sentiment analysis, document categorization, and intent recognition. Traditionally, supervised learning algorithms for text classification rely on fully annotated datasets, where each instance is labeled according to a predefined set of categories. While this approach yields strong performance in individual domains, it suffers from the limitation of requiring extensive labeled data for every new domain of application. This is a significant barrier in real-world scenarios involving multiple domains with varying label sets, especially when annotations are scarce, expensive, or inconsistent across domains. Recent advances in transfer learning have offered a promising solution by enabling model adaptation from a source domain to a target domain using shared knowledge. However, most existing cross-domain transfer learning methods make strong assumptions that the source and target label sets are either fully aligned or partially overlapping. These assumptions do not hold in practical applications, where domains can have completely different label semantics and counts, making prior approaches inadequate for such diverse settings. This paper addresses the challenge of cross-domain text classification in scenarios involving   multiple source domains   and   disparate label sets  , where the target domain may have neither directly shared labels nor examples with any of the source domains. This is a particularly challenging and under-explored problem, as it deviates from the more common assumption of label alignment or overlap. For instance, consider a news categorization system adapted for healthcare sentiment analysis, or a product review classifier repurposed for support request classification. In such cases, label semantics and granularity differ significantly, requiring adaptation techniques capable of capturing abstract, transferable patterns in the data. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel transfer learning framework that identifies and extracts knowledge from multiple source domains, even when their label sets differ significantly from the target domain. The key idea is to identify and select informative   labeled instances   across these disparate domains using criteria that prioritize semantic similarity and document representation generality. These instances are then aggregated to form an   auxiliary training set  , which serves as a pseudo-annotation reservoir for the target domain. Our method leverages both domain-invariant feature representations and minimal statistical modeling to bridge the domain and label gaps. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets, including social media and 20 Newsgroups, which represent diverse and realistic domain configurations with varying label structures.

Coreference resolution (CR) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to identify expressions in a text that refer to the same real-world entity. Its applications range from information extraction to document summarization and machine translation. A core challenge in CR systems lies in the computational modeling of anaphoric relationships — particularly those involving pronouns — which often require syntactic, semantic, and discourse-level analysis. While extensive research has been conducted on monolingual CR systems, especially for resource-rich languages such as English, relatively little attention has been devoted to cross-lingual CR. This paper presents the first machine learning-based attempt at addressing the problem of CR in the context of bilingual corpora, specifically  bitexts , where the goal is to disambiguate the referents of English pronouns by leveraging linguistic information from a parallel text in Czech. One of the key motivations for cross-lingual CR is the asymmetry of linguistic resources across languages. English, for example, benefits from large annotated corpora and well-established CR systems, in contrast to many other languages where such resources are scarce or non-existent. A bitext, which includes a source language (e.g., English) and a target language (e.g., Czech) aligned sentence by sentence, offers a structured way to transfer such rich linguistic knowledge. The cross-lingual setting is also unique from purely monolingual or parallel-to-mono projection-based systems, as it does not require explicit annotations in the target language and can take advantage of complementary cues present in the aligned sentences. This work specifically targets the resolution of English pronouns by enriching the feature vector of a standard monolingual English CR system with features derived from the Czech side of the bitext. These features include aligned word classes, lemmas, and discourse syntactic structures, which are adapted through a key component of our pipeline: a supervised pronoun aligner. This aligner surpasses the widely used GIZA++ baseline in both intrinsic evaluation (pronoun alignment accuracy) and in downstream CR performance. Our aligner generates high-quality cross-lingual links between pronouns and their potential antecedents, enabling the transfer of accurate context from the Czech side into the English CR model. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce a machine learning framework for cross-lingual CR that is agnostic to the monolingual CR system it augments. Second, we develop a novel pronoun aligner specifically tailored for monolingual pronouns in bitexts, demonstrating significant improvements in alignment performance compared to existing baselines.

Answer selection is a critical task in community question answering (CQA), where the goal is to identify the most suitable answer(s) to a given question from a pool of candidate responses. This task is fundamental to the success of CQA systems, which have gained widespread traction as a valuable information-seeking resource on the web. In platforms such as Stack Overflow, Quora, and Zhihu, users submit questions and receive answers from peers, making accurate answer selection essential for improving information retrieval and user experience. In a typical CQA setting, each question is typically presented in two components: a   subject  , which acts as a concise summary of the user's intent, and a   body  , which expands on the subject with additional context, examples, and detail. These two parts are inherently complementary, with the subject providing high-level intent and the body providing depth and nuance. However, most existing methods for answer selection in CQA have traditionally treated the question subject and body as interchangeable or concatenated elements, often using them indistinguishably in model training and inference. This approach, while convenient, overlooks the nuanced relationship between the two parts and the importance of the subject in capturing the user’s primary intent. This is particularly problematic in the context of short or ambiguous subjects, where the body is essential for disambiguation and context enrichment. Moreover, it may confuse models when the body introduces tangential or misleading information that is irrelevant to the core question, thereby degrading performance in answer selection. In this paper, we propose   Question Condensing Networks (QCN)  , a novel model architecture designed to systematically exploit the structural duality of questions in CQA. At the core of QCN lies the premise that the   subject is the primary component   of the question representation, while the   body complements it   by providing context about its intent. Our model first independently encodes the question subject and body using deep contextual representations. It then learns to integrate the body information into the subject-based representation by considering both   similarity   (how much the body elaborates on the subject) and   disparity   (how much the body adds new or divergent information). This dual perspective allows QCN to focus on the critical intent conveyed in the question while being mindful of contextual nuances provided by the body. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we conduct experiments on two widely used community question answering datasets: the Microsoft Research (MSR) Community Answers dataset and the Quora Duplicate Questions dataset (adapted for answer selection).

Recent advancements in machine translation (MT) have emphasized the importance of objective functions that define how translation quality is measured and optimized. Traditionally, MT systems are trained or tuned to optimize a single metric, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) or TER (Liu et al., 2006), which measure different aspects of fluency, adequacy, or alignment between the generated translation and a reference. A single objective metric tends to emphasize a specific facet of translation quality but may overlook other important characteristics that contribute to a human-like translation. Hence, when the MT system is optimized with respect to one metric, its performance on alternative metrics might degrade, potentially leading to a suboptimal overall translation quality. In real-world applications, however, translation quality is a multifaceted phenomenon, and relying on a single objective for optimization may restrict the system's ability to balance the various desired properties of a translation. This problem is especially pertinent when the priorities of the translation system differ across application scenarios (e.g., formal vs. colloquial, literal vs. idiomatic), where a combination of metrics is more representative of human judgments. In this paper, we propose a multi-objective optimization framework for machine translation that leverages the theory of Pareto Optimality to simultaneously optimize a translation system with respect to multiple evaluation metrics. Unlike previous ad hoc approaches that combine multiple metrics into a single, weighted objective function (such as linearly combining BLEU and TER), our approach explicitly models the trade-offs between the competing objectives and generates a set of Pareto-optimal hypotheses that represent diverse optimal solutions. Each of these hypotheses embodies a different balance between the selected metrics, capturing a broader and more representative interpretation of translation quality. This allows the system to make more informed and diversified translation decisions, particularly when the individual metrics evaluate different aspects such as fluency, factual consistency, or document-level coherence. Implementing our framework does not require modifying the underlying decoding architecture or significantly increasing the computational complexity of standard optimization methods like Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och, 2003) or PRO (Popovič et al., 2010). Instead, the framework acts as an end-to-end enhancement layer that operates by selecting subsets of translations that lie on the Pareto front, representing the optimal set of solutions where no additional gain in one metric can be achieved without sacrificing performance on another. We demonstrate that this method outperforms traditional linear combination-based approaches in terms of both translation quality, as evaluated on multiple widely used metrics, and system flexibility, as it allows for seamless incorporation of new or alternative evaluation criteria without retraining the model from scratch.

This paper introduces a novel method for predicting the trade decisions made by players in a win-lose board game using the negotiation dialogues they engage in. The Settlers of Catan, a complex board game that involves strategic resource management and negotiation, serves as the platform for our study. In this game, players must engage in trade agreements to acquire scarce resources, and these exchanges are primarily conducted through open negotiation. The significance of this task lies in the intersection of computational linguistics and game theory, as human negotiation strategies often encode a wealth of implicit information about players' goals and constraints. Understanding and modeling this dynamic interaction during the negotiation phase is crucial for simulating human-like strategic behavior in artificial agents. Negotiation dialogues offer a rich, unstructured source of information about players' preferences, intentions, and constraints. However, capturing these latent preferences over time demands robust modeling of the evolving semantics of the negotiation. A static snapshot of preferences at a single time step may be insufficient for predicting the strategic choices of players, especially in games where context and prior utterances heavily influence the discourse and resulting behaviors. Traditional methods for modeling trading in such games often rely on domain-specific rules or do not integrate spoken negotiation data into predictive models. In contrast, we propose a framework that dynamically infers the real-time evolution of each player's preference model from the spoken dialogue and uses game-theoretic principles to identify the equilibrium trade moves that are likely to be executed. Our core contribution is a system that processes the negotiation dialogues as unfolding conversations, incrementally updating each player's preference model while reasoning about which trade options are approximately in equilibrium. By considering the temporal aspect of dialogue and the strategic equilibrium implications of the player’s possible actions, our method generates predictions that are both more accurate and more context-sensitive than existing alternatives. This is demonstrated in a comprehensive evaluation where we compare our method against four established baselines, including models that ignore dialogue or lack equilibrium reasoning. The experimental results underscore the importance of integrating both the evolution of preferences and the principles of strategic reasoning for achieving high predictive performance. Such a system not only enhances the ability of AI agents to predict and simulate human negotiation behavior in competitive scenarios but also opens new possibilities for research at the intersection of natural language processing, game theory, and decision-making in multi-agent systems.

Natural language generation (NLG) is a pivotal component of spoken dialogue systems, playing a crucial role in determining the usability, engagement, and perceived quality of human-machine interactions. An effective NLG system must produce responses that are not only semantically accurate and contextually appropriate but also sound natural and diverse—qualities that are essential for maintaining user engagement and creating the illusion of human-like conversational fluency. While traditional NLG systems in spoken dialogue applications often rely on rule-based approaches and handcrafted templates, these methods are inherently limited in their flexibility and scalability. Rules tend to generate rigid and stylized outputs, which lack the fluid, human-like variation observed in natural language use. Moreover, rule-based systems struggle to generalize across domains and are labor-intensive to adapt to new applications or languages. The limitations of traditional approaches have motivated the adoption of data-driven and statistical methods for NLG, especially in the context of open-domain or multi-turn dialogues where linguistic diversity is a key factor. Among these, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks—deep learning architectures capable of modeling temporal dependencies—offer a promising framework for generating fluent and context-sensitive utterances directly from semantic inputs. By combining the advantages of neural network architectures with the capacity to learn from large unaligned corpora, LSTM-based models can simultaneously perform sentence planning and surface realization, circumventing the traditional multi-stage pipeline used in classical NLG systems. In this paper, we propose a semantically conditioned LSTM-based language generator designed specifically for spoken dialogue applications. Our model leverages semantic inputs to condition the language generation process, ensuring that the generated utterances align with the required meaning while also preserving linguistic richness and fluency. A distinguishing feature of our approach is its ability to learn from unaligned dialogue data by jointly optimizing surface realization and sentence planning in a fully end-to-end manner. This is achieved through the use of the cross-entropy training criterion, eliminating the need for manual pipeline alignment or task-specific feature engineering. Additionally, our LSTM generator supports the generation of varied outputs, enabling the system to avoid monotonous responses and better simulate human-like communication diversity by sampling from the model's output distribution. To evaluate the efficacy of our proposed method, we conducted both objective and subjective assessments in two distinct test domains. The results demonstrate significant improvements in response generation quality compared to traditional systems and previously proposed statistical approaches.

The task of constructing formal meaning representations is a central challenge in natural language understanding, with significant implications for semantic technologies, such as question answering, text generation, and logical inference. Among the various formalisms proposed to model meaning, Discourse Representation Theory (DRT; Kamp and Reyle, 1993) offers a well-established and expressive framework that captures both the propositional content of utterances and the relationships between expressions in discourse. DRT represents sentence meaning through Discourse Representation Structures (DRSs), which are hierarchical, referentially closed semantic forms that track discourse referents and the conditions under which they are introduced or modified. Parsing DRSs from natural language is a complex and challenging task due to their hierarchical and referential nature, which demands both syntactic and semantic understanding. While traditional approaches to semantic parsing have often relied on rule-based or template-driven systems, the recent rise of deep learning has opened the door for end-to-end neural models that can learn to perform this task directly from data. However, creating accurate and generalizable DRS parsers remains difficult due to the abstract, structured output format and the need to disambiguate and resolve complex semantic relationships. In this work, we introduce a neural model for open-domain Discourse Representation Structure parsing that leverages the strengths of deep learning to capture compositionality and discourse coherence. Our key contribution is a method that transforms DRSs into tree-structured representations, enabling the use of structure-aware parsing strategies. This tree transformation captures the hierarchical and referential structure of DRSs in a way that can be naturally decomposed for sequential processing. To effectively model the parsing process, we design a three-stage decoding pipeline. In the first stage, the model predicts the basic structure of the DRS, establishing the hierarchical dependencies among discourse referents and their conditions. The second stage focuses on predicting predicates and the relations that bind arguments to them. Finally, in the third stage, the model identifies referents and resolves coreference links, ensuring that variables are correctly introduced and used across the DRS. Each decoding step benefits from attention mechanisms and contextualized representations, allowing the model to focus on relevant portions of the input and maintain long-range dependencies. We evaluate our approach on the  Groningen Meaning Bank (GMB) , a large and representative corpus annotated with DRSs. Experimental results demonstrate that our structure-aware model significantly outperforms competitive baselines, including both rule-based and neural semantic parsing systems.

The task of training effective statistical machine translation (SMT) models has long been centered around optimizing the model's output with respect to a single evaluation metric, such as BLEU or METEOR. This single-metric focus is primarily a simplification of the complex process of evaluating the quality of translated text, which encompasses multiple aspects such as fluency, accuracy, lexical diversity, and fluency with respect to reference translations. Recent studies have shown that a single evaluation metric often fails to capture the full spectrum of translation quality, and optimizing for just one may not yield the best overall results. This has prompted researchers to investigate multi-metric optimization (MMO), where the translation system is tuned to optimize over a set of complementary evaluation metrics simultaneously. From an optimization perspective, MMO poses a more complex problem than traditional single-metric tuning. The inherent trade-offs between different metrics mean that optimizing for one can lead to a degradation in the performance of others. These trade-offs often result in a set of Pareto-optimal solutions, where no metric can be improved without at least one other suffering as a consequence. This provides a natural theoretical framework for MMO, as it directly aligns with the notion of Pareto optimality in multi-objective optimization. However, effectively combining multiple Pareto-optimal solutions into a single translation model remains an open challenge. In this work, we propose a suite of novel methodologies for multi-metric optimization in the context of statistical machine translation, with a specific focus on ensemble-based decoding techniques. Ensemble methods have been previously applied in the field of machine learning as a way to combine the strengths of multiple models in order to achieve improved performance. Drawing on this idea, we introduce a new ensemble-tuning algorithm designed specifically for MMO in SMT. Our method allows for the combination of multiple Pareto-optimal models in a principled way, enabling the translation system to leverage the different aspects captured by each model. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed methods using standard datasets with both single-reference and multiple-reference configurations. Our results demonstrate that multi-metric optimization not only generates statistically significant improvements in multiple metrics at once (such as BLEU and RIBES) but also avoids the typical trade-off scenario observed in single-metric optimization, where improvements in one metric are achieved at the expense of another. In fact, we observe simultaneous gains across several metrics without a meaningful loss in any other.

Event detection and classification is a foundational task in natural language processing, enabling semantic understanding of textual content and facilitating downstream applications such as information extraction, question answering, and knowledge base construction. Given the complexity and diversity of human language, where events are often described in varied and ambiguous ways, the ability to accurately identify and categorize events is crucial for real-world applications dealing with news articles, social media, and other document corpora. Traditionally, event detection has been approached using rule-based systems or statistical models that rely heavily on handcrafted features and domain-specific knowledge. However, the recent rise of neural network architectures has demonstrated superior performance in capturing the rich linguistic patterns necessary for event detection, without the need for extensive manual feature engineering. Despite the widespread adoption of neural networks for event classification, a rigorous comparative analysis of various neural architectures remains limited. Most prior studies either focus on a single model or provide only superficial comparisons without controlling for variability in training-test splits and model initialization parameters. This creates a gap in the literature regarding the systematic evaluation of different model designs for this task. Additionally, the utility of external knowledge, such as syntactic and temporal structure, in enhancing event detection performance remains underexplored. In this paper, we address these challenges by presenting a novel approach to event detection using GRU-based recurrent neural networks. Our model is specifically designed to integrate syntactic dependencies and temporal relations into the feature representation through a learnable attention mechanism. The attention module dynamically combines the outputs of the GRU with intermediate syntactic positions and temporal indicators, enabling the model to focus on event-related information while preserving the sequential nature of the text. We conduct a thorough empirical evaluation of our model across multiple training-validation-test splits of the widely used ACE 2005 dataset. Crucially, we evaluate the robustness of our model under different random initializations and training conditions to ensure the reproducibility and generalizability of our findings. Our evaluations compare the proposed GRU-based architecture with several state-of-the-art baselines, including convolutional and standard recurrent neural networks, as well as well-known pre-trained transformer models. The results demonstrate that the inclusion of syntactic and temporal attention mechanisms significantly enhances event detection performance, especially in cases where events are nested or contextually complex. Furthermore, we observe that our model achieves competitive or superior performance across all tested splits, highlighting its potential as a scalable and effective solution for real-world event detection tasks.

The task of canonicalizing named entity mentions—mapping mentions of entities in text to a standardized identifier or record in a knowledge base—is a core challenge in natural language processing with wide applications in information extraction, question answering, and semantic data integration. Traditional approaches often focus on entity disambiguation, where mentions are matched to the most probable entity in a pre-defined knowledge base (e.g., Wikipedia). However, real-world use cases frequently involve constructing a canonical table that captures not only the entity but also its structured attributes, such as occupation, birth date, or associated events. This process, which we refer to as  attribute-based canonicalization , requires resolving not only the identity of the entity but also the values and structure of its properties. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic model designed to address the task of canonicalizing named entity mentions into a well-structured table format. Distinguishing this work from prior efforts is its integration of multiple types of signals: entity context, surface features, and a dynamic modeling of attribute parts with first-order dependencies. Additionally, the model explicitly accounts for noise, which is particularly important when the input data is collected from heterogeneous and imprecise sources like web blogs or social media. By capturing these dimensions in a unified framework, the model enables a more accurate and robust mapping of mentions to their canonical forms. The key innovation of our approach lies in its use of transductive learning: given a small set of known entities (seeds) and the raw text of mentions, the model iteratively infers the most likely entity and attribute assignments while learning from the co-occurrence patterns in the data. At its core, this is achieved through a combination of Bayesian inference—updating probabilities as more evidence is accumulated—and conditional estimation techniques—prioritizing the most predictive features when resolving ambiguous cases. We evaluate the model on two real-world datasets: one derived from political blogs and the other from sports news. These diverse domains present varied linguistic and structural challenges, making them suitable for testing the generalizability of the approach. Our experiments indicate that the proposed model consistently outperforms both a simple agglomerative clustering baseline and prior work on canonicalization tasks, demonstrating significant performance gains in both entity linkage and attribute mapping. This work contributes to a growing space in structured knowledge extraction by emphasizing the value of attribute-level modeling and probabilistic reasoning in handling the complexity of named entity canonicalization.

Stock movement prediction remains one of the most challenging problems in quantitative finance due to the inherently stochastic nature of financial markets, the nonlinear interdependencies among market influencers, and the requirement to make temporally-conditioned predictions from highly noisy and chaotic data. Traditional models often focus on historical price data, technical indicators, or fundamental data. However, recent works have shown that social media content, especially tweets, can provide timely and diverse signals that reflect public sentiment and collective expectations about companies, industries, or policy changes that might otherwise be slow to appear in traditional records. Despite promising results, prior approaches mainly rely on discriminative models or standard topic models, which often fail to capture the full complexity of the underlying stochastic processes and the temporal dependencies between data sources and stock movements. This paper presents a novel deep generative model for stock movement prediction that jointly learns from both textual (Twitter) and numerical (historical price) signals. Our model is specifically designed to address three major complexities in the problem: first, the inherent stochasticity of market movements; second, the lack of effective modeling of long-term and temporal dependencies; and third, the integration of multiple modalities (i.e., text and time series) into a unified predictive framework. To address the first challenge, we introduce a framework with recurrent, continuous latent variables, enabling the model to better accommodate the uncertainty and stochasticity inherent in market predictions. This is a departure from traditional deterministic models, which cannot naturally represent such uncertainty and are prone to overfitting. To address the tractability challenge caused by intractable posterior inference in generative models, we employ neural variational inference, using encoder networks with strong temporal modeling capabilities to approximate the true posterior distribution. This allows us to perform scalable and efficient posterior inference while preserving the model’s ability to generate realistic predictive dynamics. Additionally, we propose a hybrid objective function that includes a temporal auxiliary task to explicitly enforce the model to learn and preserve predictive dependencies across time. The temporal auxiliary not only strengthens the temporal coherence of the model’s hidden representations but also serves as a regularizer to avoid overfitting to task-irrelevant patterns in the input streams. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we construct a new dataset that spans a wide spectrum of market activities and time periods. The dataset includes real-time Twitter data explicitly filtered for stock-related sentiment and the historical stock prices of over 100 publicly traded companies.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have demonstrated the importance of combining syntactic and semantic information for modeling the structure and meaning of text. Traditional approaches often rely on explicitly parsing syntactic structure at runtime, such as using a constituent or dependency parser, and subsequently incorporating this parsed information into semantic models. While effective in many cases, this approach incurs additional computational overhead and introduces error propagation, as syntactic parsers are not perfect and may compound errors in downstream semantic tasks. This paper proposes a novel method to incorporate syntactic information into semantic models without requiring explicit syntactic parsing during inference. We introduce the concept of a  syntactic scaffold : a means of enabling syntactic awareness in semantic models through a multitask training objective, leveraging only a treebank during training and avoiding costly syntactic processing at runtime. The syntactic scaffold effectively learns to encode syntactic relationships implicitly, using these relationships to support semantic goals such as understanding argument structures, identifying event frames, and resolving coreference. The key insight behind this approach is that syntactic relationships are not only crucial for parsing but also provide important signals for semantic understanding. By jointly training a model to predict semantic annotations while being implicitly guided by a treebank via a multitask learning framework, we allow the model to implicitly encode and utilize syntactic information as scaffolding for complex semantic structures. This circumvents the need for explicit parsing modules during inference and avoids the error cascade traditionally associated with chaining syntactic and semantic components. We evaluate the effectiveness of syntactic scaffolds on three canonical semantic tasks:  PropBank semantics , focusing on argument role labeling;  frame semantics , which requires identifying semantic frames and their associated frame elements; and  coreference resolution , which involves resolving anaphoric references and linking mentions of the same entity across a document. In all three tasks, we compare our approach to strong baselines that rely on explicitly incorporated syntactic features or internal representations from pre-trained models. Our results show that syntactic scaffolds lead to significant improvements over these baselines, achieving competitive performance on all tasks without requiring additional runtime syntactic processing. This work highlights the potential of multitask learning as a framework for integrating syntactic and semantic information, and opens new avenues for building accurate and efficient models that implicitly encode both structural and meaning-based knowledge. By abstracting away from traditional syntactic pipelines, our method represents a scalable and robust approach to syntactic-aware semantic modeling, with broad implications for tasks that benefit from both domains of linguistic knowledge.

The task of accurately translating natural language between languages is inherently complex, not only due to syntactic and semantic ambiguities, but also because of the polysemy of words—many words have multiple related or unrelated meanings depending on their usage in context. This polysemy often constitutes the key barrier to achieving high-quality translations in statistical machine translation (SMT). For instance, the Chinese word “银行 (yínháng)”, which can mean “bank (financial institution)” or “river bank,” will be translated to entirely different English words depending on its sense in the source text. In standard SMT systems, the context-specific meaning of the source word is not explicitly modeled, resulting in translation errors that could be avoided with knowledge of the correct word sense. To address this issue, the integration of word senses into the translation pipeline has been a promising yet underexplored research direction. Prior approaches have primarily focused on reformulating the word sense disambiguation (WSD) problem for machine translation, using supervised learning to predict likely translations based on pre-defined senses. However, such methods often neglect the nuanced and dynamic nature of word senses, which vary widely based on language-specific syntactic and semantic patterns. Moreover, the reliance on hand-labeled or manually curated sense inventories limits scalability and real-world applicability, especially in low-resource settings. In this paper, we propose a novel sense-based translation model that explicitly models and incorporates word senses in the translation process. Rather than treating word sense as an external disambiguation step, our model seamlessly integrates sense inference into the translation model itself. We develop a broad-coverage sense tagger based on a nonparametric Bayesian topic model that automatically identifies semantically meaningful clusters of word usage in the source language. These clusters serve as the inferred senses for each word in the source context. The model then utilizes maximum entropy classifiers to select the most suitable translation for each source word based on its inferred sense. This end-to-end approach allows the decoding process to take into account both the contextual meaning of the source text and the target language equivalence. Our approach is fundamentally different from prior WSD-integrated SMT models, which relied solely on external sense labels rather than learning them from the data. By directly learning word senses as topic distributions and explicitly modeling their relationships to translation choices, our model avoids inaccuracies introduced by noisy or incomplete sense inventories.

The study of meaning is one of the central problems in linguistics and artificial intelligence, with far-reaching applications in tasks such as semantic similarity, text understanding, and machine translation. In recent years,  distributional semantics  has emerged as a powerful paradigm for building computational models of meaning, based on the intuition that  words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings  (Firth, 1957). Almost all research in this area has focused on modeling meaning entirely from  textual data , using co-occurrence statistics to represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space. While these models have achieved impressive success in capturing general semantic relationships such as synonymy or antonymy (Mikolov et al., 2013; Turney & Pantel, 2010), they often lack a connection to the world via sensory or perceptual information, and consequently may underrepresent aspects of meaning that are grounded in perception and sensory experience (Murphy, 2003; Lakoff & Johnson, 1999). Recent advances in  computational perception and vision , especially in  deep learning , provide us with the tools to model percepts and grounded representations at a much finer level than previously possible. In this work, we explore the use of  vision-based  and  multimodal  distributional models of meaning, constructing vector spaces where meaning is partially grounded in perceptual representations extracted from visual data. This paper investigates the scope and limitations of incorporating visual signals for modeling the semantics of language, particularly focusing on the case of  color terms , which are intimately tied to perceptual experience. We compare the performance of visual models with traditional textual distributional models on a variety of semantic tasks and find that while visual models  perform worse overall  in most semantic similarity tasks, they significantly outperform verbal models on certain lexical subclasses, particularly color terms and other words with strong visual correlates. More surprisingly, we find that even when color terms are used in  nonliteral  or  metaphorical  settings (e.g., "being in the red," as in debt), the visual models can still provide meaningful insights, demonstrating a capacity to abstract visual gist while recognizing such figurative usage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining visual and textual data in  multimodal  models yields substantial performance gains for certain tasks, suggesting that textual and visual models capture distinct yet complementary dimensions of meaning. This result aligns with theoretical work in cognitive semantics, which emphasizes the complementarity between symbolic and embodied representations (Barsalou, 1999; Louwerse & Jeuniaux, 2009). To our knowledge, this is the first work to directly analyze and contrast the performance of perceptually grounded versus purely textual distributional models on a broad set of semantic tasks, particularly in the domain of color semantics.

Scope learning is a critical task in semantic role labeling and information extraction, where the goal is to identify the textual span dominated by a particular cue, such as a negation or speculation marker, and determine its relation to specific entities or propositions in the text. In biomedical natural language processing (NLP), such tasks are particularly relevant due to the interpretive nature of clinical and scientific texts, where the implications of a cue (e.g., "not known" or "may indicate") can profoundly affect semantic inference and downstream applications like evidence extraction and knowledge base construction. Despite its importance, scope learning poses substantial challenges due to the complex interplay of syntax, semantics, and discourse features, which often transcend boundaries defined by shallow syntactic structures. A common approach to tackle this problem involves sequence tagging models, which identify the boundaries of scope markers within surface-level syntactic chunks, such as noun phrases or verb phrases. While effective in certain settings, such chunking-based approaches are often limited in their ability to capture long-range dependencies and deep semantic relationships, which are essential for modeling the interaction between the cue and its arguments. Recent work has begun to address these limitations by integrating deeper semantic representations, such as dependency parses and semantic role labels, into scope learning architectures. However, a unifying and flexible framework that explicitly models the structural relationship between cues and their associated arguments remains lacking. This paper proposes a novel approach to scope learning that is grounded in the concept of simplified shallow semantic parsing. Rather than treating the task as an isolated sequence tagging problem, we frame it as a semantic argument identification task by modeling the cue as the predicate and mapping its scope into a collection of linguistic constituents that function as its arguments. This shift in perspective enables us to incorporate structural information into the modeling process and capture the hierarchical relationship between the cue and its syntactically and semantically relevant constituents. Our framework does not rely on full-scale semantic parsers but instead uses a lightweight yet powerful representation that focuses on the cue-argument dependency and syntactic cohesion, making it both computationally efficient and adaptable to different processing pipelines. We evaluate our approach on the BioScope corpus (Kim et al., 2016), a widely used dataset for scope learning in biomedical texts involving negation and speculation cues. Experimental results demonstrate that our parsing-based approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art chunking-based methods in both precision and recall, underscoring the value of incorporating structural semantics in modeling cue-argument relations.

This paper introduces a novel neural attention-based model designed for the task of disfluency detection. Disfluency detection is a key problem in natural language processing, often encountered in spontaneous speech, where speakers frequently produce revisions such as self-corrections, insertions, and repetitions that disrupt the fluency of the sentence. The removal or correction of disfluencies is essential for improving the performance of downstream tasks such as machine translation, speech recognition, and dialogue systems. Traditional approaches to disfluency detection typically rely on handcrafted rules or statistical taggers such as conditional random fields (CRFs), which model the dependencies between neighboring words in a sentence. While CRF-based methods have shown decent performance, they are limited in capturing long-range dependencies and handling complex disfluency structures in naturalistic speech data. In contrast, our approach leverages the encoder-decoder architecture, a powerful framework in sequence modeling, and transforms the problem into a sequence-to-sequence learning task. This approach allows the model to consider the entire structure of the sentence when identifying which parts are disfluent, thereby enabling it to capture not only immediate word dependencies but also non-local elements that may directly or indirectly contribute to disfluency. Central to our model is the use of a neural attention mechanism as a pointer to select an ordered subsequence of the input sentence that is grammatically correct and rhythmically natural. The model is composed of a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network as the encoder, which captures contextual information from both past and future words in the sequence. The decoder, equipped with an attention module, dynamically aligns the encoder’s output with the target sequence, effectively determining which parts of the input should be retained and which should be discarded or corrected as disfluent. This allows the model to generate a fluent version of the sentence without explicitly needing to classify all words as fluent or disfluent. The key advantage of this architecture is its ability to model complex sentence structures and long-range dependencies, which are both critical for accurate disfluency detection. We evaluate our model on the widely used English Switchboard corpus, a benchmark dataset containing transcribed spontaneous speech annotated for disfluencies. The results show that our model achieves an F-score of 86.7%, which is a significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we extend our evaluation beyond English by testing the model on an in-house annotated Chinese dataset.

Word sense disambiguation (WSD) remains a challenging subtask in natural language processing (NLP) due to the polysemy and homonymy prevalent in human language. Despite decades of research, achieving robust accuracy in WSD is complicated by the need for rich, high-quality lexical resources and contextual modeling that generalizes well across domains and use cases. Traditional supervised WSD approaches rely on annotated corpora such as SemCor or OntoNotes to train classifiers by extracting contextual features around a target word, including part-of-speech tags, neighboring words, and syntactic dependencies. While these feature sets yield reasonable accuracy, the performance of these models often plateaus, suggesting a gap in the exploitation of available linguistic knowledge and the limits of small-scale annotated data in capturing semantic nuances. This paper presents a novel method to augment supervised sense disambiguation by incorporating unlabeled, large-scale corpora through features extracted from   selectors  , a class of context-sensitive words that appear in parallel, semantically aligned contexts to a given lexical instance. The core intuition underpinning our approach is that, even in unannotated text, words cooccurring in shared semantic environments across different corpora—especially at web scale—can provide distributionsal evidence about a target word’s sense. By including these selectors as additional features in a support vector machine (SVM) sense classifier, we effectively bridge the gap between manually annotated training data and the vast, rich semantic context available in unstructured web text. Our contributions are threefold. First, we define the notion of a selector and propose a method for systematically identifying such words in an unsupervised manner based on contextual similarity. Second, we demonstrate through extensive empirical evaluation that the inclusion of these selectors as features consistently and significantly improves supervised sense disambiguation performance across both coarse-grained and fine-grained WSD tasks. Our experiments achieve error reductions of 15.4% and 6.9%, respectively, over baseline models. Third, we show that the selector-based feature representation enhances the classification step of named-entity recognition (NER), reducing errors by 9.3% on the OntoNotes corpus. Notably, these improvements come at no additional cost in terms of human annotation effort beyond the initial training data, as the proposed methodology leverages web-scale unlabeled corpora. By expanding the set of available features for supervised WSD with the context-based insight of selectors, this work opens up new avenues for improving semantic modeling in NLP tasks requiring language-level understanding without relying on the scarcity of labeled examples.

The task of constructing a coherent and comprehensive timeline from fragmented medical narratives is a critical challenge in clinical natural language processing (NLP). Clinical narratives, such as discharge summaries, progress notes, and consultation reports, are typically written by different healthcare providers and often follow varying formats, making it difficult to extract consistent temporal sequences of events across them. Accurate temporal ordering is essential for tasks like risk prediction, treatment monitoring, and overall patient care planning. However, traditional methods that focus solely on within-document event sequencing fall short in capturing cross-narrative temporal relations, which are necessary to form a unified and accurate understanding of a patient’s clinical history. In clinical narratives, events are often spread across multiple documents, each containing partial and potentially redundant information. The temporal relations between these events are not always explicitly stated, requiring the system to infer temporal order from implicit cues such as relative expressions (e.g., “after the surgery,” “prior to admission”), document dates, and event types. Previous work on temporal relation extraction has primarily focused on intra-document event ordering (Baldwin et al., 2014; Uzuner et al., 2011), where the events and their relations are confined to a single text. Extending these methods to a cross-narrative setting introduces new challenges, such as aligning temporally related events that appear in distinct documents, handling ambiguity in coreference between mentions of the same event, and resolving conflicting temporal information across sources. This paper addresses the cross-narrative temporal ordering problem by developing and comparing two approaches for aligning and temporally organizing medical events across multiple clinical documents. Our first approach introduces a novel weighted finite state transducer (FST) representation for medical event sequences. This formalism allows compact and flexible modeling of temporal relations and coreference, enabling efficient composition and decoding of the most probable global timeline using standard FST operations. We show how FSTs can encode both the local temporal relations between events and the cross-narrative dependencies between mentioned events. The second approach we propose is based on dynamic programming with iterative pairwise alignment. This method performs a sequence of pairwise alignments using global alignment (Needleman-Wunsch) and local alignment (Smith-Waterman) strategies and combines the results to form a global ordering. Unlike the FST-based approach, the dynamic programming method is not designed for scalable decoding of global timelines but is intended to provide an alternative baseline that is intuitive and well-aligned with traditional sequence alignment techniques.

Recent advancements in machine translation have significantly benefited from statistical and neural models capable of learning complex patterns directly from data. Among such approaches, forest-based translation has gained attention due to its ability to harness syntactic ambiguity in source sentences by considering multiple parse trees simultaneously. Forest-based methods compactly represent an exponential number of source parse trees through chart structures, enabling improved coverage and more coherent translation outputs. However, generating accurate translation rules from forest structures—particularly in efficiently encoding the attachment of target function words—remains a significant challenge. A crucial but often underutilized aspect of translation is the role of   function words  , which are low-level, syntactically rich elements such as articles, auxiliaries, prepositions, and particles. In the target language, these words are indispensable for well-formed grammar and sentence structure but pose a challenge in rule-based translation systems due to their ambiguity and their frequent omission or structural shifts during translation. This is especially true in target languages like Japanese, where function words are lexically and syntactically sparse but still vital for disambiguation and grammatical correctness. In this paper, we address the underrepresentation and misplacement of function words in forest-to-string translation by proposing a method that effectively leverages these words in the construction of generalized tree-to-string translation rules. Specifically, given aligned   forest-string pairs  , we extract translation rules that model the attachment of both aligned and unaligned function words in the target language. Our approach is based on the observation that function words are often grammatically constrained and semantically bound to nearby syntactic chunks. Therefore, we propose to incorporate   target-side dependency parser outputs  —which yield syntactic chunks—to effectively bind function words to relevant source linguistic structures. To this end, we design a rule extraction method that uses the forest structure to generate   tree-to-string translation rules   that respect the local syntactic dependencies inferred by the target parser. By limiting the attachment of function words to local chunks, we avoid the overgeneration of attachment hypotheses, which can dramatically improve rule precision. This local binding strategy not only enhances the fidelity of source-to-target syntactic mappings but also strengthens the modeling of function word positions during decoding. The proposed method is evaluated on a large-scale   English-to-Japanese   translation task. Through rigorous experimentation, we demonstrate that our approach significantly improves upon the state-of-the-art forest-to-string translation system by achieving a   1.8 points absolute improvement in BLEU score  , confirming the efficacy of function words as critical features in forest-based rule generalization.

The way scientific knowledge is disseminated and built upon hinges heavily on the citation network, where researchers use references to acknowledge, support, and contextualize their work. Citations facilitate the mapping of knowledge evolution, enable academic evaluation, and are a cornerstone for systems such as recommendation engines, topic modeling, and impact analysis. However, a key limitation of current citation-based evaluations is the assumption that all references are   equal in intensity  —that is, each citation is treated as having the same level of semantic weight and importance, regardless of its underlying purpose. This simplification overlooks the nuanced and heterogeneous nature of citation practices in scientific literature, where the same citation can be used for contrasting purposes such as validating a prior finding, criticizing a methodology, or simply providing background information. If we consider the multitude of reasons for citing—a necessary function within the structure of scholarly communication—we see that the intensity or emphasis placed on each reference in the body of a paper often varies significantly. For example, a citation incorporated into a statement of agreement may carry more "semantic weight" than another that’s used to present an opposing viewpoint, even if both are essential to the argument. Ignoring these differences in citation intensity can lead to distorted interpretations of scientific impact and hinder the effectiveness of citation-based applications like author credit allocation, paper recommenders, or evaluation of research productivity. In this work, we argue that   measuring the intensity of citations is fundamental   not only to achieving a more accurate understanding of the role of a reference in a scientific discourse but also for enhancing the performance and relevance of citation-based technologies. Intensity, in this context, refers to the degree of reliance or emphasis a reference is given within a text. It ranges from implicit mentions to direct usage of a cited claim and is encoded in the linguistics and structure of the citation context. Quantifying this intensity enables us to reflect the true impact and relevance of cited works in a document. To advance this vision, we take the following key steps: first, we curate and release a   richly annotated dataset   containing references labeled for intensity. This human-annotated data serves as the foundation for modeling reference intensity as a classification task. Second, we introduce   GraLap  , a novel   graph-based semi-supervised learning model   designed to explicitly capture the semantic and relational structure between references and the text in which they appear.

The dynamic nature of real-world information poses a significant challenge for maintaining the accuracy and relevance of Knowledge Bases (KBs). Most existing KBs, such as DBpedia or YAGO, are static by design, meaning their contents are not frequently updated in response to new or changing facts. However, such updates are crucial in temporal domains like spousal relationships, political positions, or job titles, where entities’ relationships evolve over time. An accurate and up-to-date KB requires detecting and integrating such changes automatically, which necessitates a system capable of recognizing time-varying facts and their relevant verbs—what we call  state-changing verbs  (SCVs). These verbs, such as  marry ,  divorce ,  elect , or  appoint , typically denote an event that triggers a change in the state of a relation or a specific entity. Thus, the automatic identification of SCVs is key to building systems that can enhance the timeliness and fidelity of KBs. This problem, however, is challenging due to the lack of annotated data mapping verbs to KB relation updates and the ambiguity of which textual changes correspond to factual changes. One possible solution lies in leveraging the rich and vast, albeit noisy, source of information provided by Wikipedia and, in particular, its revision history. Wikipedia infoboxes, which are structured summaries of key entity facts, are commonly updated whenever the entity's information changes. Changes to these infoboxes, in turn, are often reflected in the surrounding text of the articles through the addition or deletion of verbs. For example, the spousal relation between two individuals is often initialized with the verb  engage  being added to the text and later terminated when  divorce  is inserted following the modification of the infobox. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learning state-changing verbs by leveraging Wikipedia’s edit history as weak supervision. Our method distantly supervises the mapping of textual verb changes to infobox updates using edit logs and the temporal alignment of article text and infobox fields. By observing the correlation between the addition or deletion of verbs in the article and subsequent updates to the infobox, we are able to infer potential SCVs and their associated state transitions. Furthermore, we incorporate hard and soft constraints to disambiguate between different verbs that could influence the same relation, ensuring more robust mapping. To evaluate our approach, we run experiments by predicting infobox updates based solely on the verbs observed in the text.

End-to-end relation extraction is a core task in natural language processing, aiming to automatically identify named entities and their semantic relations within unstructured text. Traditional approaches to this task often rely on cascading pipelines, where entity recognition and relation classification are conducted in separate stages with potentially conflicting errors compounding in later phases. Feature-based systems, although successful in certain domains, typically require hand-crafted linguistic features and domain-specific heuristics, which are labor-intensive and often limit scalability across different languages or genres of texts. In recent years, deep learning approaches have emerged as promising alternatives, offering the potential to model complex linguistic patterns in a more principled and generalizable manner. In this paper, we propose a novel end-to-end neural model for the joint extraction of entities and their relationships using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). Our model architecture is designed to capture two complementary aspects of linguistic structure—linear word sequence information and hierarchical syntactic dependencies. To achieve this, we stack bidirectional tree-structured LSTM-RNNs on top of bidirectional sequential LSTM-RNNs. This allows our model to effectively integrate both sequential and structural representations into a unified framework for relation extraction. By sharing parameters between the entity recognition and relation classification tasks, we enable the model to learn joint representations of entities and their interactions, improving coherence and task performance. A key innovation of our method is the use of dependency tree structures, encoded via tree-structured LSTMs, to model the local syntactic context that is vital for capturing the relationships between entities. For example, the grammatical role of a noun phrase—whether it is a subject, object, or modifier—often determines the relation it has with other entities in the sentence. Our model captures this through hierarchical composition over dependency subtrees, allowing it to dynamically aggregate relevant features for the task. We also incorporate two additional mechanisms to improve training and generalization: entity pretraining and scheduled sampling. Entity pretraining is a preprocessing step in which the model is first trained on the entity detection task alone before being fine-tuned on the joint task. This encourages the model to focus on entity boundaries during early stages, which is especially beneficial for relation extraction. Scheduled sampling, on the other hand, dynamically blends gold-standard entity labels with model-generated intermediate predictions during training, gradually increasing the model's reliance on its own outputs.

The semantics of natural language is a core area of study in linguistics and computational linguistics. A particularly interesting property of real-world language is  semantic compositionality , the ability to derive the meaning of a complex expression from the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined. This principle is often considered a cornerstone of linguistic theory (Fodor and Lepore, 1998). Sentences and multiword expressions in particular offer a rich testbed for studying how semantic compositionality works across human languages. A special but ubiquitous class of multiword expressions is  compound nouns , which appear in many languages, often in highly productive and formulaic ways. German is especially notable in this regard, as compound nouns are a dominant and easily identifiable feature of the language and are well-documented in both linguistic and computational studies. German’s rich inflectional system and productive compounding rules provide fertile ground for testing general theories of compositionality. In assembling compound nouns, German grammar generally permits a concatenate structure of parts that may carry rich semantic relations (e.g., modification, classification, location), but without clear ordering constraints or syntactic structure. This raises the question: To what extent do the representational properties of a German compound noun reflect the compositional structure of its component words, and can we reverse-engineer this composition process using distributional models of meaning? This paper presents a novel empirical investigation into the semantic compositionality of German compound nouns using vector space models (VSMs) and various formal composition models. We begin by assuming that the meaning of a compound can be estimated from the distributional context co-occurrences in a large corpus. However, rather than taking these distributions as a final point, our objective is to  reverse-engineer  the compound’s meaning by using its  constituents . That is, we attempt to reconstruct the observed distributional vector of the compound from the vectors of its parts using different models of semantic composition. This process allows us to evaluate the extent to which meaning in German compounds is, in fact, compositional rather than idiosyncratic. To analyze compositionality, the paper uses a large dataset of German compound nouns, each manually annotated for immediate syntactic constituents. We employ state-of-the-art models of semantic composition—such as additive models, multiplicative models, and more sophisticated approaches like recursive neural networks—alongside a new model we propose that demonstrates superior performance in composition accuracy. Our models are evaluated based on how closely the reconstructed vectors approximate the original distributional vectors, using standard metrics of vector similarity.

Chinese treebanking is a foundational task in computational linguistics, enabling a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications such as syntactic parsing, machine translation, and information extraction. Over the years, syntactic annotation of Chinese has primarily focused on either phrase-structure (PS) trees or dependency (DP) trees, with significant differences in the representation, scope, and linguistic theories underpinning each approach. Phrase-structure grammars, popularized by frameworks such as the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB; Marcus et al., 1994), offer a hierarchical representation of sentence constituents that are essential for capturing the grammatical structure of a language. On the other hand, dependency grammars, as advocated by the Universal Dependencies (UD; Nivre et al., 2016) and other frameworks, provide a more compact and linguistically expressive representation focused on the relationships between syntactic head and dependent words. These two views often address different linguistic questions and, as a result, have been developed independently. The divergence between these two structural perspectives has led to challenges, including the need for cross-view conversion and the limited flexibility for exploring different syntactic theories when benchmarking NLP systems. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing a multi-view treebanking framework specifically for Chinese. The proposed framework establishes dependency structures as the base annotation layer and enables the derivation of phrase structures with minimal loss of information. This design choice is motivated by the growing prominence of dependency parsing in modern NLP and its compatibility with large-scale cross-lingual and cross-theoretical applications. By starting with a dependency structure and incorporating phrasal components derived algorithmically or semi-automatically, our framework facilitates the creation of a unified annotation scheme that is modular, linguistically robust, and syntactically precise. To realize this vision, we have built a large-scale multi-view Chinese treebank (PMT 1.0) under the proposed framework. The first publicly available release of the treebank comprises 14,463 annotated sentences. Each sentence is equipped with both dependency and phrase structure annotations. This dual annotation allows researchers to study syntactic representation from two complementary perspectives without requiring redundant manual annotation efforts. Given the complexity of converting from dependency to phrase structures, special attention was paid during construction to ensure the conversion process preserves as much syntactic information as possible. To evaluate the effectiveness of the multi-view framework, we trained and tested a transition-based dependency parser using features derived from the phrase structure view, demonstrating significant improvements in parsing performance compared to a model trained solely on the dependency structure.

The ability to infer new knowledge from textual data is crucial for expanding the scope of information available to both humans and machines. Despite the vastness of the Web, many questions cannot be directly answered by the factual content it contains. For example, while it may be explicitly stated that Barack Obama is the father of Malia Obama and Sasha Obama, it may not be explicitly noted that Malia Obama and Sasha Obama are sisters. In such cases, inference is a powerful mechanism to uncover implicit knowledge. However, inference requires a set of logical rules, or   inference rules  , which can deduce new facts from existing ones. The challenge, then, becomes: how can these rules be automatically learned from text in a general and flexible way? This paper explores the problem of learning first-order Horn clauses — a logical formalism that generalizes propositional logic — from Web text in an unsupervised, domain-independent manner. The extracted rules are then used to infer new facts that are not explicitly stated. We present   SHERLOCK  , a scalable system for inductive logic programming that learns over 30,000 Horn clauses from unstructured Web text. Unlike domain-specific or manually crafted rule sets, SHERLOCK learns general rules across a broad range of topics, from geography and human relations to scientific domains such as chemistry and biology. The success of any such system hinges on the ability to reason effectively in the presence of   noise, ambiguity, and incompleteness   in the data. Traditional statistical methods for rule learning often struggle under these conditions, especially when the extracted relational facts are sparse and may contain many false positives. To address this challenge, SHERLOCK introduces a novel   rule scoring function   inspired by the   Statistical Relevance   framework of Salmon et al. (1971). This function evaluates the relevance of each rule to a set of known facts and emphasizes rules that are statistically supported and generalizable. We evaluate SHERLOCK using comparison with the    TEXTRUNNER    system, a popular tool for fact extraction that does not perform inference. Our experiments demonstrate that inference over the rules learned by SHERLOCK is significantly more effective. At a precision level of 0.8, SHERLOCK's inferred knowledge base contains   three times more facts   than explicitly extracted data. This result highlights the potential of learning inference rules from raw text, even in the absence of annotated training data. Our approach opens up new possibilities for knowledge discovery and reasoning using real-world textual data.

The task of fine-grained named entity typing (F-NET) involves detecting and classifying entities into highly detailed semantic categories, often with thousands of possible types within a structured ontology like WordNet. This task becomes particularly challenging in short, noisy, or context-dependent inputs such as tweets and news headlines, where contextual ambiguity and data sparsity are rampant. Traditional approaches, often based on either flat taxonomies or hierarchical models with limited supervision, struggle with the high-dimensional space of fine-grained types and the variability of expressions. In addition, many existing systems are designed to operate on well-structured documents or assume access to large annotated corpora, which severely limits their applicability to real-world short-form text. Our goal is to address the critical limitations of previous models by developing a system that is both fine-grained and context-aware. The proposed system, FINET, is the first end-to-end framework for named entity typing that supports WordNet's super fine-grained classification scheme while explicitly addressing the challenges of data scarcity and noisy intermediate representations. FINET extends the traditional pipeline by incorporating principles from word sense disambiguation and unsupervised type generation, enabling it to generalize over entities that have no labeled training data. Rather than relying solely on pre-annotated examples, FINET constructs training data by leveraging ontological relationships and cross-resource alignment, making it both scalable and robust. A key contribution of this work is the development of a modular, multi-stage architecture that begins with the extraction of potential types from multiple sources—such as surface syntactic cues, semantic role labels, and entity linkers—and culminates in an end-to-end system that scores and selects the most contextually appropriate type. To reduce overfitting and improve generalization, the system is trained using noisy labels generated from WordNet hypernyms and other open-source knowledge bases. Our experiments, conducted on both standard benchmark datasets and our own collection of 1000 short-form sentences derived from personal experiences, show that FINET significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of precision, recall, and coverage of entity types. Notably, the system is capable of recognizing types at three levels of granularity, demonstrating strong performance even on the most fine-grained level. This paper also explores the practical benefits of FINET in tasks that demand high-precision typing, such as information extraction for knowledge graph construction, semantic parsing, and question answering. Through its novel treatment of data scarcity, robust type candidate generation, and end-to-end fine-grained selection, FINET provides a strong foundation for future research in context-aware NLP.

Recent advances in dependency parsing have significantly improved the accuracy and efficiency of syntactic analysis in natural language processing. Dependency parsing, especially in a graph-based framework, seeks to identify the syntactic relations between words by modeling their dependencies as a graph structure where each word is a node and each dependency is an edge connecting a head to its modifier (McDonald et al., 2005). These parsers typically rely on ranking or scoring all possible edges efficiently using a classifier such as a perceptron or support vector machine. However, the widespread use of   hand-crafted feature templates  —such as word identities, part-of-speech tags, and grammatical functions—has introduced several limitations.
