As such, syntactic information has been considered an essential ingredient in building robust SRL models. However, over the last few years, the emergence of neural network-based models has begun to upend these classical assumptions. Recent studies have demonstrated that end-to-end deep learning architectures, such as BiLSTMs, Transformers, and task-specific networks, can achieve competitive – even superior – performance on SRL tasks without explicit syntactic input. These models learn distributed representations of words and their contexts through large-scale training and seem less reliant on explicit syntactic features. This led many researchers to question whether syntax remains a necessary or even beneficial component in modern neural SRL systems. In this paper, we aim to revisit and quantify the role of syntactic information in  neural syntactic-dependent  SRL frameworks. We argue that while neural models can achieve decent performance without syntactic features, syntactic signals still provide valuable inductive biases that can lead to better generalization, particularly in complex linguistic environments, low-resource scenarios, and cross-lingual settings. To this end, we present a neural SRL model that explicitly incorporates syntactic dependencies through an enhanced argument labeling architecture. We also introduce an extended  k-order argument pruning  algorithm, which allows us to filter out unlikely candidates during the argument prediction stage, leveraging syntactic proximity for faster and more informed decision-making. Our approach is evaluated on the widely adopted CoNLL benchmarks (2008 and 2009) for English and Chinese.

Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled models to analyze and predict sentiment in text with remarkable accuracy, especially when using annotated datasets and traditional feature-based approaches. However, more complex sentiment analysis tasks, such as predicting distributions over multiple sentiment or emotional labels rather than simple positive/negative classifications, remain a challenging problem. In addition, many real-world sentiment data often exist in the form of open-ended textual expressions that reflect nuanced, multifaceted emotions. A person may feel both sadness and relief, or anger and hope, in a single narrative, requiring models to go beyond binary classification to adequately capture this complexity. This paper introduces a novel approach to predict sentiment distributions using a semi-supervised recursive autoencoder (RAE) framework, which not only encodes hierarchical sentence structures but also learns distributed representations of phrases in a purely data-driven manner. Our model makes two key contributions to the field of sentiment analysis. First, by framing sentiment prediction as a multinomial classification problem, we explicitly model the distribution of emotional responses in continuous probability space rather than relying on discrete, binary classifications. This distributional approach provides a more nuanced and interpretable representation of sentiment, which is particularly useful for qualitative, multilabel datasets. Second, we propose a recursive autoencoder as the backbone for learning rich contextual and compositional representations of language at the phrase and sentence level without relying on manually curated sentiment lexica or polarity transformation rules. Autoencoders, originally introduced in the context of unsupervised deep learning, have been predominantly used for tasks like denoising or dimensionality reduction. In contrast, our proposed architecture leverages the inductive bias of recursive autoencoders to model the hierarchical structure of language, which is crucial for capturing the syntactic and semantic relationships among words and phrases essential for sentiment analysis. The semi-supervised nature of our approach allows us to utilize the abundance of unlabeled text data to learn meaningful sentence embeddings and only leverage limited labeled data for training the sentiment distribution prediction layer. This is particularly valuable in real-world applications, where annotated multi-label datasets are difficult to acquire at scale. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments on two benchmark datasets. First, we apply our model to a well-studied movie review dataset that has served as a standard benchmark in sentiment analysis. Here, our recursive autoencoder achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting a distributional sentiment label, outperforming existing models that rely on heuristic-based features, sentiment lexicons, or other pre-defined resources.

Bilingual lexicons play a foundational role in various natural language processing tasks, notably in machine translation and cross-lingual information retrieval. These resources provide essential mappings between equivalent terms in two languages and help bridge linguistic and conceptual gaps between language systems. Traditionally, the process of creating bilingual lexicons has been a labor-intensive and expensive endeavor, requiring deep linguistic and domain-specific knowledge from human experts. As such, the development of high-quality, specialized bilingual lexicons has been largely confined to high-resource language pairs and general-purpose vocabularies. With the rise of machine learning and computational linguistics, researchers have explored a variety of automated methods to construct bilingual lexicons from parallel corpora or monolingual text, reducing the reliance on manual annotation. However, such approaches often suffer from well-known limitations, including the scarcity of cross-lingual parallel data and the difficulty of handling domain-specific terminology. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for building specialized bilingual lexicons that leverages the vast, multilingual structure of Wikipedia as a source of background knowledge. Wikipedia not only offers extensive coverage in hundreds of languages but also provides a structured and semantically rich lexical and domain landscape that can be systematically exploited for cross-lingual lexical acquisition. Our approach is designed to overcome the limitations of existing methods by (1) extracting domain-specific terminology from Wikipedia categories, (2) aligning these domains across languages using interlanguage links and semantic relations, and (3) constructing domain-specific translation dictionaries by combining lexical and contextual information from multilingual Wikipedia articles. The generality and scalability of our method are two of its key contributions. By using Wikipedia as a backbone for linguistic alignment, the method is applicable to a diverse range of language pairs, including low-resource or less commonly studied ones, as long as the languages are represented in Wikipedia. This is particularly important in facilitating cross-lingual technologies for endangered or underrepresented languages. We present a comprehensive evaluation of the method across four specialized domains and two language pairs—French-English and Romanian-English, two language pairs representing different typological settings and resource abundance. The performance of our proposed approach is benchmarked against three state-of-the-art methods, including unsupervised word embedding-based approaches and lexicon alignment techniques using existing bilingual dictionaries. The experimental results demonstrate the competitive strength of the proposed method across all tested configurations, with consistent improvements in translation accuracy for domain-specific terms.

The digital transformation of political discourse has led to an explosion of user-generated content, particularly in the form of online political blogs. These platforms serve as vital hubs for democratic participation, enabling citizens to express opinions, initiate debates, and engage with a broad audience. At the heart of this interactive environment are blog posts and their subsequent comments, which together form a rich and dynamic source of data about public sentiment and political engagement. However, understanding the factors that drive a blog post to generate a particular set of comments—such as emotional tone, topic, authorship, or community norms—remains a formidable challenge. Traditional analyses often rely on manual coding or simplistic keyword-based approaches, which struggle to capture the nuanced nature of language and user behavior in such discourse. Recent advances in probabilistic topic models have demonstrated their utility for analyzing large-scale text collections by uncovering latent thematic structures. Among them, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) is widely used for modeling the topics present in a collection of documents. However, applying such models to online political blogs presents unique challenges. Unlike news articles or academic texts, blog posts are inherently personal, often authored by individuals rather than institutions, and are accompanied by a stream of user-generated comments that form an organic response to the content. These comments are not only reactive but also shaped by the social dynamics of the community, including levels of verbosity, polarization, and prior interactions among users. Modeling the generation of both blog posts and their comments requires extending traditional topic models to account for the interplay between content and context in this interactive medium. In this paper, we introduce a family of advanced topic models that extend the LDA paradigm to jointly capture the generation of blog posts and related comment threads. Our models account for key features of the data, such as the authorship patterns in blog posts, the thematic alignment between posts and comments, and the heterogeneity in user engagement that varies across different communities and topics. These models are trained to infer latent topics that are useful not only for interpreting the content of discussions but also for predicting which blog users will respond to a given post. We frame this as a novel comment prediction task, where the goal is to identify, based on a post’s topic and style, the subsets of users within the blog community who are most likely to engage.

Gender classification on social media and online user data is an important task in natural language processing with broad applications ranging from demographic analysis to personalized recommendation systems. Despite the significance of the task, one major challenge in gender classification is the lack of large-scale, reliable, and publicly available labeled datasets, particularly in multilingual and cross-platform scenarios. In contrast, large volumes of unlabeled user data are readily available, providing an opportunity to leverage semi-supervised learning approaches. These methods aim to harness information from both limited annotated data and abundant unlabeled data to improve classification accuracy. Traditional gender classification techniques mainly rely on textual features derived from user-generated content, such as user profiles, tweets, posts, or comments. Features such as word usage, n-grams, and stylistic markers have been shown to correlate with gender. However, textual features alone can often be ambiguous or insufficient, especially when the text content is sparse, lacks gender-specific cues, or is written in a gender-neutral style. To better model user gender, recent studies have started incorporating social network information into the classification pipeline. This includes connections such as friendship, followings, group memberships, and shared interests, which can provide additional signals for gender inference, especially when combined with textual features. Inspired by the strong correlation between gender and user interaction patterns, we propose a factor graph-based semi-supervised approach for gender classification that jointly models textual and social information. Specifically, we focus on a particular type of indirect link, termed "same-interest" links, which reflect connections between users who share common topics or themes in their online behavior. Such links, derived from shared content preferences or overlapping activities, are expected to carry implicit gender signals and therefore can be used as an auxiliary source of information to enhance classification performance. Our model, called the Textual and Social Factor Graph (TSFG), is a probabilistic graphical model that integrates both textual features and the structure of the social network. The textual features are modeled using standard text classification components, while the social links are treated as relational constraints. These constraints capture the idea that users who share similar interests are more likely to belong to the same gender. By combining these components within a unified framework, TSFG enables efficient inference that jointly considers both sources of information during the learning process. The inference procedure is carried out with a semi-supervised learning strategy based on label propagation and expectation maximization techniques.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive improvements in sentiment classification tasks. Traditional models for sentiment analysis primarily rely on the text content of reviews or documents to predict sentiment scores or labels, often overlooking the rich contextual information associated with users and products. However, reviews are not just texts—they are contextualized opinions shaped by the writing styles, biases, and expression nuances of individual users, as well as the specific characteristics and reputation of the products being reviewed. Incorporating this contextual information can significantly enhance sentiment analysis, especially in scenarios where review data is noisy or sparse. This is particularly relevant for cold-start users and products, whose limited number of reviews makes it difficult to build robust user or product representations using conventional methods. Cold-start users are those who have written only a few reviews, and cold-start products are those with very limited historical feedback. Most traditional sentiment classification models are not specifically designed to handle the cold-start problem and may suffer from performance degradation in such scenarios. The lack of historical reviews for these entities limits the ability to construct accurate and representative features, leading to poor generalization and unreliable sentiment predictions. Thus, addressing the cold-start issue is crucial for improving the robustness and scalability of sentiment analysis systems, particularly in real-world scenarios with large and dynamic user and product bases. In response to this challenge, we propose the   Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC)   – a novel framework that incorporates user and product information into the sentiment classification process while explicitly addressing the cold-start problem. Our method introduces a dual-module architecture consisting of (1) a fast word encoder for generating contextualized word embeddings and (2) a Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA) mechanism that adaptively integrates user and product information into the classification process. The word encoder captures both short- and long-range contextual dependencies in the review text, while the CSAA module dynamically adjusts the attention weights depending on the availability of user and product information. To address the cold-start problem, HCSC introduces  shared vectors  derived from similar users or products. These shared vectors act as proxies when a specific user or product has insufficient review data to infer reliable features. The mechanism of switching between original (user/product-specific) vectors and shared ones is governed by a   frequency-guided selective gate vector  , which determines whether the cold-start signal should be activated based on the sparsity level of the source.

Minimum error rate training (MERT) has emerged as a pivotal methodology in optimizing NLP systems, particularly in domains such as machine translation and speech recognition. Its objective is to train system parameters by directly minimizing a task-specific error rate, such as the BLEU score or word error rate, using a small set of reference-human parallel sentences. This empirical risk minimization approach often yields substantial gains in performance over traditional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) due to its direct alignment with the task's ultimate evaluation metrics. Despite its efficacy, MERT faces significant challenges, primarily due to the complex and non-convex nature of the evaluation functions it seeks to optimize. These functions can have multiple local optima, leading to suboptimal parameter settings and unstable training behavior when using heuristic search strategies like the Och algorithm, which relies on local gradient-based updates and random perturbations. This paper presents   LP-MERT  , an innovative and exact search algorithm for MERT that guarantees global optimality by reducing the optimization problem to a series of linear programming (LP) operations. Traditional MERT methods often rely on local, greedy, or sampling-based strategies that may fail to reach the true minimum over the vast, non-smooth error surface. Our approach instead formulates the minimum error rate training problem as a constrained linear optimization problem over a finite-dimensional parameter space, where the search is conducted exhaustively but efficiently. By leveraging the power of linear programming, LP-MERT ensures that the best possible model is selected within the scope of the provided N-best lists for a set of S input sentences. We begin by modeling the training process as a linear problem, where the system score is expressed as a linear combination of features derived from the N-best hypotheses generated for each input sentence. The central idea is to combine all candidate hypotheses in a way that globally minimizes the evaluation function while fulfilling the constraints imposed by the N-best lists. The key advantage of this approach is that it is polynomial in the number of hypotheses (N) and the size of the feature space, making it suitable for problems with moderate-size feature spaces. However, the computational complexity grows exponentially with the number of input sentences (S), which limits its scalability for very large datasets. We address this limitation through two major extensions: 1) a selective sampling strategy to focus the search on promising regions of the parameter space, and 2) a beam-search variant of LP-MERT that reduces the computational load without sacrificing too much accuracy.

The dynamic and ever-growing nature of social media platforms like Twitter presents both challenges and opportunities for researchers and practitioners in the domain of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval. Twitter, in particular, hosts an unprecedented volume of real-time content, often reflecting current events, public sentiment, and trending topics. The ability to efficiently summarize and analyze such content is crucial, especially in the context of monitoring public discourse, breaking news events, and social trends. A widely adopted approach to this task is the extraction and ranking of keyphrases, which serve as concise and informative summaries of the salient topics present in a given dataset of tweets or social media posts. Among the various methods for keyphrase extraction, topical keyphrase extraction has emerged as a particularly powerful technique for summarization of social media content. Unlike traditional keyphrase extraction techniques that focus on specific domains or generic language, topical keyphrase extraction aims to identify the most relevant and representative terms within a given topic cluster or event. This task is especially challenging in the context of Twitter, where the microblogging format limits the verbosity of discourse and hides important contextual cues typically used in longer textual genres. Additionally, the language on Twitter is often informal, contains slang, and is prone to ambiguity, making the application of standard NLP tools and approaches less effective. To address these challenges, we propose a novel two-stage method for topical keyphrase extraction from Twitter. Our approach first employs a context-sensitive version of the PageRank algorithm, which is adapted to model the interconnected web of terms within a particular topic or event. By considering the co-occurrence patterns of terms across tweets, we are able to infer a network structure where the keyphrases are treated as nodes and their semantic and contextual relationships as edges. This allows our method to prioritize not only frequent keyphrases, but also those with high structural prominence within the topic network. The second stage of our method introduces a probabilistic scoring function that combines both relevance and interestingness of the candidate keyphrases. Relevance measures how strongly a keyphrase is associated with the target topic, while interestingness captures the surprising or novel nature of the phrase within the broader context of Twitter discourse. This dual-scoring mechanism ensures that the extracted keyphrases are both representative of the topic and distinctive enough to draw attention or provide value in tasks such as news summarization or topic modeling.

Language acquisition is a complex and multifaceted process in which children develop an understanding of multiple levels of linguistic structure, such as phonology, morphology, and syntax, in parallel. Despite the observational evidence of this multiplicity, many theoretical and computational models of language acquisition have traditionally focused on a single level at a time. These models often implicitly assume a sequential learning process, where children first master one level (e.g., phonology) before progressing to a more abstract level (e.g., syntax). However, recent empirical studies in child language acquisition suggest that linguistic competence is developed in an integrated and coordinated manner from early stages. This raises the question of whether simulating a joint learning process of multiple linguistic levels—specifically, morphology and syntax—can offer a more accurate and insightful model of how language is learned, especially in the rich and noisy input of child-directed speech. This paper explores the utility of joint morphological and syntactic learning from child-directed speech by developing and evaluating a model that simultaneously induces morphological segmentations and syntactic categories for utterances in two typologically different languages: English, which is morphologically simpler, and Spanish, which is more morphologically complex. By combining two established computational models—one designed for morphological segmentation and the other for syntactic categorization—we aim to assess whether the interaction between these tasks can yield improvements in performance over existing task-specific models. The model is evaluated on datasets of child-directed speech, focusing on the naturalistic and often ungrammatical input faced by infants as they acquire their first language. Previous studies in computational linguistics have demonstrated the value of joint learning in various domains, including phonological and syntactic processing, and semantic parsing. In the context of child language acquisition, however, the potential of integrating multiple components remains underexplored. This paper provides a novel contribution by testing the hypothesis that a joint model can leverage the interdependencies between morphology and syntax during learning. In English, where morphological cues are sparse, the joint model achieves improved morphological segmentation. In Spanish, conversely, the joint model enhances syntactic categorization. These results not only validate the efficacy of a joint learning framework but also highlight the influence of typological properties on the learning dynamics. As such, this work contributes to both cognitive science and computational modeling by demonstrating how the integration of multiple linguistic levels can be beneficial in modeling language acquisition, particularly in ecologically valid settings such as early child-directed speech.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify expressions within a text that refer to the same real-world entity. The ability to correctly resolve coreference links is crucial for downstream applications such as information extraction, summarization, machine translation, and question answering, where a coherent understanding of entity mentions across sentences is essential. Despite decades of research, coreference resolution remains a challenging problem due to the ambiguities and complex linguistic structures that often arise in natural language texts. A large body of prior research on coreference resolution typically frames the task as a sequence of two-class classification problems: during the processing of the input text, the system needs to determine whether a given mention links back to a previously resolved antecedent or marks the introduction of a new entity. Conventional machine learning approaches for coreference resolution optimize training objectives by minimizing the classification error on training instances, commonly using loss functions such as logistic loss or hinge loss for binary classification tasks. However, such formulations often fail to directly optimize the final task objectives — in coreference resolution, this typically involves maximizing evaluation metrics such as the MUC score, B3, or CEAF, which quantify the accuracy of the coreference chains in a system's output. This discrepancy between the training objective and the evaluation metric can lead to suboptimal performance on standard benchmarks, even when a model shows strong performance in individual classification decisions. Recent work has demonstrated that evaluation metrics, such as the MUC (Message Understanding Conference) metric and the B-CUBED (based on the harmonic mean of precision and recall for mentions), are not aligned with the simple minimization of error rates. Instead, they assess global configurations of the coreference chains and are more sensitive to the interplay of many decisions across the entire document. To address this problem, we propose a novel training strategy for coreference resolution that aligns the training objective with the evaluation metric by maximizing the score of the target metric directly during training. Specifically, our framework introduces two key components: 1)   instance weighting   to assign higher importance to coreference decisions that have a larger impact on the overall metric score, and 2)   beam search-based inference   to jointly optimize the metric score across all mentions in a document. By incorporating domain-specific knowledge about the evaluation metric during training, the model learns to optimize not only for local decisions but for overall coherence and correctness of the entire set of coreference links.

The human ability to process spoken or written language is remarkable in its speed and efficiency, particularly when it comes to integrating information across utterances to update and maintain a coherent mental representation of the discourse. This process is guided by a combination of syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic knowledge, as well as probabilistic expectations derived from context. In recent years, computational models of human sentence processing have increasingly focused on   predictive processing  —the idea that language comprehension is driven by the brain's ability to predict upcoming information based on prior knowledge and constraints. One key theoretical framework that underpins this perspective is the concept of   surprisal  , an information-theoretic measure that quantifies the degree of unexpectedness of a linguistic element given the current context. Surprisal has been shown to correspond closely with human processing effort, as measured by eye movements, fixation times, and other psycholinguistic and neurological metrics. The computational modeling of surprisal traditionally relies on   inference mechanisms  —probabilistic models that generate expectations about upcoming inputs based on the structural, semantic, and distributional properties of language. A central challenge in this domain is building models that can account for both the   local syntactic structure   and   long-distance discourse dependencies  , as these are critical for accurately predicting and resolving co-reference relations in complex utterances. While syntactic models such as probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) and, more recently, models based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) have offered useful frameworks for syntactic prediction, they often fail to capture the nuanced ways in which discourse structures influence language comprehension and prediction. In this paper, we present a novel computational model of   discourse-based predictions   in human sentence processing. Our model integrates two core components: a   Hidden Markov Model (HMM) noun phrase chunker  , which incrementally parses and models syntactic structure during real-time processing, and a   co-reference classifier  , which resolves coreferential links between nominals and prior discourse entities. Both models are trained to be   fully incremental and generative  , enabling them to assign probabilities to lexical elements based on their syntactic and discourse context. This compositional architecture allows us to compute   surprisal as the negative log probability   of a predicted word or phrase, based on both syntactic and co-referential constraints. We hypothesize that incorporating co-reference information into the prediction mechanism significantly improves the model's capacity to simulate real human processing dynamics, as it enables the system to maintain a coherent, context-sensitive representation of the emerging discourse.

Recent advancements in machine translation (MT) have largely focused on formal domains such as news articles or legal documents, where sentences are structured and context is relatively stable. However, the increasing demand for translating informal, naturalistic, and conversational texts—such as dialogues, social media, and chat—presents unique challenges that traditional MT approaches struggle to address. Dialogues, in particular, are characterized by a diverse set of linguistic features, including dialogue acts (e.g., questions, assertions, requests), speaker identity, gender, and varying levels of formality or register. These elements affect the structure, content, and style of the language, making translation not only a matter of syntactic and semantic accuracy but also of appropriateness and fluency in a conversational context. Despite the ubiquity of dialogues in media and communication, research on their translation, especially from the perspective of statistical machine translation (SMT), has been limited. Most studies in MT assume a document-centric, formal, and monolexical approach, with little regard for the conversational nuances that play a significant role in day-to-day language. This paper addresses this gap by directly exploring the effect of four conversational aspects—dialogue acts, speaker identity, gender, and register—on the quality of machine-translated dialogues. We focus on fictional dialogues, drawn from multilingual film subtitles, which provide a rich and standardized source of dialogue examples, and we take the first step toward building a comprehensive framework for analyzing and improving MT quality in the conversational domain. A central contribution of our work is the creation and public release of a novel, multilingual corpus of movie dialogues annotated with the four dialogue-specific aspects mentioned above. This is a valuable resource for the MT community, as it allows for the systematic evaluation of how dialogue-specific features influence translation accuracy and fluency. To measure the impact of these aspects on translation quality, we perform an extensive evaluation using the BLEU metric and find that BLEU score fluctuations between categories are often significantly larger than expected by chance. This suggests that certain conversational features are more challenging for SMT systems to handle accurately, thus motivating domain-specific adaptation strategies. Based on our findings, we hypothesize that SMT systems can be substantially improved by tailoring them to the specific characteristics of dialogues, such as adapting models based on dialogue acts and text register. This adaptation leads to a measurable gain in translation quality, particularly in domains where conversational patterns are prevalent.

Recent advancements in statistical machine translation (MT) have emphasized the integration of syntactic information to enhance the fluency and grammaticality of generated text. Traditional phrase-based MT systems often rely heavily on lexical and phrase-level statistics extracted from aligned bilingual corpora, with limited incorporation of syntactic structures. While such systems demonstrate remarkable performance, they can struggle with long-range dependencies, word order reconstruction, and generating grammatically diverse outputs—especially in languages with complex or free word order (Nivre et al., 2006; Hajič and van Genabith, 2005). Dependency parsing has emerged as a promising method for capturing syntactic information due to its robustness, simplicity, and ease of integration into the MT decoding framework. A major bottleneck in leveraging dependency structures, however, has been computational complexity. Cubic-time algorithms for dependency parsing, such as the Eisner algorithm and its variants (Kuhlmann et al., 2003), are computationally expensive and ill-suited for real-time or large-scale MT systems. This has historically limited their practical adoption, even though they provide high-precision syntactic analyses. The development of polynomial-time dependency parsing—particularly quadratic-time methods—offers a way forward. In a groundbreaking insight, McDonald and colleagues (2005b) recast dependency parsing as a maximum spanning tree (MST) problem, leveraging graph-based algorithms with a quadratic time complexity, making the approach both theoretically elegant and computationally feasible. This has sparked renewed interest in integrating syntactic parsing into language modeling and translation frameworks, particularly for tasks where grammaticality and structural complexity are critical. This paper explores the integration of quadratic-time MST-based dependency parsing into the phrase-based MT decoding pipeline as a means of enhancing syntactic fluency. We implement a quadratic-time dependency parser adapted from the MST framework (McDonald et al., 2005b) and integrate it as part of the language model scoring process within a phrase-based decoder. The dependency parser is trained on monolingual corpora and deployed during decoding to penalize syntactically unlikely translations. Our experiments are evaluated on the widely used NIST Chinese-English translation benchmarks, a domain characterized by high syntactic variability and complex semantic alignment challenges. Our results demonstrate that the inclusion of dependency language models based on MST parsing yields consistent improvements in translation quality. Specifically, we observe a 0.92% reduction in Translation Error Rate (TER) and a 0.45% increase in BLEU score compared to a strong phrase-based baseline. Additionally, we conduct an error analysis to investigate the effect of syntactic roles in translation fluency and alignment accuracy.

Transliteration — the process of mapping a source language surface form to a target language orthographic representation — plays a crucial role in cross-lingual and multilingual natural language processing applications, particularly in scenarios where words or names from non-target languages appear in the input. Accurate transliteration is essential in tasks such as machine translation (MT), cross-lingual information retrieval, and named entity recognition. While phonetic and rule-based transliteration approaches have been widely studied, recent work has increasingly focused on discriminative, data-driven models due to their improved generalization capabilities and flexibility in capturing relevant source-target mappings. Early discriminative transliteration models, such as those based on conditional random fields (CRFs) and maximum entropy Markov models (MEMMs), typically model transliteration at the character level, using discriminative features to condition the decoding process on source characters and their contextual interactions. A notable advancement was introduced by Sherif and Kondrak (2007b), who proposed a substring-based decoder that enables more compact representations and modeling of recurring character patterns. This is particularly useful for capturing morphological or orthographic structure that may not be directly accessible through character-level alignments. In this paper, we build upon the work of Sherif and Kondrak (2007b) by introducing a   discriminative substring decoder   that further improves transliteration accuracy by leveraging additional resources: specifically, a list of known target-language words. By incorporating this external knowledge during decoding, the model can bias its predictions toward valid or likely transliterations, particularly for rare or out-of-vocabulary source forms. Our proposed system achieves a   28.5% relative improvement in transliteration accuracy   on the Japanese katakana-to-English task over the state-of-the-art model, demonstrating the significant boost in performance enabled by this enhancement. Additionally, the paper presents a controlled study comparing two feature paradigms for discriminative training:   indicator features   and   hybrid generative features  . While indicator features are rich and directly discriminative, expressing precise conditions about the input and context, hybrid generative features introduce elements from traditional generative models, such as source-to-target character or substring probabilities. Surprisingly, we find that the   hybrid generative approach outperforms the purely discriminative counterpart  , despite the reduced access to complex source context features. This result underscores the potential value of incorporating goenvironmental cues from generative mechanisms even in a discriminative pipeline. Finally, we evaluate the utility of our improved transliteration system in the context of machine translation. We find that substituting fluently machine-transliterated strings into MT outputs leads to a measurable   0.5-point improvement on a 4-point human judgment scale  , indicating that high-quality transliteration significantly enhances the fluency and naturalness of cross-lingual output.

Phrase reordering is a fundamental challenge in statistical machine translation (SMT), especially in hierarchical phrase-based (HPB) systems, which extend phrase-based translation by allowing tree-like structures that more accurately depict syntactic dependencies. While HPB systems are powerful in capturing both local and long-distance reordering phenomena through hierarchical rules, the reordering decisions they make are typically based solely on the observed linguistic patterns in phrase rules and lack explicit modeling of contextual information. This deficiency can lead to suboptimal reordering choices, particularly in contexts where the correct ordering depends on factors beyond local syntactic structure or phrase alignment. Phrase reordering in SMT has traditionally relied on pre-defined reordering models or heuristic rule-based strategies, which often fail to account for the rich and complex contextual cues present in natural language. For example, in Chinese-to-English translation, specific reordering patterns such as rightward or leftward shifts and bubble features are commonly modeled. However, in many cases, the appropriate reordering must consider surrounding linguistic structure, functional words, positional information, and other features that are not explicitly captured in the phrase rule ordering component of the model. This paper proposes a context-dependent phrase reordering approach that addresses this limitation by incorporating a maximum entropy (MaxEnt) model into the decoding process of an HPB system. Our approach explicitly models reordering decisions using a wide range of contextual features, such as the position of the source phrases, the surrounding neighboring phrases, and the lengths and positions of the aligned target segments. We categorize translation rules into different reordering patterns and construct a MaxEnt model for each pattern, allowing the decoder to dynamically select the most appropriate reordering strategy given the current context. The features are extracted during decoding and used to train the MaxEnt model on annotated data, enabling the system to learn context-sensitive reordering preferences. The model is seamlessly integrated into the standard hierarchical phrase-based framework, enhancing the translation process without requiring significant changes to the underlying architecture. We conduct experiments on large-scale Chinese-to-English translation tasks using standard benchmark datasets. Our results show that the proposed method achieves significant improvements over the baseline HPB system. Specifically, the BLEU score (case-insensitive) is improved by 1.2 to 2.1 absolute points, confirming the effectiveness of contextual modeling in phrase reordering. These improvements indicate that the MaxEnt model's ability to incorporate rich contextual information leads to more accurate and linguistically plausible reordering decisions.

Keyphrase extraction is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), relevant for applications such as document indexing, information retrieval, and summarization. The extracted keyphrases often serve as compact and representative summaries of the content of a document and are typically validated against a set of reference keyphrases using evaluation metrics. However, standard evaluation metrics for keyphrase extraction, such as precision, recall, and F1, are based on exact matching of n-grams, which limits their ability to account for near-misses where component words are semantically similar or syntactically related to the reference keyphrases. Such cases are common in the evaluation of keyphrases, especially when the extracted phrases differ only slightly from references, either through synonyms, reordering of words, or minor syntactic variations. These near-misses are left unaccounted for by traditional metrics, leading to underestimation of system performance in evaluative studies. In an effort to address this limitation, several evaluation metrics originally developed for tasks such as machine translation and text summarization have been adapted for use in keyphrase extraction, with the aim of capturing the nuances of partial overlaps and semantic relatedness between extracted and reference keyphrases. Metrics such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Liu et al., 2006), and ROUGE (Lin, 2004) compute similarity based on overlapping n-grams or paraphrastic relations and are increasingly used as alternatives to or supplements for traditional exact match metrics. Additionally, R-precision (Pereira and Tegmark, 2002), a less commonly used metric in the context of keyphrase extraction, has also been adapted to assess the correlation between the best keyphrases ranked by a system and those annotated by human evaluators. In this paper, we present an empirical study evaluating the feasibility and effectiveness of various n-gram-based evaluation metrics for keyphrase extraction, with a particular focus on whether these metrics can adequately capture near-misses and provide a more comprehensive and linguistically informed evaluation. Our experiments involve measuring the correlation between automatic evaluation scores and human annotations across multiple datasets. We find that R-precision consistently achieves the highest correlation with human judgment, suggesting that a ranking-based approach to evaluation may offer an advantage over standard set-based metrics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the degree of semantic similarity between partially matched components of extracted and reference keyphrases is not uniform and is, in fact, influenced by the position of the matched words within the phrases. This indicates that the effectiveness of partial match evaluation metrics may depend on syntactic and positional factors, and that future evaluation frameworks should take into account the grammatical roles and coherence of component terms.

Document-level sentiment analysis is a crucial task in natural language processing, particularly in understanding how people or entities interact and express opinions toward one another in text. Traditional sentiment analysis systems often focus on sentence-level or aspect-level sentiment, where the task is to classify the sentiment polarity of individual expressions or phrases. However, in many real-world scenarios — such as analyzing political discourse, news articles, or social media content — the goal is to infer  directed  sentiment at the document level, i.e., to determine who holds a positive or negative opinion toward whom, across all mentioned entities in the text. This task is particularly challenging because it requires capturing the complex interplay of sentiment, entity relationships, and contextual cues that exist beyond a single sentence. Previous work on document-level sentiment inference has typically focused on pairwise relationships where entities co-occur in the same sentence or sentence fragment. While this approach can capture some inter-entity sentiment, it is limited in its ability to infer sentiments between entities mentioned in different parts of the document or to reason about transitive or indirect relationships. Additionally, such methods often ignore higher-level, theory-driven constraints that can help prune inconsistent hypotheses and encourage more coherent global inferences. In this work, we address these limitations by presenting a novel approach to document-level sentiment inference that jointly models three key contexts: (1)   sentence- and discourse-level sentiment cues  , (2)   factual evidence about entity factions  , and (3)   global constraints grounded in social science theories   such as homophily (the tendency for similar entities to have aligned sentiment), social balance, and reciprocity (the mutual alignment of sentiment between two entities). These components are combined within an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) framework, allowing for joint and structured inference over all entity pairs in the document. Our framework enables the model to consider how sentiment signals propagate through the text, the relationships between different groups or factions (e.g., political parties, corporate entities), and the theoretical expectations of social structures. For example, if two individuals are known to be part of the same faction (e.g., based on explicit factual data), the model can infer that their alignment in sentiment is more likely, helping reduce noise and increase consistency in predictions. Similarly, when applied to professional or organizational entities, such as CEOs and the companies they lead, the model can reason that these entities are expected to share a similar stance or sentiment toward their stakeholders or competitors.

Parsing a sentence into a dependency structure is a fundamental task in natural language processing, essential for downstream applications such as semantic role labeling, syntactic simplification, and machine translation. Dependency parsing, in particular, seeks to represent grammatical relations as directed edges between word tokens, with a single root node as the syntactic center of the sentence. While projective dependency structures, where all the edges can be drawn without crossing, are well-studied and amenable to efficient algorithms, many languages exhibit non-projective structures, where crossing dependencies are necessary to represent accurate syntactic relations. Non-projective parsing thus poses a greater algorithmic challenge but is crucial for processing morphologically rich or syntactically flexible languages like Czech, Welsh, or the Romance languages. Transition-based parsing has emerged as an efficient and effective approach for projective dependency parsing. It employs a stack-based formalism, applying a series of push and pop operations guided by features extracted from the current state of the parser. The system incrementally constructs the structure and has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance, thanks to its ability to integrate rich contextual features and be trained using discriminative methods like perceptrons or neural networks. However, adapting transition-based parsing to non-projective scenarios remains a challenge. Extensions to non-projective settings often involve more complex state representations and higher computational costs, while maintaining both accuracy and efficiency. One common strategy for handling non-projectivity is to split the parsing process into multiple stages, each addressing a specific set of grammatical dependencies. This modular approach allows the parser to leverage specialized knowledge for different types of arcs in the dependency graph, which can also improve error isolation and interpretability. In this paper, we present a novel transition-based system for non-projective dependency parsing that operates in three distinct steps. The key insight is to decompose the parsing task into components: the first step applies a classical projective transition-based parser to handle all projective dependencies, while the second and third steps separately handle non-projective leftward and rightward dependencies. This multi-step processing affords the ability to leverage existing high-performing techniques for individual dependency types while allowing for optimization through dedicated classification heads. The novelty of our approach lies in the decomposition of non-projective parsing into a sequence of linear-time processes: the first step uses the well-established arc-eager algorithm for projective parsing; the second predicts leftward non-projective arcs; the third predicts rightward non-projective arcs.

Ontologies play a critical role in representing structured semantic knowledge, enabling a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as information retrieval, text classification, and word-sense disambiguation (WSD). These hierarchical systems are typically designed based on human-encoded semantics, and their success in downstream NLP tasks relies heavily on how well they model the lexical and conceptual relationships inherent in the language of the target domain. However, despite their formal structure and semantic richness, ontologies often fail to fully align with the dynamic and nuanced usage patterns observed in natural language. This misalignment can result in diminished performance when ontologies are utilized for NLP tasks not originally intended to benefit from them, such as biomedical WSD, where the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) is one of the most commonly employed ontologies. In this paper, we present a novel approach for evaluating the quality and relevance of ontologies in the context of specific NLP tasks by leveraging the mechanism of spreading activation, a well-established technique in cognitive science for simulating semantic similarity and propagation of knowledge through interconnected networks. Our method provides a principled way to assess how effectively an ontology can serve as a knowledge base for a given domain, by quantifying the distributions of activation spread across both the instances and relationships of the ontology when applied to domain-specific textual data. Unlike traditional ontology metrics—which often rely purely on structural features or lexical properties—isolated from the linguistic context in which these ontologies are used—our activation-based model offers domain-sensitive evaluations and can highlight regions of the ontology that may be biased, underrepresented, or misaligned with target linguistic phenomena. Building upon this evaluation strategy, we further demonstrate how the insights derived can be used to improve the ontology's utility for NLP tasks through automated optimization of its graph structure. Specifically, we apply our method to the UMLS ontology in the domain of biomedical NLP, where WSD accuracy is crucial for interpreting the diverse and context-sensitive meanings of technical and clinical terms. By simulating spreading activation within domain text, we identify areas of the ontology that contribute positively or negatively to WSD performance. Using these insights, we refine the ontology's structure and representation, incorporating a fall-back mechanism based on word-sense probability to address ambiguous cases. The resulting system significantly outperforms existing graph-based methods for WSD, achieving an accuracy of 0.82.

The study of semantic representation has long occupied a central place in cognitive science and computational linguistics. The traditional approach in natural language processing has largely focused on modeling word meaning using solely the linguistic environment—such as co-occurrence counts, distributional statistics, and syntactic patterns—under the implicit assumption that language is self-sufficient for capturing meaning. This abstraction has led to the development of powerful models such as distributional semantic models and their neural extensions (e.g., word embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe), which excel at capturing semantic similarities, analogies, and relations based purely on textual data. However, mounting evidence from cognitive science suggests that language is deeply grounded in human sensory and motor experiences—what is often termed the “embodied” or “perceptual symbol system” view of meaning (Barsalou, 1999, 2008). According to this perspective, the comprehension and production of language are inextricably linked to perceptual, bodily, and action-based representations. Despite this compelling theory, the integration of perceptual and sensorimotor data into semantic models remains underexplored, particularly in tasks that directly involve modeling word meaning. In this paper, we address the question of whether and how combining both linguistic and perceptual information can enhance semantic representations. We investigate a range of models that integrate these data modalities using different architectural strategies. Linguistic data is modeled via large, naturally occurring corpora, capturing the contextual distribution of words in language. Perceptual data, on the other hand, is represented using feature norms, which are derived from human judgments about which perceptual and sensorimotor attributes are central to a word’s meaning (e.g., color, texture, or interactivity). For instance, the word  apple  may be strongly associated with attributes such as  round ,  sweet , or  edible , while  hammer  might evoke  heavy ,  hard , and  tool-like . These feature-based representations serve as proxies for the sensorimotor experiences associated with processing words. Crucially, we explore different integration mechanisms for merging the information from these two sources. We compare two primary approaches: (1) direct concatenation of linguistic and perceptual vectors, and (2) latent space alignment techniques that seek a shared manifold over the modalities. Our results reveal that the latter, where the shared latent space implicitly models the co-variation between linguistic input and perceptual features, leads to semantic representations that are more aligned with human judgments of word similarity. These findings suggest that the most effective models of word meaning may be those that leverage both modalities in a way that reflects the intrinsic co-ordination between language, perception, and action—an outcome that is more nuanced and cognitively plausible than the string concatenation of independent representations.

Parameter tuning is a critical step in the development of statistical machine translation (SMT) systems. The performance of a translation system is heavily dependent on the accurate setting of its parameters, which influence aspects such as phrase selection, language model weights, and syntactic constraints. Despite the importance of this stage, traditional tuning methods face significant challenges in scalability and computational efficiency, especially when dealing with systems with an increasing number of features. One of the most widely known and used methods is Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) introduced by Och (2003). MERT is a gradient descent-based optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts the parameters of the translation model to minimize a specific error metric, typically the BLEU score. However, while MERT works effectively for models with a relatively small number of parameters, it becomes computationally prohibitive when applied to systems with hundreds or even thousands of features. This is due to the exponential increase in the number of parameter combinations that must be evaluated during the optimization process. To address these limitations, researchers have explored alternative methods based on the MIRA (Margin Infused Relaxed Algorithm) framework (Crammer and Singer, 2003). MIRA offers a structured approach to parameter optimization by using a margin-based ranking framework to update feature weights. However, despite its appealing theoretical properties, MIRA-based approaches have been criticized for being complex to implement and requiring the development of specialized optimization code, which limits their practical applicability and adoption in the community. In this paper, we propose a parameter tuning method that addresses the shortcomings of both MERT and MIRA by viewing the optimization problem in a pairwise ranking framework. Drawing on the work of Herbrich et al. (1999), we formulate tuning as a ranking problem, where the objective is to rank better translations higher than their suboptimal counterparts. Our pairwise ranking optimization (PRO) method is built on the assumption that, given a diverse set of candidate translations generated by the decoding process, we can learn to assign weights to features that effectively distinguish between high-quality and low-quality translations. One of the key advantages of the PRO approach is its ability to scale gracefully with the number of features. Unlike MERT, which is constrained by the computational complexity of full-scale gradient optimization, PRO reduces the problem to a sequence of binary classification tasks, each of which can be efficiently solved using off-the-shelf linear binary classifier software such as SVM or logistic regression.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, primarily due to the adoption of deep learning techniques that enable end-to-end modeling of translation tasks. NMT systems are typically trained using a word-level loss function under the teacher forcing algorithm, where each word in the target sentence is predicted one at a time based on the ground-truth previous words. While teacher forcing is effective for training and simplifies gradient computation, it inherently evaluates the translation at the level of individual words rather than full sentences, which can result in suboptimal translation quality. Moreover, this method introduces the problem of exposure bias during training, where the model is exposed to correct previous outputs during training but must handle its own potentially error-prone predictions during inference, leading to error propagation and poor generalization. In contrast, sequence-level training approaches seek to address these limitations by directly optimizing the model using a loss function that considers the whole translated sentence. Reinforcement learning (RL) and maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) are prime examples of such methods, which aim to align the training objective more closely with the evaluation metric, such as BLEU score. Although RL-based methods can improve translation fluency and coherence, they suffer from high variance in gradient estimation due to the stochasticity involved in generating sequences and the complexity of the reward function. This results in unstable training and often suboptimal performance. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new sequence-level training method based on probabilistic n-gram matching, which captures the distribution of n-grams at the level of the generated sentence. This approach avoids the reinforcement framework by defining a differentiable and tractable sequence-level loss function that incentivizes the model to favor the production of meaningful and fluent n-grams in the target language. Unlike word-level loss, the probabilistic n-gram loss evaluates how well the n-grams generated by the model align with those observed in the reference translations, thereby guiding the model to learn better sentence-level translation strategies. In addition to the sequence-level training, our method employs greedy search during both training and inference. This mimics the inference procedure more closely by using the model's own predictions as context for generating the next target word, unlike beam search which explores multiple paths simultaneously and can be computationally expensive. Greedy search with probabilistic n-gram matching helps mitigate the issue of exposure bias, as the model is consistently exposed to self-generated contexts throughout the training phase, thus maintaining better alignment between training and inference dynamics.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have spurred increasing interest in the acquisition and application of inference knowledge, such as entailment and paraphrase rules, often encoded over syntactic or semantic representations of linguistic expressions. Such rules are pivotal in various NLP tasks—including question answering, information retrieval, and semantic text simplification—as they allow systems to extend the reach of their reasoning capabilities by making inferences based on relationships between expressions. For instance, a rule might capture logical entailment by asserting that  “Alice smiles”  entails  “Alice is happy” , or a paraphrase rule might assert that  “He ran quickly”  is semantically equivalent to  “He sprinted” . The effectiveness of these rules is contingent not only on their content but also on how they are implemented during inference, especially when dealing with high-dimensional or large-scale syntactic knowledge bases. However, the computational and memory costs associated with inference over such rules can be formidable. Traditional methods often perform inference naively—iterating over all rules for a given input—and may not scale well to real-world knowledge bases, which typically contain vast numbers of rules. This is exacerbated by the need for inference over hierarchical or tree-structured syntactic representations, such as those derived from context-free grammars or dependency trees, where the application of inference rules must consider the overlapping and nested nature of the linguistic structures involved. Thus, designing efficient algorithms and compact representations for storing and processing entailment and paraphrase rules is an important and challenging problem. To address these limitations, we present a novel framework for scalable inference, which centers around a compact data structure called a   Compact Forest  . This structure effectively packs information from multiple syntactic representations and inference rules into a shared, hierarchical space, allowing for efficient traversal and inference through a unified mechanism. Our key insight is to preprocess and compress the syntactic dependencies and their associated inference rules into a single data representation that can be queried efficiently. The data structure is informed by a formal logical semantics for rule application, and we provide theoretical guarantees of its validity and correctness under the assumption of deterministic syntactic derivations. Moreover, we introduce an algorithm that operates on this compact representation, demonstrating how inference can be implemented in a highly scalable and memory-efficient manner. The algorithm avoids redundant calculations by explicitly tracking rule interactions during traversal and avoids full exploration of the rule space through careful prioritization informed by syntactic coverage.

Tokenization is a critical preprocessing step for any statistical machine translation (SMT) system. However, for languages like Chinese and Korean—where word boundaries are not explicitly marked—tokenization is inherently ambiguous, and this ambiguity poses a significant challenge to translation systems. Traditional approaches often rely on a fixed tokenization (1-best) or a lattice that encodes multiple tokenization possibilities. While lattices provide a more robust representation of tokenization ambiguity than a single best transcription, they still maintain a clear separation between tokenization and translation. In this paper, we introduce a new paradigm that aims to bridge the tokenization-translation divide by jointly decoding both the source-side tokenization and the target-side translation. This is particularly beneficial for morphologically rich and tokenization-ambiguous languages like Chinese and Korean, where traditional pipeline approaches are prone to compounding errors due to suboptimal intermediate representation decisions. Although the initial separation of tasks has dominated SMT pipelines, it is often at odds with the interleaving nature of linguistic processing in real-world scenarios. Sentence modeling involves syntactic, semantic, and phonological phenomena, and the resulting segmentation of a string into tokens is directly influenced by the syntactic role, semantic composition, and grammatical context of each unit. A tokenization that is optimal for the language model may not be the best for translation, and vice versa. This task-specific optimization introduces a dependency between the tokenization and translation stages that, when decoupled, can lead to suboptimal performance. By jointly modeling them within a unified framework, we can leverage the interdependencies between these two tasks in a way that improvements in one also benefit the other. We consider the input to the system as a sequence of atomic units (e.g., characters in Chinese and subwords in Korean), allowing for multiple syntactically and contextually plausible tokenizations. Given this input, the joint decoder searches over the space of possible tokenizations and translations simultaneously, integrating discriminative features derived from both tokenization and translation hypotheses. The joint model includes features for token boundary prediction, source-side language modeling, alignment patterns, and target-side language modeling. These features are scored using a log-linear model that assigns a weighted objective to the entire joint sequence of source tokens and target words. Empirically, we demonstrate that our joint decoder significantly outperforms various strong baselines, including those based on 1-best tokenizations and lattice-based tokenization alternatives. On the Chinese-to-English and Korean-to-Chinese translation tasks, our system achieves substantial improvements in BLEU scores, while also showing strong performance as a tokenizer when compared to standalone monolingual Chinese tokenizers.

Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) is an essential task in natural language understanding, aiming to identify the predicate-argument structure in a sentence, and assign each argument with a semantic role that captures its relationship with the predicate. Traditional SRL systems typically follow pipeline architectures, often built specifically for one semantic lexicon, like PropBank ( Palmer et al., 2005 ), which defines the   "doer" (agents), "done-to" (patients), and other roles   in a first-order event perspective; or NomBank   (Carreras and Marquez, 2005)  , which elevates the predicates to noun phrases and labels the predicates of nominalizations. While pipeline methods have achieved high performance, they often suffer from error propagation across successive stages and are not able to capture cross-instance interactions between the two disparate annotation schemes. Recently, integrated SRL systems that jointly model features extracted from   multiple semantic lexicons   have shown promising results. Such frameworks, often using   dependency-based parsing   with a rich feature space, aim to enable the system to benefit from the unique strengths of each ontology while maintaining consistent output. One such approach is   semantic dependency parsing   ( PD-Cx ), where syntactic and semantic dependencies are jointly modeled to build structured semantic role graphs. However, the feature-based complexity of these approaches often leads to high computational cost and suboptimal performance unless mitigated with effective   feature selection strategies  . This paper introduces a novel and efficient   integrated semantic dependency parsing approach   for   NomBank and PropBank   that unifies the two in a single labeling framework. Our system   1.   leverages advanced feature extraction techniques to incorporate   a wide range of linguistic and contextual features   into the model through   assistant argument labels  , which allow the model to consider context about both verbal and nominal predicates   2.   employs an efficient   large-scale feature selection algorithm  , where hierarchical filtering techniques are applied to identify   two optimal feature template sets  : one tailored to the   PropBank-style roles   and the other specifically toward   NomBank roles  . Through this process, the model retains high discriminative power while significantly reducing redundancy and noise from the feature space. We demonstrate that such an   integrated semantic dependency system   not only reduces modeling complexity but also improves overall consistency in role attachment and argument class discrimination. The experiments are conducted on the dataset from the   CoNLL-2008 shared task   — a real-world, large-scale evaluation dataset, known for its inclusion of both PropBank and NomBank annotations. The results indicate that our system achieves performance that is   comparable to the state-of-the-art pipeline SRL systems  , while operating within a unified model that reduces overfitting and eliminates error propagation.

The task of constructing concise and informative overviews from a set of news articles is a significant challenge in the field of natural language processing. While multi-document summarization has long been studied for generating compact summaries, these typically aim to extract representative content and condense redundant information to produce a topic-centric summary. However, the problem of assembling an   overview article  —a coherent, reader-friendly, and well-structured narrative that synthesizes all relevant aspects of a news event—requires a different set of strategies. This task, which we refer to as   news synthesis  , goes beyond simple redundancy reduction and focuses on organizing information in a way that provides a complete understanding of the event, enabling users to grasp who is involved, what happened, when and where, and why it is significant. The motivation for developing an automated overview synthesis system is driven by the exponential growth of online news content, particularly during major news events. While readers often look for a single source of summary to avoid sifting through multiple reports, news outlets tend to specialize in different facets or angles of the event. This fragmentation makes it difficult to obtain a comprehensive overview without manual effort. Automatically compiling such overviews can help news consumers and professionals, such as journalists and analysts, quickly gain a full picture of a developing news event. In this paper, we present a novel approach to constructing news overview articles by leveraging a task-specific news synthesis pipeline. Our method addresses the challenges of verbosity, redundancy, and inconsistency across news articles by incorporating the following components:   passage segmentation  ,   relevance ranking  ,   sentence selection  , and   content merging  . Our approach organizes the key elements of the event into a coherent narrative by identifying central entities, important temporal and spatial markers, and salient details while removing repetitive and irrelevant information. Furthermore, we ensure that the final output remains faithful to the original source news articles while conforming to the structural and linguistic norms of news writing. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments using the   Wikinews dataset  , a publicly available collection of multi-paragraph articles that serve as high-quality human-constructed overviews of real-world events. We compare our method with several established multi-document summarization techniques and demonstrate that our news synthesis approach outperforms them on standard automatic evaluation metrics, such as ROUGE and BLEU scores, as well as in a manual evaluation where human judges rate the overall quality, coherence, and usefulness of the generated overviews.

Idiom understanding remains a challenging task in natural language processing (NLP) due to the dual nature of idiomatic expressions — they often have non-compositional meanings that deviate from the literal interpretations of their constituent words. A core challenge in idiom processing is to distinguish between the figurative and literal usage of potentially idiomatic phrases in real-world contexts. This task, known as idiom token classification, is particularly important for downstream NLP applications such as machine translation, information extraction, and semantic role labeling, where correct interpretation of phrase usage can significantly impact downstream system performance. Several previous approaches to idiom token classification rely on rule-based methods or traditional machine learning techniques, leveraging hand-crafted lexical, syntactic, and discourse features to distinguish idiomatic from literal usages. More recently, deep learning models have been explored to better capture the contextual and semantic nuances of idiom usage. Despite their effectiveness, many of these approaches depend heavily on assembling accurate and rich contextual representations, often incorporated at the discourse or paragraph level. This introduces a reliance on external discourse models, which may not always be accurate, available, or domain-independent, especially in open-ended or domain-unseen text. In this work, we propose a novel approach to idiom token classification using sentential distributed semantics, specifically Skip-Thought Vectors (STVs), which are designed to encode rich semantic representations of sentences. Unlike traditional vector models such as word embeddings, which represent individual tokens, STVs represent entire sentences and capture the contextualized meaning of expressions within their use. This makes them particularly suitable for our task, where the classification decision must be grounded in the semantics of the surrounding context rather than the static meaning of words or phrases. We investigate the effectiveness of STVs as features for training classifiers that determine whether a given idiom token is used literally or figuratively. Our key hypothesis is that such sentence-level representations can encode sufficient contextual and semantic information to support accurate idiom classification without requiring explicit discourse-level modeling. The proposed models are trained to classify individual occurrences of idiom candidates within their sentence contexts, making them less susceptible to errors propagated by potentially inaccurate discourse models. We evaluate our approach on benchmark datasets for idiom token classification and demonstrate that models using Skip-Thought Vectors achieve competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art baselines. More importantly, our models do not require access to discourse-level information, reducing their dependency on the accuracy of contextual features that may vary across tasks, domains, or languages.

Automatic Text Scoring (ATS) systems have emerged as a powerful and efficient alternative to traditional human marking processes in educational and linguistic assessment. ATS enables the rapid, objective evaluation of large volumes of student-generated texts, particularly in standardized testing scenarios where consistency is paramount. While traditional ATS systems have primarily relied on hand-crafted features—such as syntactic complexity, lexical diversity, and fluency indicators—these approaches often require substantial domain expertise and are not inherently generalizable across different types of tasks or language varieties. In recent years, deep learning techniques have demonstrated significant success in capturing complex and high-level representations of text for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, enabling more robust and flexible models. This study introduces a fully automated ATS framework based on neural networks that eliminates the need for manual feature engineering by learning representations directly from raw text. Our approach employs Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to encode the sequential structure of text, capturing both the contextual and semantic dependencies that correlate with text quality. The key innovation of our model lies in its ability to simultaneously learn not only the overall score of a text but also the relative importance of lexical elements that influence that score. By iteratively adjusting word-level contributions during the learning process, the model implicitly identifies linguistic patterns and stylistic features that are crucial for evaluation. These representations are then aggregated over time and task to produce a predictive score at the sentence or document level. In addition to performance, our study emphasizes the interpretability of neural ATS models. Inspired by recent work in visualizing deep learning systems, we propose a novel method to highlight the regions of a text that are most discriminative in determining its final score. This interpretability component not only increases transparency—thereby fostering trust and acceptability among users—but also allows for feedback-driven improvements, enabling educators and researchers to understand the strengths and weaknesses of submitted texts from the model’s perspective.
