Recent advances have incorporated neural network-based models, such as Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) networks, to better capture long-range dependencies and contextual information. However, these models are often trained in a batch fashion, which is computationally expensive, particularly when working with high-dimensional feature spaces over large-scale datasets. To improve the efficiency of model training, this paper introduces a novel training method:   Frequency-Adaptive Learning Rates   for online gradient descent. Our method dynamically adjusts the learning rates of model parameters based on the frequency of feature appearances in the training data, allowing frequent features (typically more predictable or stable) to be learned quickly while allocating more learning updates to infrequent or informative features. This results in significantly faster convergence, even when dealing with high-dimensional features. We also introduce a new set of features for the joint modeling of word segmentation and new word detection. These include word-based features and   enhanced edge (label-transition)   features, which capture not only about individual word identities but also the syntactic and positional relations between adjacent segments. These high-dimensional features provide more detailed information for the learning model and lead to better performance. Despite the increased feature complexity, our frequency-adaptive training method ensures that the training remains efficient. Empirical results on standard benchmark datasets show that our proposed method not only achieves   higher or equal accuracy   when compared with state-of-the-art models but also reduces training time by   an order of magnitude  , making it more scalable and suitable for real-world applications. Furthermore, our training method is a   general-purpose optimization approach   that can go beyond the specific tasks of word segmentation and new word detection.

Semi-supervised text classification is a crucial task in natural language processing, especially in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or costly to obtain, but unlabeled data is abundant. The goal is to build accurate classifiers by combining a small set of labeled examples with a large pool of unlabeled data. This problem is particularly challenging in deep learning contexts due to the high model capacity of neural networks, which require substantial supervision to generalize well. Classic self-training and co-training approaches have demonstrated effectiveness but often lack mechanisms to systematically incorporate top-down modeling into the learning process, which is essential for maintaining consistency and preventing error propagation from noisy pseudo-labels. Deep learning models, on the other hand, thrive on supervised signals and struggle when exposed only to unlabeled data, hence the necessity for hybrid strategies that bridge the gap between traditional semi-supervised learning and deep architecture training. In this paper, we address the limitations of existing methods by introducing a   deep hybrid model   with a novel   bottom-up-top-down learning algorithm   for semi-supervised text classification. Our architecture integrates both a   generative model   for distribution estimation, to capture the underlying structure of the unlabeled data, and a   discriminative model   for classification, which takes advantage of the labeled examples. The key innovation lies in the fine-tuning process, which operates in an online learning setting. During each iteration of the training process, the model first performs a   bottom-up, generative pass   to assign pseudo-labels to unlabeled samples. These pseudo-labels are then used to modify the parameters of the classifier in a   top-down, discriminative update  . This two-stage fine-tuning approach effectively enforces joint consistency between the generative and discriminative components of the model, and it is designed to propagate supervisory signals in a hierarchical and interactive manner. The hybrid design is particularly well-suited to semi-supervised text classification because it simultaneously captures local linguistic patterns and global semantic structure, two key aspects of language modeling. By leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data within a unified computational framework, our method avoids the heuristic nature of many traditional semi-supervised approaches while still benefitting from their intuitive properties, such as incorporating indirect supervision through pseudo-labeling. We evaluate our model across multiple standard text classification benchmarks, using a wide range of supervised-unlabeled data splits to simulate varying levels of annotation effort. The results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning baselines and classical semi-supervised approaches, especially in low-label regimes where labeled data is extremely limited.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning have enabled the analysis of vast collections of textual data, especially in domains such as social media, news corpora, and scientific publications. Among these, topic modeling has emerged as a powerful technique for uncovering latent thematic structures in document corpora. Traditional topic modeling methods, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), require batch processing of the entire dataset and are not efficiently tailored for scenarios involving continuously arriving text documents. Such scenarios call for efficient online modeling techniques, which can incrementally update model parameters and scale effectively to handle massive and dynamic datasets. In response to these challenges, stochastic variational inference (SVI) has been introduced as a flexible and computationally efficient method for online topic modeling. SVI enables the use of approximate inference techniques to update model parameters in an online manner, making it an attractive solution for large-scale and real-time applications. Despite the efficiency of SVI, the performance of online topic modeling depends heavily on the optimization algorithm used. Among the most popular optimization algorithms for gradient-based methods is AdaGrad, which adapts the learning rate for each parameter based on the historical sum of squared gradients. AdaGrad has gained widespread adoption due to its ability to perform well on sparse data and its early stopping-like behavior by reducing learning rates for frequently updated parameters. However, this same feature becomes a drawback in the context of online topic modeling, where large gradient magnitudes are common. In such scenarios, AdaGrad's mechanism of accumulating squared gradients in the denominator of the learning rate results in excessively small learning rates very quickly. As a result, the model parameters fail to converge to their optimal values within a reasonable training period, leading to suboptimal topic representations and reduced model performance. This paper investigates the suitability of AdaGrad as an optimization algorithm in the context of online topic modeling with SVI. Our analysis reveals that the accumulation of large gradients in AdaGrad fails to account for the necessary learning dynamics in topic modeling tasks, thereby severely hindering convergence. In contrast to the general belief that adaptive learning rates are universally beneficial, we demonstrate that their effectiveness is highly context-dependent, and in the case of online topic modeling, AdaGrad's design leads to premature saturation of learning rates. The implications of our findings are significant: they underscore the importance of carefully selecting optimization algorithms when deploying topic modeling techniques on large-scale, streaming textual data.

The task of relation classification has proven to be an essential problem in natural language processing, with broad applications ranging from information extraction to semantic parsing and question answering. Its objective is to identify the semantic relationship between two entities mentioned in a text, a problem that requires robust modeling of both local and global textual features. In recent years, deep neural network architectures have emerged as a dominant paradigm for tackling this problem, demonstrating consistent improvements over traditional rule-based and shallow learning methods. Despite these successes, the research community has largely explored individual models on a limited number of datasets, typically focusing on a small subset of the available benchmarks and neglecting the influence of architectural choices across a wide range of data domains. This narrow focus makes it difficult to assess the generalizability, robustness, and adaptability of the models, as well as to establish a clearer understanding of what architectural components or linguistic features are most beneficial for relation classification across diverse tasks. The lack of broad exploration is especially concerning given the increasing variety of neural model designs and linguistic feature representations in continuous word representations (e.g., GloVe, BERT), attention mechanisms, and hierarchical recurrent and convolutional frameworks. These innovations introduce a complex design space with subtle, often unintuitive trade-offs between model capacity, training efficiency, and performance. To address this gap, we present a systematic evaluation of a wide array of neural relation classification architectures, all evaluated on six benchmark datasets – Mateo Ordonez, PDTB, TACRED, TACREV, SemEval-2010 Task8, and the WN18RR relational knowledge base – which collectively span different domains, document types, and linguistic phenomena. These datasets are particularly diverse in their characteristics, ranging from unlabeled discourse relation corpora in the case of PDTB to knowledge base-style triplets in WN18RR. Our contributions include (1) the largest empirical analysis of neural relation classification models to date, covering a wide array of linguistic features and architectural components; (2) the introduction of a novel neural model combining a  multi-channel  LSTM with a CNN (termed M-MASS: Multi-Channel LSTM + CNN for Relation Classification), which we propose as a flexible and performance-optimized solution for the task; and (3) actionable insights into architectural choices and their impact on performance and adaptability across different datasets and tasks. By performing a large-scale exploration, this work not only pushes the state-of-the-art on two of the benchmarks but also identifies key architectural trade-offs and persistent challenges in modeling complex, context-sensitive relations in natural language.

Recent advancements in knowledge-based question answering (KBQA) have led to remarkable progress in retrieving structured data from knowledge graphs (KGs) to answer natural language questions. Among the most widely adopted benchmark datasets are WebQuestions (Berant et al., 2013) and SimpleQuestions (Bordes et al., 2014), which primarily consist of factual questions that can be answered by a single relation in the underlying knowledge base. These datasets have played a pivotal role in the development and evaluation of KBQA systems. However, as questions in real-world scenarios often involve multiple constraints requiring the composition of several knowledge base relations, the simplicity of WebQuestions and SimpleQuestions limits their ability to capture the true complexity and diversity of the real-world question-answering (QA) task. The current generation of KBQA approaches often achieve impressive performance on these datasets, but their efficacy on more realistic and complex questions—those incorporating multiple constraints and requiring deep compositional reasoning—remains insufficiently evaluated and poorly understood. To bridge this gap and inspire future research on challenging, multi-constraint QA, we introduce   ComplexQuestions  , a novel benchmark dataset designed to evaluate KBQA systems on questions that require the integration of multiple knowledge base relations to arrive at the correct answer. The creation of   ComplexQuestions   is guided by the observation that many real-world questions involve a composition of constraints derived from interconnected facts within the knowledge graph, a requirement not adequately captured by existing datasets. By incorporating such nuanced scenarios,   ComplexQuestions   provides a more rigorous and realistic evaluation framework for KBQA systems, particularly those relying on deep semantic understanding and constraint satisfaction strategies. In addition to presenting the   ComplexQuestions   dataset, we also propose a systematic and effective   constraint-based KBQA approach   tailored for solving multi-constraint questions. This approach encodes question semantics as a logical expression involving multiple constraints from the knowledge base, which are then matched and resolved through hierarchical filtering and relational composition. By explicitly modeling the interplay between constraints, our method demonstrates robust generalization over both simple and complex question settings. Empirical evaluations on   WebQuestions  ,   SimpleQuestions  , and our newly proposed   ComplexQuestions   show that our method not only achieves performance on par with state-of-the-art models on the established benchmarks but also significantly outperforms existing approaches on the more challenging   ComplexQuestions   dataset. These results highlight the importance of incorporating complexity and constraint-based reasoning in the design of KBQA systems and underscore the value of   ComplexQuestions   as a critical addition to the KBQA research landscape.

The semantics of verbs is a central topic in linguistic theory, cognitive science, and natural language processing (NLP). Verbs not only encode grammatical properties, such as tense and argument structure, but also capture rich conceptual information about events and actions. A robust semantic representation of verbs is essential for modeling compositional meaning, supporting cross-linguistic comparison, and improving the performance of NLP systems such as parsers, machine translation engines, and semantic role labelers. VerbNet (VN), one of the most prominent resources for English verbs, provides a lexical hierarchy of verbs and their syntactic classes. However, despite its theoretical underpinnings and widespread use, its semantic predicates lack empirical validation. Traditionally, VerbNet defines the meanings of verbs using theoretical semantic features or semantic primitives, which are not directly grounded in observable behavior or perceptual experiences. Thus, while the current semantic representation is consistent and predictive in a formal sense, its validity in capturing how meaning is understood by human subjects remains an open question. The lack of empirical validation for semantic predicates in VerbNet limits the robustness of its applications in both computational and theoretical domains. One possible solution to this problem is to move toward an empirically grounded semantic decomposition—constructing semantic predicates that are not only theoretically coherent but also supported by human judgments. This paper introduces The VerbCorner Project, a research initiative that harnesses crowdsourcing methodologies to improve the empirical validation of the semantic predicates in VerbNet. The project aims to assess and refine the current semantic representations by incorporating human intuitions about the event structures verbs describe. The principles guiding the decomposition of verbs into semantic features are often abstract and not easily subject to direct verification. For instance, the verb  spray , a representative of the  Spray  class in VerbNet, is associated with features like  MOTION ,  NOT , and  LOCATION , which collectively indicate an event where an agent causes a theme to move from a non-location to a new location. However, the interpretation of such predicates, and their assignment to specific verbs, is not inherently verifiable through human judgment tasks unless reframed into a perceptual or event-based framework. The VerbCorner Project addresses this by transforming theoretical predicates into experimentally testable hypotheses. Rather than relying solely on expert curation, this project leverages the crowd to participate in the annotation of verbs, where participants are presented with semantic features or event-based scenarios and asked to judge whether a given verb applies to or characterizes a particular action or event.

Grammar is a cornerstone of effective communication, yet grammatical correctness remains a difficult and often ambiguous measure to evaluate in the domain of natural language processing. Grammatical Error Detection (GED), as part of broader grammar correction systems, is a long-standing research problem that has gained renewed interest in the context of automatic language assistance tools and educational technologies. While there have been significant advances in the development of GED systems over the years, the evaluation of these systems has often been critiqued for lacking clarity, consistency, and rigor. In many cases, meaningful comparisons between different approaches remain challenging, even when the same evaluation dataset is used. This paper aims to systematically examine the central issues that arise in the evaluation of GED systems and to offer insights into practices that can lead to more reliable and interpretable results. At first glance, evaluating a GED system appears to be a straightforward classification task: given a sentence and a set of possible grammatical errors, the system must correctly identify the errors. However, the reality is more complex due to the three-way contingency between the original sentence, the corrected version provided by an annotator or expert, and the system output. Unlike in binary classification problems where the concepts of true positive and false positive are cleanly defined, the ambiguity introduced by the annotated correction and the system's response complicates evaluation. The possibility that the correct "ground truth" may differ between annotators or methodologies further contributes to this challenge. To address this, we present an evaluation framework that simplifies the task into a more intuitive and comparable scheme, ensuring that results from different systems are not only statistically significant but also substantively meaningful. A second critical issue in the evaluation of GED systems is the class imbalance—errors are typically much less frequent than non-errors in training and test data. This imbalance skews the performance of most standard evaluation metrics such as accuracy and F1-score, often rendering them ineffective as benchmarks. To mitigate this issue and provide a more accurate picture of system performance, we recommend the direct reporting of raw performance counts, including true positives, false negatives, false positives, and true negatives. These raw values allow a finer-grained analysis and give scientists and practitioners a better way to understand the performance characteristics of a system, such as overcorrection or undercorrection. Beyond the technical challenges of evaluation metrics, there are various conceptual and methodological pitfalls in GED that warrant attention.

Speech recognition systems have made substantial progress over the past few decades, enabling robust performance in a variety of domains. However, even the most advanced systems still face significant challenges when dealing with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. These are words that appear in speech data but are not present in the system's predefined vocabulary. In open-domain tasks such as broadcast news, lectures, or spontaneous speech, OOV words often include named entities, technical terms, foreign language words, and neologisms that are essential to conveying important information but are not captured by a fixed vocabulary. Traditional speech recognition systems, which rely on word-based models, are inherently limited in their ability to handle such out-of-vocabulary content because they produce error or no output when encountering unknown words. One common approach to addressing this issue is the use of hybrid word/sub-word recognition systems. These systems extend the vocabulary representation by incorporating sub-word units—such as phonemes, syllables, or byte-pair encodings—to decompose new words into known components. When combined with context modeling, this allows the system to not only detect, but even transcribe, OOV words via hypotheses involving sequences of sub-word units. In most prior work, sub-word units are derived using heuristic or data-driven approaches that rely heavily on the phonetic properties of target languages. These methods often extract common phone sequences from a phoneme-aligned text corpus using basic statistical measures such as frequency or n-gram counts. While these strategies are simple and efficient, they are not guaranteed to be optimal for a given recognition task and may not account for the linguistic variability in different domains or the acoustic patterns present in speech. Additionally, the process of building the sub-word lexicon is often decoupled from the speech recognition model training process, leading to suboptimal integration and performance bottlenecks. To address these limitations, this work proposes a probabilistic model that jointly learns sub-word units tailored specifically for the task of open vocabulary speech recognition. Instead of relying on heuristic rules or static statistics, our model learns the sub-word lexicon in an end-to-end fashion that is optimized for a target task—namely, the detection and recognition of OOV words. The learned sub-words are designed to capture not only phonetic patterns but also the functional and morphological properties that are essential for accurate decomposition and recombination in speech recognition.

Morphological analysis is a foundational task in computational linguistics, enabling a wide range of downstream applications such as machine translation, information retrieval, and syntactic parsing. The goal is to annotate words with their morphological features, such as part of speech, tense, gender, number, and case—often in the absence of parallel annotated data for the target language. While traditional supervised approaches yield high performance, they require substantial annotated resources, which are available only for a relatively small number of languages. Such annotated data is particularly scarce for low-resource languages and is not trivial to collect manually. In the context of resource-poor languages, unsupervised methods for morphological analysis have thus become a key research focus. Conventional unsupervised approaches to morphological analysis typically rely on minimizing description length criteria, such as the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. These methods assume that the most linguistically meaningful and predictive features are the ones that allow the most compact description of the lexicon. However, such models tend to suffer from overfitting and inductive bias mismatches, as they are often tailored to the idiosyncratic patterns of the lexical forms in a target language without explicit generalization guidance from other languages. Moreover, these approaches struggle to capture both the global and structured nature of morphological systems, often producing local approximations that are insufficient for describing the complex interdependencies among features. In this paper, we shift the focus and approach the problem of unsupervised morphological analysis from a structured prediction perspective. Rather than trying to induce morphological features in isolation for each language, we propose a framework where the problem is viewed as a retrieval task in a shared, universal feature space. Here, each language—annotated or not—is embedded in a common morphological representation where predictive relationships can be learned and transferred across languages. Our key contribution is the development of a   structured nearest neighbor prediction   algorithm designed precisely for this purpose. The method assumes that morphological analyses for a target language should be close to those of a set of source languages whose annotated data is available. By formulating the problem in a universal feature space, we avoid the assumption of parallel data across languages, a common limitation in transfer learning. Instead, we build a shared semantic landscape where languages with different typological structures can contribute to the induction of morphological features. To evaluate our approach, we apply it to a set of eight typologically diverse inflecting languages and show that our model substantially outperforms traditional MDL-based baselines in nominal morphology induction.

The task of sentiment classification has been a central focus in natural language processing (NLP) due to its applications in opinion mining, customer feedback analysis, and social media monitoring. Effective sentiment classification systems heavily depend on the availability of high-quality sentiment resources, such as labeled datasets and sentiment lexicons. However, these resources are often disproportionately available across languages; high-resource languages like English benefit from extensive research and data collection efforts, while low-resource languages struggle with a lack of annotated corpora. This disparity in resource availability has motivated the development of cross-language sentiment classification (CLSC), a paradigm that transfers the knowledge from a source language with abundant resources to a target language with scarce data. CLSC represents a promising approach to address linguistic data imbalance and improve multilingual NLP capabilities. Recent advances in cross-lingual transfer learning have demonstrated the utility of bilingual embeddings in bridging the semantic gap between source and target languages. Traditional multilingual word embeddings (MWEs), often trained on large-scale parallel corpora, aim to place words from different languages into a shared semantic space, enabling the transfer of knowledge without retraining language-specific models from scratch. However, while these embeddings effectively capture syntactic and semantic relationships between words across languages, they are typically agnostic to sentiment. As a result, when applied to CLSC tasks, they may not preserve the affective properties of words, such as positive or negative polarity, which are often critical for effective sentiment classification. This paper proposes a novel approach to learn bilingual sentiment word embeddings (BSWE) for the task of English-Chinese cross-language sentiment classification. Unlike traditional bilingual embeddings that focus solely on syntactic and semantic alignment, BSWE explicitly incorporate sentiment information into the shared cross-lingual vector space. By integrating both semantic and sentiment knowledge during the embedding learning process, BSWE aims to improve the accuracy of CLSC by preserving not only the meaning of words but also their affective properties across languages. Our method does not require large-scale parallel corpora, which are expensive to collect and annotate. Instead, it leverages small amounts of labeled data in the source and target languages along with minimal translation resources. This makes it particularly suitable for resource-scarce language pairs, where large parallel datasets are unavailable. The bilingual sentiment embeddings are learned through a dual-objective optimization framework that combines traditional alignment criteria with sentiment consistency constraints. The model ensures that source and target words with the same sentiment meaning are mapped closely in the shared space while maintaining the structural and semantic features of the original language representations.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to identify and classify entities such as person names, locations, organizations, and other concepts from text into predefined categories. NER systems typically rely on supervised learning, where models are trained on annotated data. However, in many real-world applications, the performance of these systems significantly drops when they are applied to texts from an unseen   domain  , due to the   domain shift  —a change in the distribution of documents between the   source domain   (where training data is available) and the   target domain   (where the model is deployed). This challenge, known as   domain adaptation  , is critical to building robust NER systems that can generalize across diverse applications and languages, ranging from web news and scientific literature to social media, medical reports, and e-commerce product descriptions. A major difficulty in domain adaptation for NER is the   domain-specific vocabulary and term usage   in the target domain. Entities such as "Microsoft" in software documentation may appear differently compared to their appearance in a product sales report, and these distributional differences often lead to a degradation in the model’s performance. Traditional adaptation methods require a certain amount of   labeled target-domain data   to fine-tune the NER model. However, annotating such data is   labor-intensive  ,   time-consuming  , and often   infeasible   for new or niche domains, especially in low-resource languages such as Chinese or other non-English languages. It is, therefore, highly desirable to develop domain adaptation techniques that can bridge the domain gap   without   requiring manual labeling in the target domain. In this paper, we address the domain adaptation problem in NER by proposing a novel method based on   Latent Semantic Association   (LaSA). The key intuition behind LaSA is to   capture the underlying semantic relationships between words   using the   co-occurrence patterns in unlabeled text   from both the source and target domains. This is achieved by grouping words that frequently appear in similar   contextual snippets   into shared   latent concepts  , effectively mapping them into a domain-invariant   concept space  . By projecting both the source and target domain term spaces into this   semantic concept space  , we can   align the distributions   of entity-related terms across domains and bridge the domain mismatch. Once the concept space is established, we incorporate these semantic association features into the NER model as additional signals during the adaptation process. This allows the model to better generalize across domain-specific language variations, without relying on target domain labels.

Automatic essay scoring has emerged as a valuable tool in educational assessment, enabling efficient and consistent evaluation of student writing. Traditional approaches often focus on global measures such as grammar, vocabulary, and fluency. More recent research has extended the scope of automated assessment to include domain-specific dimensions of essay quality, such as coherence, relevance to the prompt, and argumentation quality. However, one critical dimension that remains underexplored is thesis clarity. A clear thesis is a cornerstone of effective writing, providing a central idea around which the essay is structured and argued. Yet, there is a dearth of work in the natural language processing (NLP) literature on how to automatically assess and model this crucial dimension of academic writing. Our goal is to address this gap by investigating how to model and evaluate thesis clarity in student essays. To enable this exploration, we introduce a new annotated corpus where essays are labeled according to their thesis clarity scores. This resource is built to support both scoring and error analysis tasks. We propose a learning-based approach that leverages continuous representations of text in combination with task-specific features to predict an essay's thesis clarity score. Our model achieves strong correlation with human judgments, demonstrating its robustness and effectiveness. Moreover, in addition to scoring, we aim to provide actionable feedback to writers and human evaluators by identifying the specific aspects of an essay that contribute to a lower score in thesis clarity. To this end, we present a second learning-based system that classifies the types of errors present in an essay that impact its thesis clarity. Examples of such errors include lack of a clear central claim, failure to maintain focus on the thesis in body paragraphs, or vague or overly broad thesis statements. We validate our approaches on the annotated corpus, and our results show that both the scoring model and the error classifier perform well in comparison to baselines and are robust across different essay lengths and writing styles. Our work represents a step toward more comprehensive and feedback-rich automated essay evaluation systems that go beyond simple scoring and provide meaningful insight into the quality of student writing. This paper is structured as follows: in Section 2, we discuss related work on essay evaluation and thesis statement modeling; in Section 3, we describe our annotated dataset and experimental setup; in Sections 4 and 5, we present our scoring model and error classifier respectively; in Section 6, we analyze our results and discuss implications for learning-based essay evaluation; and finally, we conclude in Section 7 with future research directions.

Multilingual neural machine translation (NMT) is an important direction in modern machine translation research. The goal of this paradigm is to train a single model capable of translating between multiple source and target language pairs, rather than training separate models for each language pair in isolation. This has several advantages, including reduced inference and storage costs, better generalization when some language pairs are under-resourced, and the potential for cross-lingual knowledge transfer. However, a key challenge in multilingual NMT is how to balance parameter sharing across languages with the need to specialize the model to the idiosyncratic characteristics of individual language pairs. While sharing parameters within a shared encoder-decoder architecture is a natural approach to lever- age linguistic regularities and reduce training data requirements, it can also lead to a dilution of language-specific patterns and degrade performance on specific translation tasks, especially when the source or target language is very different in syntax or semantics from the most commonly represented languages in the training data. The attention mechanism plays a critical role in NMT by dynamically modeling the input-output relationships, and is particularly influenced by the ordering, structure, and linguistic properties of the source and target languages. In multilingual settings, attention is applied across all language pairs using a fixed mechanism, which implicitly assumes that the same contextual patterns hold across all target language directions. However, languages vary significantly in their syntactic and semantic dependency structures – for example, while English and Dutch share similar left-to-right word order, the SOV structure of Japanese and Czech presents a different attention dynamic when translating toward or from these languages. Motivated by this, we propose the use of   task-specific attention models   in multilingual NMT. Our approach introduces additional attention layers specifically tuned to the source-target language pair during decoding, allowing the model to dynamically adapt its attention behavior based on the translation task while maintaining the parameter sharing of the encoder and decoder. The key idea is to retain the generalization benefits of multilingual parameter sharing while introducing   task-specific components   that allow for fine-tuned adaptation of the attention mechanism. Our experiments are conducted on a multilingual setup involving the four languages of the Europarl corpus. We compare a baseline model where all parameters, including the attention mechanism, are shared across all language pairs, to our model with task-specific attention heads for each target language.

The task of cross-domain adaptation in natural language processing (NLP) is a persistent challenge. Named Entity Recognition (NER), which aims to identify and classify entity mentions in text into categories such as person, organization, or location, is a particularly acute example. While supervised NER models trained on standard domain corpora like newswire (e.g., CoNLL-2003) perform impressively on in-domain test data, they often falter when applied to out-of-domain text, such as social media, search queries, or web snippets. This is largely due to the significant lexical, structural, and distributional differences between the source domain (e.g., news) and the target domain (e.g., web queries). Efforts to adapt models to such unseen data have typically relied on domain-specific labeled examples, rich linguistic annotations, or pre-training on domain-matched unlabeled data, which are not always accessible or scalable. In this paper, we investigate a novel and scalable method— Piggyback —for addressing cross-domain NER, using the output of search engines to obtain additional contextual information about a token. Our motivation is that even though NER models may misclassify a token in an unfamiliar domain due to lack of prior exposure to similar contexts, the real-world usage of that token in diverse contexts can be mined by leveraging web-scale services like search engines. The core idea of Piggyback is to treat web search engines not as end users of NLP systems, but as collaborators in the NER process. When faced with an ambiguous or unfamiliar token in the input text, the model submits the token together with a surrounding contextual window to a search engine. It then retrieves a set of search results and uses the frequency and types of entities present in those results to inform the classification decision. Essentially, the model piggybacks on the search engine's ability to associate entities with their contexts in web content and learns to integrate that external signal with the local syntactic and semantic cues in the input text. This strategy is particularly well-suited for high-variability tasks like NER in web queries. Web queries often contain snippets of partial mentions, non-standard spellings, or rare domain entities that are unlikely to appear in training corpora. However, by querying a search engine and observing what related contexts have been indexed, the model gains implicit, domain-invariant knowledge of the token’s usage in the broader linguistic ecosystem. This paper contributes several key elements to the advancement of robust and cross-domain NER.

There is a growing interest in understanding how language can emerge from interaction among autonomous agents in artificial environments. This line of research is particularly relevant to the design of flexible and adaptable communication systems that mimic aspects of human linguistic behavior. One of the classic settings for studying emergent communication is the referential game, where agents take turns in describing and guessing visual stimuli to achieve a shared goal. Recent studies have demonstrated that agents can develop language-like systems in such settings, characterized by symbol-based communication and structured grammatical patterns. However, much of this research has focused on the syntactic and semantic properties of the symbols themselves and how they are used, rather than on the underlying perceptual representations that agents build from their visual inputs. In this paper, we shift focus to the visual representations induced by agents during their interaction in a referential communication game. Specifically, we investigate the system introduced by Lazaridou et al. (2017), where agents iteratively communicate about images containing abstract shapes. This setting is particularly suitable for studying the interplay between perception and language, as the agents' communication is grounded in visual stimuli, and the task necessitates a shared understanding of these images. We analyze the representational capacity of the agents—particularly, how they encode the visual information from their input and whether their representations align with human conceptual categories or higher-level object properties. Surprisingly, our analysis reveals that although the agents' visual representations are highly aligned with each other, they do not reflect the conceptual features of the objects depicted in the images. That is, the representations learned by the agents seem optimized for the communicative task rather than for capturing perceptual or semantic regularities in the input. This result challenges the assumption that agents in emergent communication tasks automatically build representations that align with human-like perceptual or cognitive categories. Instead, it suggests that the communication signals they deploy are decoupled from the underlying visual semantics. Consequently, if we aim to build communication systems that are meaningful and interpretable, it is essential to pay attention not just to the linguistic structures that emerge, but also to the latent visual semantics that agents learn (or fail to learn) as a result of their interaction. Our findings highlight a critical dimension that is often overlooked in the study of emergent language: the nature of agents' visual understanding. In settings where language must be grounded in perception, the representations constructed by the agents play a foundational role.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a foundational task in natural language processing, aiming to identify and classify entities such as person names, locations, organizations, and temporal expressions from text. However, these systems remain limited in low-resource settings due to a lack of transcription standards, scarcity of labeled examples, and the dependence on language-specific information. Unlike purely surface-level orthographic models, our approach encodes the pronunciation and phonological structure of words, making it more robust in settings where the spelling is ambiguous, inconsistent, or encodes dialectal or phonological variation. Our work contributes to both the monolingual and cross-lingual NER tasks. For monolingual settings, we demonstrate that the model achieves strong performance on task without requiring manual feature engineering or language-specific pre-processing, reducing reliance on resource-intensive domain adaptation. For low-resource or zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, the phoneological awareness of the model facilitates adaptation across unrelated languages, even when no labeled data is available in the target language. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have underscored the importance of task-specific word representations that effectively model semantic and syntactic nuances of language beyond generic dense vector embeddings like those generated by Word2Vec or GloVe. Task-specific word representations are typically learned by training a model on a carefully chosen set of linguistic data, allowing the model to acquire features optimized for the particular task at hand, such as named entity recognition (NER), sentiment analysis, or sentence similarity. A critical yet often overlooked aspect of this learning process is the  learning order —that is, the sequence in which the model is exposed to the training instances. This decision has direct implications for the model's learning trajectory, influencing how effectively it generalizes from the training data to unseen examples. Traditionally, the training order is either determined by the natural left-to-right sequence of the corpus or is arbitrarily randomized, assuming these approaches are sufficient to promote robust learning. However, assembling a  curriculum —a structured, strategic learning order that starts with simpler instances and gradually increases in complexity—can enable the model to benefit from an ordering that mimics the cognitive process of human learning. The concept of curriculum learning, drawing from educational theory, posits that learning progresses most efficiently when the learner is exposed to easier examples initially, followed by increasingly challenging ones. While successful in computer vision and speech processing, curriculum learning has remained largely heuristic-driven in NLP, with curriculum construction often dependent on domain-specific intuition or simple heuristics based on instance length or depth. In this work, we propose a novel Bayesian-optimization-based approach to automatically learn the optimal curriculum for task-specific word representation learning. Our key insight is to treat the curriculum as a continuous search problem over possible orderings of training instances, where the objective function to be optimized is the performance on a downstream NLP task that relies on the learned word representations as features. To model the curriculum, we define a linear ranking function that assigns a scalar score to each training instance based on a learned weight vector and a hand-crafted feature vector capturing various aspects of instance complexity. These features include lexical, syntactic, and semantic properties that are believed to influence the difficulty of the instance for the target task. We frame the curriculum learning as a global optimization problem using Bayesian optimization, a sample-efficient strategy well-suited for high-dimensional, noisy search spaces.

Natural language processing (NLP) systems have achieved remarkable success in processing well-formed, standardized text across a wide range of languages. However, real-world text, especially user-generated content (UGC), often contains a host of inconsistencies, including misspellings, non-standard abbreviations, phonetic variants, and idiosyncratic lexical choices. These characteristics make NLP tasks more difficult, particularly in under-resourced or morphologically rich languages like Arabic. The problem is further compounded when dealing with dialectal varieties, which exhibit significant lexical, orthographic, and morphosyntactic divergence from the standard form. Such variations considerably increase the data sparsity problem in NLP models, leading to reduced accuracy and robustness, particularly in the context of morphological analysis. Among the many Arabic dialects, Egyptian Arabic (EA) is one of the most widely spoken and has the largest amount of textual and speech data in the world due to its media presence and popularity as a lingua franca. However, even with this abundance of data, morphological disambiguation remains a non-trivial task, primarily due to the high flexibility in the use of lexical forms, lack of standardization, and heavy reliance on morphological cues for syntactic and semantic interpretation. Morphological disambiguation, the process of assigning the correct morphological features to a surface word form from among a potentially large set of possible analyses, is a critical first step for many downstream NLP tasks, including parsing, syntactic analysis, machine translation, and information retrieval. Traditional approaches to morphological tagging often rely on well-formed, orthographically consistent data, and fail to generalize to real-world scenarios where such assumptions are violated. For dialectal Arabic, where data noise and variability are even more pronounced, the need for a robust, data-efficient model becomes even more pressing. In this paper, we present a neural morphological tagging and disambiguation architecture tailored specifically for Egyptian Arabic that is capable of handling the inherent noise and variability in UGC. Our contributions include (1) the development of a robust neural model based on modern sequence labeling architectures extended to capture long-range dependencies; (2) the introduction of several noise-robust training strategies, such as character-level representations, subword segmentation, and dropout with morphological sensitivity; and (3) various architectural enhancements, including multi-task learning and the use of pre-trained language models, to improve the model’s capacity to generalize from noisy or inconsistent textual input. Empirically, we evaluate our system on a comprehensive annotation of Egyptian Arabic text covering both written and spoken corpora.

Sensory information is a fundamental part of human perception and plays a crucial role in how we interpret and understand language. Everyday language is rich with expressions and terms that connote visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile experiences. For instance, when we hear a phrase like “the scent of fresh rain,” it immediately evokes a sensory memory that enriches our understanding of the moment. While humans naturally use this sensory information to infer a deeper meaning, computers lack this ability and typically rely on syntactic or semantic features to analyze text, without capturing the sensorial connotations embedded in the language. Such an understanding, however, is often key to tasks like content interpretation, sentiment analysis, and multimodal reasoning, where the integration of sensorial information can add significant value. The goal of this paper is to bridge this gap by introducing   Sensicon  , the first automatically constructed sensorial lexicon in English. Sensicon maps words to the five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—facilitating the modeling of language grounded in sensory experiences. Building such a resource is not only a linguistic endeavor but also a computational challenge that requires methods capable of acquiring, validating, and organizing sensorial associations at scale. Human annotation is one way to build a sensory lexicon, as done in smaller-scale datasets. However, due to its labor-intensive nature and high costs, this method is not scalable for large, dynamic, and constantly evolving language corpora. Moreover, the lack of a systematic and publicly available sensorial resource in existing computational linguistics literature motivates the development of an automatic method to generate a reliable sensorial lexicon. Our approach to building Sensicon is based on a combination of   bootstrapping   and   corpus statistics  , using a seed set of sensorially labeled words and expanding iteratively through co-occurrence patterns observed in large text corpora. We refine candidate words by leveraging contextual information and applying frequency-based filtering to ensure robustness. To evaluate the quality of the resulting lexicon, we create a   gold standard dataset   via   crowdsourcing  , where human annotators independently label a subset of the lexicon for accurate benchmarking. We evaluate Sensicon on two sensorial classification tasks: at the word level and at the sentence level. In both settings, we show that a simple classifier enhanced with Sensicon significantly outperforms baseline models, including an unlexicalized statistical model and a feature-based baseline derived from semantic embeddings alone. Our results not only demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methodology for building a high-quality sensorial lexicon but also highlight the utility of Sensicon in downstream tasks where sensorial knowledge is beneficial.

Sentence compression is a key task in natural language processing, aiming to shorten a sentence while retaining its essential meaning. This is especially useful in applications such as text summarization, machine reading, and document condensation. In previous work, neural network models, particularly those based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have demonstrated promising performance on sentence compression by learning to identify and remove non-essential words. However, these models are often trained on data from specific domains, which can lead to a significant drop in performance when applied to new domains. This is because the distribution of linguistic patterns, the structure of sentences, and the semantics of content often vary across different genres, such as news, clinical reports, or scientific articles. In this paper, we address the problem of improving the domain adaptability of LSTM-based deletion models for sentence compression. Our central hypothesis is that incorporating explicit syntactic information and imposing syntactic structure constraints can make neural models more robust when deployed in new domains. Syntax is a prime source of inductive bias; for example, syntactic relationships such as subject-verb agreement, modifying phrases, and clause structure provide consistent patterns that can be leveraged across different types of sentences. By taking advantage of such patterns, we believe that a model can generalize better and avoid domain-specific biases that might be learned from training data. To test this hypothesis, we propose two major methodological innovations. First, we augment the input representation of the LSTM model with explicit syntactic features derived from dependency parses, including head and dependency relation types for each word in the sentence. These features provide the model with direct access to syntactic information that might not be implicitly captured by the learned representations alone. Second, we introduce a post-processing step in the form of an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation, which ensures that the output of the model is a well-formed, grammatically correct sentence. The ILP constraints enforce syntactic rules such as preserving the main clause and ensuring coherence of the resulting compressed text. We evaluate our proposed model on a cross-domain setting, specifically moving from the widely studied Gigaword (newswire) dataset to the Travel domain dataset. We compare our model with a standard LSTM-based sentence compression approach as well as with a traditional non-neural baseline. Our results show that the inclusion of syntactic features and constraints leads to consistent improvements in compression quality, as measured by both standard evaluation metrics such as ROUGE and qualitative assessments of fluency and coherence.

The task of temporal relation classification plays a crucial role in natural language understanding, especially in domains such as information extraction, question answering, and narrative analysis, where temporal coherence is essential for inferring the sequence of events or their relative timing with respect to time expressions. Temporal reasoning constitutes the backbone of semantic processing for text, allowing systems to model real-world events and their inter-temporal dependencies with greater precision. While previous research has made significant progress in this area, existing approaches often face several limitations that hinder their effectiveness, including a simplified classification schema, overreliance on surface-level syntactic patterns, and the neglect of deeper semantic or discourse knowledge that underpins temporal relations. One of the key challenges in temporal relation classification is the static and restrictive nature of many prior classification frameworks. Most state-of-the-art systems rely on a coarse-grained classification schema that collapses the 14 original DTL (Document Time Link) relations of the TimeBank corpus into just six categories. While this simplification may aid in training robust machine learning models with limited supervision, it inevitably leads to the loss of important distinguishing characteristics of the relations. A finer-grained classification over the full set of 14 relations, on the other hand, is more reflective of the complexity of temporal phenomena in natural language and is more aligned with the objectives of downstream tasks that require nuanced temporal analysis. In light of these limitations, we propose a method for temporal relation classification that (1) employs the original 14 temporal relations as the classification target, thereby preserving the richness of the temporal taxonomy; (2) integrates a broad and sophisticated array of linguistic knowledge derived from semantic and discourse features, including syntactic structures, semantic roles, modality, and discourse signals, rather than focusing solely on morpho-syntactic properties; and (3) adopts a novel hybrid approach that combines rule-based systems with machine learning-based models, leveraging the strengths of both paradigms to enhance classification performance. The linguistic knowledge considered in our approach is sourced from both static linguistic resources, such as WordNet and ontological knowledge bases, and dynamic features extracted from semantic role labeling, discourse parsing, and event alignment tools. This knowledge is utilized to enrich the feature representations of event-event or event-time pairs, providing the learning system with a deeper understanding of the underlying meaning and temporal dynamics. Furthermore, the rule-based component of our system incorporates manually crafted temporal inference rules derived from domain experts, which are used to generate pseudo-labels or to filter ambiguous predictions made by the learning model.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for sequence-to-sequence modeling, offering a more end-to-end and potentially simpler approach to translation compared to traditional statistical machine translation methods. These models, especially those based on deep learning architectures such as the Transformer or the long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved impressive results in terms of translation quality. However, the cost of this performance is the necessity for NMT systems to be large in terms of model size and inference speed, which poses challenges for deployment on devices with limited computational resources. Reducing the size of NMT models while maintaining or only minimally impacting translation performance is therefore a key challenge in practical NMT application. Knowledge distillation is a well-known technique in deep learning for compressing large, complex models (often referred to as teacher models) into more compact, deployable models (referred to as student models). In the context of machine translation, knowledge distillation can be applied at different granularities: at the word level, which is the most common approach, or at the sequence level, which provides a more holistic view of the translation process. Prior work has demonstrated the effectiveness of word-level knowledge distillation in improving the performance of compact translation models. In this paper, we investigate the application of knowledge distillation in NMT, with a particular focus on extending the approach beyond the word level to sequence-level distillation. Our contributions include not only the application of standard knowledge distillation techniques to word prediction in NMT models but also the proposal of two novel sequence-level knowledge distillation methods. Our first method introduces a novel loss function that encourages the student model to align not only the words but also the structure and semantics of predicted sequences with the teacher model. The second method extends this idea by incorporating a sequence-level attention mechanism, allowing the student to learn the global dependencies the teacher emphasizes during translation. Surprisingly, we find that both sequence-level distillation approaches significantly improve the performance of student models, often to the point where standard beam search decoding techniques become unnecessary, even when the teacher model relies on them. This simplification of decoding further enhances the efficiency of the student model without compromising translation quality. We evaluate our models on two widely used translation benchmarks and demonstrate that our best student model achieves a speedup of up to 10 times compared to the teacher model, delivering a slight trade-off in performance (4.2 BLEU with greedy decoding and 1.7 BLEU with beam search).

Question classification (QC) is a fundamental preprocessing step in many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly in question answering (QA) systems and dialogue systems. Its goal is to identify the topic or intent of a given question, categorizing it into predefined classes such as person, place, event, or numerical. Accurate question classification is essential for selecting appropriate components of a system, such as document retrieval modules, knowledge base query interfaces, or tailored response generators. Over the years, QC has been explored using a variety of approaches, ranging from machine learning techniques to statistical and rule-based methods. While machine learning models often achieve strong performance with sufficient training data, they may struggle in scenarios with limited or imbalanced data and typically offer less transparency in their decision-making process. On the contrary, rule-based methods are more interpretable and can achieve impressive results by directly encoding domain knowledge into explicit rules, although they are often perceived as less scalable due to the manual effort required for rule development. This paper presents a purely rule-based approach to question classification that leverages both the syntactic and semantic properties of questions, achieving a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 97.2%. By combining the advantages of structured question analysis and semantic concept mapping, we reduce the reliance on annotated training data while maintaining, and even improving upon, the performance of machine learning-based systems in this domain. Our method is composed of two main stages: first, we perform syntactic analysis to extract relevant words or phrases from the question structure that are strong cues for classification. Second, we classify the question by mapping these extracted elements to a predefined set of semantic Concepts via carefully crafted linguistic rules. The extracted words are selected based on grammatical roles and discourse features such as the subject, object, verbs, and question words (e.g., "who," "where," "when"). These cues are known to contain the highest predictive value for most question types. In the second stage, we construct a rule-based classifier that associates the extracted words to Concept categories using a handcrafted mapping that reflects the semantic relationships between language patterns and question intents. Through systematic experiments on a standard benchmark dataset, we demonstrate that this purely rule-based system significantly outperforms previous approaches. Our results not only illustrate the scalability of rule-based methods in the QC domain but also open the door for hybrid approaches where our rule-based system can serve as a reliable and interpretable foundation for machine learning models.

The global rise in the prevalence of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) has spurred a critical need for early and accurate assessment tools that can identify individuals at risk and monitor disease progression. Alzheimer’s, the most common cause of dementia, is a neurodegenerative disorder with a long preclinical phase, during which early detection can enable timely intervention and improve care outcomes. However, the availability of high-quality, longitudinal datasets for cognitive assessment remains a significant challenge, particularly in the context of underrepresented or small populations. In many cases, these datasets are inherently   multiview  , as they incorporate heterogeneous sources of information such as linguistic behavior, demographic indicators, clinical measurements, neuropsychological test scores, and biomarkers—each reflecting a distinct dimension of cognitive decline. One promising approach for analyzing such multiview datasets is   multiview representation learning  , which aims to encode the relationships between diverse feature spaces into a joint low-dimensional embedding. These embeddings can capture latent associations between the views while preserving task-relevant patterns that are critical for downstream applications like classification and regression. A key challenge, however, lies in fusing the views effectively without losing the unique discriminative signals from each mode of data. In this work, we propose a framework for learning multiview embeddings tailored for dementia assessment. Focusing on the   DementiaBank   dataset—composed of spoken language samples from individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD, alongside linguistic, demographic, and clinical metadata—we exploit the inherent multiview structure of the data. We apply   Generalized Canonical Correlation Analysis (GCCA)  , a multilinear extension of CCA, to learn a shared low-dimensional representation that aligns the views through their correlations while preserving the distinctiveness of each individual space. This method allows us to integrate complementary signals from lexical features, speech transcriptions, patient age, gender, verbal fluency scores, and other relevant measures. To evaluate the effectiveness of the learned embeddings, we consider two key clinical tasks: (1) classifying whether a patient presents with AD or not, and (2) predicting a continuous clinical score that reflects severity or progression. In both cases, we demonstrate significant performance gains when incorporating the multiview embeddings compared to using individual view features in isolation. Specifically, our model achieves an   F1 score of 0.82   in classifying AD and a   Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 3.42   in predicting clinical scores—highlighting the practical utility of the multiview embedding framework. Additionally, we explore the generalizability of our approach by demonstrating how multiview embeddings can also be derived from other publicly accessible datasets with similar multimodal structures, suggesting potential for adaptation to broader dementia populations.

Maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) is a foundational technique in training deep learning models for structured prediction tasks, particularly in natural language processing (NPG) applications such as machine translation and abstractive summarization. In MLE, a model is trained to predict each word in a sequence conditionally, maximizing the likelihood of the ground-truth word at each time step, given the prior context. While MLE is effective for sequence generation, it inherently focuses on localized word-level prediction accuracy and often fails to align with the overall sequence-level objectives that define evaluation success in practical applications. This mismatch, known as the “wrong objective” problem, results in suboptimal performance on discrete sequence-level metrics like ROUGE and BLEU, which are designed to evaluate fluency, relevance, and similarity of generated sequences to reference outputs. In addition to this misalignment, MLE suffers from the exposure bias issue, where the model sees teacher-forced ground-truth inputs during training but must infer from its own potentially incorrect outputs during inference. This discrepancy can lead to error propagation, especially over long sequences, causing degradation in generation quality. One prominent alternative to MLE is the use of policy gradient methods, which optimize directly for sequence-level metrics by framing the training problem as a reinforcement learning (RL) task. These methods assign a global reward to the generated sequence based on its similarity to reference outputs and use gradient ascent to update model parameters accordingly. While policy gradient approaches have shown promising improvements in aligning training objectives with evaluation metrics, they are inherently unstable due to the high variance in reward sampling. This variance can lead to noisy gradient estimates and slow or inconsistent convergence during training, especially when the reward is sparse or sparse with respect to the search space of possible outputs. To address these shortcomings, we propose  CALCS (Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence) , a novel differentiable objective that models sequence-level similarity without requiring discrete reinforcement signals. Our approach centers around the  Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) , a standard measure for comparing the structural overlap between sequences while tolerating insertions, deletions, and substitutions. However, LCS is inherently non-differentiable and thus unsuitable for direct gradient-based optimization. To overcome this, we develop a continuous relaxation of the LCS metric that is amenable to gradient descent. CALCS approximates the LCS through a soft relaxation of sequence alignment via a neural alignment matrix, enabling the model to optimize for improvements in sequence-level structural similarity at the cost of linearity in computation and ease of integration with standard seq-to-seq architectures.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning have emphasized the importance of learning meaningful and generalizable representations of textual and structured data. Traditional methods often rely on curated linguistic features or handcrafted representations, which can be restrictive and domain-dependent. In contrast, distributed representations, such as those learned through word embeddings and sentence models, have shown great success in capturing the nuances of language in a continuous vector space. However, in many NLP applications—especially those integrating information from knowledge bases (KBs)—it is crucial to model not only individual words or documents but also structured entities and their semantic relationships. Such representations can enable a range of downstream tasks, including entity typing, document classification, semantic similarity, and question answering. A knowledge base (KB) typically stores entities and the relations between them, often with accompanying textual descriptions or annotations. These KB descriptions provide valuable signals for building joint representations of entities and documents, as they encode rich semantic and contextual information. By leveraging the structural and linguistic details present in KBs, researchers can train models to learn high-quality, task-agnostic representations that bridge the gap between structured and unstructured data. One of the primary goals of such representation learning is to ensure that semantically related entities and their corresponding documents are embedded in close proximity in the vector space, enabling more effective similarity computation and reasoning. In this work, we present   TextEnt  , a novel neural network model designed to learn joint, distributed representations of entities and documents directly from the raw textual content of a knowledge base. Given a document—such as a Wikipedia page—that describes an entity and includes annotations identifying that entity, our model is trained to: (1) predict the target entity of the document, and (2) map both the document and the entity into a shared embedding space where they are close in proximity. This dual objective ensures that the learned representations are not only task-specific but also semantically aligned with the structure of the KB. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model, we conduct experiments on two common NLP tasks: (1)  fine-grained entity typing , where the goal is to assign a set of fine-grained semantic types to an entity, and (2)  multiclass text classification , which involves assigning a single semantic label to a text document. Our results demonstrate that TextEnt outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both tasks.

Natural language inference (NLI), also referred to as textual entailment, is a fundamental task in natural language understanding, aiming to determine whether a given hypothesis can be inferred from a premise. In recent years, attention-based models have emerged as powerful tools in this domain, leveraging pairwise interactions between words in the premise and hypothesis through soft alignment. These mechanisms have achieved remarkable success, particularly in tasks requiring deep contextual understanding and cross-sentence comparisons. However, a key limitation of attention mechanisms lies in their sequential and pairwise treatment of interactions, which may not fully capture the broader structural and compositional patterns relevant to the inference process. To address this shortcoming, we propose the Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), a novel model architecture tailored to capture rich and complex interaction patterns between two sentences. Unlike attention-based approaches that establish pointwise alignments between tokens, CIN employs convolutional layers to dynamically generate filters based on one sentence (e.g., the hypothesis), which are then applied to the representation of the other sentence (e.g., the premise). This design allows the model to simultaneously consider local and multi-span interactions, enabling it to leverage a spectrum of interaction patterns directly from the data. The dynamic filter generation mechanism is a core feature of CIN and offers significant flexibility. The number and size of the filters can be configured during training, allowing the model to adapt to varying task requirements and data distributions. Furthermore, this convolution-based interaction strategy sidesteps the need for explicit alignment, while still maintaining an efficient and parallelizable computational structure. Importantly, the convolution operation inherently supports capturing dependencies across multiple linguistic units, making CIN particularly well-suited for modeling syntactic and semantic structures that are critical to NLI tasks. Experiments conducted on three large-scale NLI datasets—SNLI, MultiNLI, and SciTail—demonstrate that CIN not only matches the performance of the state-of-the-art attention-based models but also exhibits robust generalization across diverse linguistic phenomena. Quantitative analysis further reveals that CIN excels in modeling long-range interactions and handling ambiguous or compositional patterns, which are often challenging for existing NLI systems. The success of CIN suggests that convolutional-based architectures can serve as a viable and effective alternative to attention mechanisms for NLI. By explicitly modeling the interaction space through dynamic filters, CIN provides a fresh perspective on how complex sentence interactions can be systematically and efficiently encoded. More broadly, the work contributes to the growing literature on interaction-based models for NLI and highlights the potential of integrating design principles from computer vision with traditional sequential language modeling.

Opinion mining has emerged as a pivotal field in natural language processing, driven by the increasing availability of user-generated content such as online reviews, social media posts, and forum discussions. Among various tasks within opinion mining, the extraction of   opinion targets  —that is, the entities or aspects being evaluated in a given opinion—stands out as a core and essential step. This task allows for the   fine-grained analysis of product reviews  , enabling applications such as summarization, recommendation systems, and sentiment analysis at the aspect level. The extraction of opinion targets is particularly challenging in informal texts, where the structure is often fragmented, the use of grammatical rules is inconsistent, and syntactic cues may be ambiguous. Two primary paradigms have emerged to tackle this challenge:   syntax-based methods   and   alignment-based methods  . The former focuses on leveraging syntactic relationships between adjectives, adverbs, and nouns extracted via   dependency parsing  , assembling   syntactic patterns   (e.g., subject-verb-object configurations, modifier relations) to identify opinion targets. However, as these methods heavily rely on the output of syntactic parsers, they are   susceptible to parsing errors  , especially when applied to noisy, informal written texts like online reviews. In contrast,   alignment-based methods   bypass the need for syntactic parsing by using   word alignment models  , often inspired by statistical machine translation methodologies. These models aim to   align opinion words (e.g., adjectives or adverbs)   with their corresponding   targets  , based on co-occurrence and contextual patterns within the sentences. While these methods avoid the inaccuracies of syntactic parsing, they may suffer from   oversimplification or lack of linguistic context  , which can hinder generalization across diverse domains and languages. Despite the existence of these two paradigms, there is a notable   gap in the empirical analysis   of their relative performance under varying conditions such as   corpus size, domain, and language  . This is a critical question in practical application, where data availability and text processing constraints often play a major role in model choice. Additionally, there remains minimal exploration into whether integrating alignment and syntactic features via a   partially supervised framework   can yield performance improvements, particularly in   low-resource settings  . In this paper, we conduct an   empirical study comparing the effectiveness   of syntax-based and alignment-based methods for opinion target extraction. We investigate how the performance of each method varies across domains, languages, and data sizes, aiming to identify   characteristic strengths and limitations   in different contexts. Additionally, we propose a   combination approach  , in which we integrate syntactic roles with alignment-based associations using a   partially supervised learning framework  .

Transliteration — the process of mapping a text in one script to another — is a crucial yet challenging task in natural language processing. It plays a particularly important role in machine translation (MT) and information retrieval by enabling the transfer of proper names, specialized terms, and other expressions across languages. In low-resource settings or when parallel corpora are limited, bootstrapping transliteration systems from automatically extracted phrase pairs represents an important avenue for research. However, a major challenge in this approach lies in the noise introduced during the phrase pair extraction, which can include misaligned terms, false positives, and semantically unrelated expressions. Existing character-level or word-level alignment methods often lack the ability to robustly distinguish between true transliteration pairs and noisy examples, which can degrade system performance and limit scalability. This paper introduces a   noise-aware character alignment method   designed specifically for bootstrapping   statistical machine transliteration (SMT)   from   automatically extracted phrase pairs  . Our model extends a Bayesian many-to-many alignment framework to explicitly account for the presence of non-transliteration components (noise) within phrase pairs.
